fields.title: Fire Against the Dark
fields.subtitle: The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, Book One
fields.description: In the smoky city of Emberwick the sun has been pale for three hundred years, and the lamps on the city wall are failing. Wren Ashby, a chimney-sweep and a thief who believes nothing in life is free, finds a battered brass lamp hidden in a sealed chimney. It burns without oil, it relights itself when she blows it out, and it keeps coming back however hard she tries to sell it. Soon the Lamp Guild calls it witch-light, the Warden wants it, a captain in grey has come to bargain for it, and the Hollows are coming over the wall. With Tobin, the Warden's son who is secretly afraid of the dark, and Old Ash, the last true Lamplighter, Wren must learn the lamp's one law before the last light in Emberwick goes out.
fields.about_html:
Fire Against the Dark is the first book of The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, an adventure series written by Ochorus for readers aged nine to twelve, and a good book to read aloud to younger children too. It is a story of chimneys and rooftops, a city wall lit by failing lamps, shadow-creatures that drain the colour out of everything they touch, a clever ember-fox, a gang of thieving soot-imps, and two children who have to be braver than they think they are.

Underneath the adventure it is a story about grace. The lamp at its heart cannot be bought, stolen or earned, only given, and what is given grows. Wren has spent her whole life believing that everything costs, and the book follows her slowly learning to receive a gift, and then to give one away when giving seems to cost her everything. Like the classic Christian fantasies it follows, it never preaches and never names the One it points to; it lets the story carry the meaning, for children to discover and for parents to talk about.

The book has fifteen chapters, about the length of a classic children's fantasy, each one a good evening's reading. Five more books will follow Wren, Tobin and Old Ash on the long road to the Bright Mountain, where the Flame began.

qa.question: What age is Fire Against the Dark written for?
qa.answer: It is written for readers aged nine to twelve, and it reads aloud well to younger children from about seven. The peril is real but never gory, and there is plenty of humour.

qa.question: What is the story about?
qa.answer: A chimney-sweep orphan called Wren finds a brass lamp that burns without oil and cannot be sold. When the city's wall of lamps fails and shadow-creatures called Hollows pour in, she and her friends must decide what the lamp is for.

qa.question: What is the lamp's law?
qa.answer: Old Ash teaches it in Chapter 8: it cannot be bought, stolen or earned, only given. And its second half: what is given, grows.

qa.question: Is it a Christian book?
qa.answer: Yes. Like the classic Christian fantasies, it tells the gospel's shape as a story rather than a sermon: grace that cannot be earned, a light the darkness cannot put out, and a Lampwright whose story readers will recognise. It never names God or quotes Scripture directly.

qa.question: Who are the main characters?
qa.answer: Wren Ashby, a quick-tongued sweep and thief; Tobin Harrowgate, the Warden's clever son, who is secretly afraid of the dark; Old Ash, the last true Lamplighter; and Cinder, his ember-fox, who sneezes sparks.

qa.question: Who is the Lampwright?
qa.answer: In the old stories he came down from the Bright Mountain with true fire, lit lamps for anyone who asked and never charged, and was snuffed out on Cinder Hill, until on the third morning the Flame burned again on the mountain. Readers may notice that he is closer to the story than anyone thinks.

qa.question: How long is the book?
qa.answer: Fifteen chapters and about forty-eight thousand words, much the length of a classic children's fantasy. Each chapter is a good evening's reading.

qa.question: Is it part of a series?
qa.answer: Yes. It is the first of six books in The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven. Each can be read on its own, and together they follow the long road to the Bright Mountain.

fields.title: A Lamp in the Flue
fields.body_html:
In the city of Emberwick it was noon, and you would never have known it. The sun was up — it was always up at noon, as it had been every day for three hundred years — but it hung above the chimneys as pale as a coin seen through dirty water, and it gave about as much warmth as a coin does. Its light was thin and grey. It lay on the rooftops like dust. It turned the canals into strips of slate and the people into something very like their own shadows.

Nobody in Emberwick thought this was strange. That is the trouble with a curse that lasts long enough: people stop calling it a curse and start calling it the weather. If you had asked anyone in the city what colour the sky used to be, they would have scratched their heads and said, “Well — sky-coloured, I suppose,” and gone back to work. The names of most colours had dropped out of the world, the way the names of very old kings drop out of it, and only a handful were left: grey, which was everywhere, and brown, and dun, and a tired, washed-out blue-ish that people called “dull” when they bothered to call it anything.

On this particular grey noon, high on the roof of Thornbury House, a girl sat astride a chimney-pot, eating the last crust of her breakfast and glaring at the sun as if it owed her money.

Her name was Wren Ashby. She was twelve, or near enough — nobody had ever told her the exact day — and she was small and wiry and sharp in the chin, with black hair she cut herself with a knife whenever it got into her eyes, so that it stuck out in tufts like the feathers of the little brown bird she was named after. She was a chimney-sweep, which meant she was black from her cap to her bare heels, and did not mind. Soot is a kind of coat, when you have no other. The only thing about her that was not black was a ribbon tied round her left wrist: a narrow, frayed, faded thing, the colour of a grey dawn with a little pink in it. It had been her mother’s. It was the only thing she owned that nobody had sold her or let her have on account, and she never took it off.

Thornbury House stood at the edge of the Hill, where the tall houses of the rich gave way to the crooked roofs of everyone else, and it had been shut up for fifty years. Its chimneys rose from the roof in tall twisting stacks, some spiralled like barley-sugar and some leaning together like old men telling secrets. People in Soot Lane said it had belonged to the last family of Lamplighters, back before the Guild, and that it was haunted, and that anyone who went inside came out with white hair. Wren had been inside all morning. Her hair was as black as ever.

She was there because of Gristle Mott, her sweep-master. And Mott was not there — he was in the back room of the Three Wicks with a mug of something — because of a gentleman.

“Gentleman come by the yard,” Mott had wheezed that morning, rubbing his great red knuckles. “Good coat. Clean boots. Agent for some buyer what wants the old Thornbury place. Wants to know if the chimneys is sound. Paid in advance.” He had patted his pocket, which clinked. “So down every flue in the place, Ashby, and if there’s one brick loose I want to know it.”

“Do I get any of what he paid?” said Wren.

Mott had laughed — a dreadful noise, like a bellows full of gravel — and told her she could have the honour of working off another day of her board money, and wasn’t she lucky to have a roof over her head at all. Wren owed Mott board money. She had owed it for as long as she could remember, and however many chimneys she swept, the sum never got any smaller. She had worked out long ago that it was not meant to.

“Everything costs,” she told the sun now, round her crust. “And if it doesn’t cost you, it’ll cost you later.” She had never yet known it to be wrong.

She licked her thumb, took up her brush and scraper, and dropped into the chimney like a stone into a well.

If you have never been inside a chimney, you may imagine it is a dreadful place, close and black and choking. And so it is. But Wren had been going up and down chimneys since she was five, and she knew them the way you know the inside of your own pocket. She knew how to brace her back on one wall and her knees on the other and wriggle down like a caterpillar. And she knew the dark. The dark did not frighten her in the least. The dark was simply where the work was; and in the dark, nobody could see that you were small.

The chimneys of Thornbury were the strangest she had ever been in. They twisted and doubled and joined and parted again, so that she would go down one flue and come out in another, three rooms away. It was like climbing about inside a knot. She tapped the bricks with her scraper as she went and found, rather to her annoyance, hardly a loose one anywhere.

It was somewhere in the middle of the afternoon that she first heard the scritching. It came from above her, and then below, and then from somewhere off to one side where there should not have been room for anything. It was a small, busy sound, like mice wearing boots.

“Gutterlings,” said Wren, wedged in the dark with her elbows out. “Course there are. Fifty years of nobody.”

Two white eyes opened above her head, round and enormous and colourless, like two peeled eggs. More opened beside them, until the chimney seemed full of eyes.

“Sweepy-girl, sweepy-girl!” squeaked a voice, thin as a whistle. “Come to call, come to call!”

“Brushy-brushy, give-give!”

“Shiny-shiny, mine-mine!”

Gutterlings, I should explain, are not wicked — not exactly. They are knee-high soot-imps who live in chimneys and flues, black as the soot itself, with long thin fingers and big white eyes. They speak in rhymes because they think rhymes are clever, and they steal anything that glints because they think glinting things are cleverer still. They are a nuisance rather than a danger.

“Clear off,” said Wren. “I’m working.”

“Working, working, never shirking!” squeaked the eyes by her knee, and something tugged at her brush.

Wren kicked. There was a scuffle, a great deal of squeaking and a shower of soot down the back of her neck, and when it was over she had her scraper and the Gutterlings had her brush, and they were carrying it away up the flue, singing.

“Brushy-brushy, ours-ours! Sweepy-girl for hours-hours!”

“That’s Mott’s brush!” Wren shouted. “He’ll have it out of my hide!”

She went up after them, very cross, round a bend and down into a place where three flues met in a brick chamber no bigger than a cupboard. The Gutterlings were there, crowded into one corner — and they were not looking at her at all. They had dropped the brush. They were scratching at the wall.

The largest of them, who had a bent ear and a long nose like a candle-snuffer, had his face pressed flat to the bricks. “Warm-warm,” he was squeaking softly. “Shiny-warm. Snib wants. Snib wants.”

Wren had felt it too, the moment she dropped into the chamber: the air was warm. Not the stuffy, coal-smelling warmth of a chimney with a fire below; this was soft and clean and steady, like a loaf just out of the oven, or a cat that has been sitting in the one patch of sun on a windowsill. And there had been no fire in Thornbury House for fifty years.

“Shift,” said Wren, and pushed in among them, and laid her hand where Snib’s nose had been.

The bricks were warm. And they were loose. Somebody, long ago, had bricked up a gap here in a hurry, and the bricks moved under her palm like bad teeth.

I do not know what you would have done in Wren’s place. Perhaps you would have reported a loose patch in the third-floor flues and gone home. But Wren had been hungry nearly every day of her life, and when you are hungry every day you learn one thing above all: if something is hidden, somebody thought it was worth hiding.

She worked her scraper into the crumbling mortar while the Gutterlings hopped round her ankles squeaking advice. One brick came out, and warm air breathed through the hole onto her face. Then a whole section fell inward with a soft rattle, and she was looking into a sealed-off flue no wider than her shoulders, running up into the dark.

Only it was not quite dark. Halfway up, in a little niche cut into the brick, something was shining.

Wren pulled herself through and up, ahead of the Gutterlings, and got there first. She hung in the narrow flue with her knees braced and looked, and for a long moment she did not do anything at all.

It was a lamp. A small one, small enough to sit in her two hands, made of brass that had been knocked about a good deal; it was dented in three places and scuffed all over. It had a little hook on top for hanging, and a glass chimney with a fine crack running up one side, thin as a hair. It was the kind of thing you might find at the bottom of a box in Crookback Market and never look at twice.

Except that it was alight.

Inside the cracked glass burned a flame no bigger than the tip of Wren’s little finger. It did not flicker. It did not smoke. It stood up straight and clear, and it was not grey, and it was not brown, and it was not dun or dull. It was a colour Wren had never seen and had no word for. If you and I had been there, we should have said at once that it was golden — golden and white at the heart, like the best sort of morning. Wren could only stare.

All the warmth had come from it — through the bricks and into the chamber — from this one tiny flame. She held her fingers near it the way you do near a fire, and the warmth went into them and up her arms, and she noticed, far off, that it smelled faintly of new bread, and of something else she could not name.

She picked it up. It was warm in her hands but not hot. She tipped it to see how much oil was left — and then turned it right over. The lamp had no oil. It had no place for oil: no reservoir, no cap to unscrew. Only the flame, standing in the brass on nothing at all, as if it had every right to.

“That’s not possible,” Wren whispered.

“Shiny-shiny!” squealed Snib, right behind her. “Shiny-shiny, mine-mine!”

The Gutterlings had crowded into the flue below her, white eyes fixed on the lamp, long fingers reaching. Snib had scrambled up the wall beside her like a spider, his nose nearly touching the glass.

“Snib found! Snib found first!”

“You found a wall,” said Wren. “I found this.”

She did the only thing she could think of. She put her face to the glass and blew the flame out.

Darkness dropped on the flue like a sack. The Gutterlings wailed. Wren clutched the lamp to her chest and held her breath, waiting for them to lose interest, as Gutterlings do when the shiny thing is gone.

She counted one. She counted two.

On three, the lamp lit itself again.

It did not sputter back. It needed no spark. One moment there was nothing, and the next the little flame was simply there, upright and golden and calm, as though it had only blinked. And Wren, holding the lamp against her chest, looked down and saw her ribbon.

It lay round her wrist, just beside the glass. And in that light it was not faded, and it was not grey with a little pink in it. It was a colour so deep and warm and alive that she felt it more than saw it, the way you feel a kind word. You and I would have called it red — a true, glad, berry red. Wren had no word for it. Nobody had used that word in her hearing in her whole life. She only knew that her mother’s ribbon was suddenly the most beautiful thing she had ever seen, and that she had worn it for eight years without once seeing it at all.

“Rot,” she whispered. It was all she could manage.

Then she shoved the lamp inside her coat, did up every button over it, and went down that flue faster than any sweep in Emberwick has ever gone down anything.

The Gutterlings chased her for a while, but with the lamp hidden they could not see it, and Gutterlings have short memories for what they cannot see. In the end they went back to squabbling over Mott’s brush. The last thing Wren heard as she dropped out of the great kitchen fireplace into the grey afternoon was Snib, small and far away up the chimney, squeaking sadly: “Shiny-shiny. Snib’s shiny. Snib remembers.”

She went home the long way, over the roofs. All the way she could feel the lamp against her ribs, warm and steady like a hand resting there, and the warmth seemed to spread until even her bare toes on the cold slates did not feel quite so cold.

And she planned. A brass lamp that burned without oil! There was not a pawnbroker in the city who would not give his eyeteeth for it. She would take it to Silas Grubb at Crookback Market first thing in the morning, and she would not let Grubb cheat her, not this time. She would sell it for silver. She would eat for a month. She would buy hot pies from the stall on Tallow Bridge, the ones with gravy in them, and eat them one after the other until she burst. She would buy Nettle a pair of stockings.

By the time she climbed down into Mott’s yard at the bottom of Soot Lane, the gloaming had come — the grey of the day deepening into the grey of evening, which in Emberwick was all the difference there was — and she was very nearly smiling.

“Where,” roared Gristle Mott, “is my brush?”

He filled the doorway of the sweep-house: a huge man, wide and wheezing, with a face like a boiled ham, smelling as always of gin and soot.

“Gutterlings had it,” said Wren. “Dozens of them.”

“Gutterlings!” Mott spat. “Two shillings, that brush. That’s two shillings on your board, Ashby. And sixpence for the trouble of listening to you.”

Wren did a quick sum. She would now owe Mott money until she was roughly a hundred and four. She opened her mouth to say so — and shut it again. Under her coat the lamp was warm, and Mott had a nose for anything worth money the way a dog has a nose for a bone.

“Get to bed,” said Mott. “And no supper, not with two-and-six on your slate.”

Wren said nothing about the lamp. She walked past him with her hands in her pockets and her chin up, which is the best way of walking past people when you want them to think you have nothing worth taking.

Someone was waiting by the water-butt. It was Nettle, the smallest sweep in the yard — seven years old, so freckled you could hardly see her face for them, with two front teeth missing and arms like sticks. Nettle followed Wren everywhere. Wren pretended to mind.

“You were gone ageth,” said Nettle, who could not say her s’s for the gap in her teeth. “Mott thaid you’d fallen down a chimney and he’d thell your thpare thocks.”

“I haven’t got spare socks.”

“That’th what I told him.” Nettle slipped her little hand into Wren’s — and looked up, surprised. “Wren. Your handth are warm.”

“Must be the running,” said Wren. Nettle’s fingers were like ice, as they always were. Nettle was always cold. “Go on. Bed. I’ll see you in the morning.”

“Will you have anything for breakfatht?”

“Maybe,” said Wren, thinking of silver. “Maybe I will.”

Wren’s room was a garret at the top of the leaning house beside Mott’s yard. It had a roof so steep you could only stand straight in the middle, a window the size of a book, a straw mattress, and one thin blanket with a hole in it. Along one side ran the chimney-breast from the rooms below; but Mott never bought coal for anybody but himself, so the bricks were always cold. If you have ever tried to sleep in a room where the fire has gone out, you will know the kind of cold I mean. It is a slow, patient cold that gets in under your blanket and sits on your chest and waits for you to give up.

Wren shut the door, pushed the broken chair against it, and listened. Below, Mott was singing in the Three Wicks — badly. Then, slowly, she took out the lamp.

The flame was still burning, as straight and calm as in the hidden flue. Its light filled the little garret. It was not much light, but it was golden, and Wren had never had golden light in that room before. And her ribbon — she held her wrist up close — was red again, so red that she sat down on the mattress quite suddenly and simply looked at it.

“Where did you come from?” she whispered. “Who put you in that wall?”

The lamp said nothing. It only burned.

She wrapped it in her coat and pushed the bundle into the corner under the slope of the roof, where it glowed through the cloth like a coal through ash. Then she lay down under her blanket and waited for the cold to come and sit on her chest, the way it always did.

It did not come.

She noticed that her feet were warm. Then her hands, and the tip of her nose, which was always the last thing to be warm. The air in the garret was soft and still and kind; and when she reached out in the dark and touched the chimney-breast, the bricks were warm too, as though someone had lit a fire in the grate below for the first time in years. Nobody had. She knew perfectly well that nobody had.

“Rot,” said Wren softly into the dark. But she did not say it as if she meant it.

She meant to lie awake and plan — Grubb, and silver, and how to slip out before Mott was up. Instead, without in the least intending to, she curled up on the straw with her ribboned wrist under her cheek and the golden glow in the corner of her eye, and fell asleep.

That was the first night in Wren’s life that she was warm all the way through. It was not, I am glad to say, the last.

Only the flame, standing in the brass on nothing at all, as if it had every right to. “That’s not possible,” Wren whispered. “Shiny-shiny!” squealed Snib, right behind her. “Shiny-shiny, mine-mine!” The Gutterlings had crowded into the flue below her, white eyes fixed on the lamp, long fingers reaching. Snib had scrambled up the wall beside her like a spider, his nose nearly touching the glass. “Snib found! Snib found first!” “You found a wall,” said Wren. “I found this.” She did the only thing she could think of. She put her face to the glass and blew the flame out. Darkness dropped on the flue like a sack. The Gutterlings wailed. Wren clutched the lamp to her chest and held her breath, waiting for them to lose interest, as Gutterlings do when the shiny thing is gone. She counted one. She counted two. On three, the lamp lit itself again. It did not sputter back. It needed no spark. One moment there was nothing, and the next the little flame was simply there, upright and golden and calm, as though it had only blinked. And Wren, holding the lamp against her chest, looked down and saw her ribbon. It lay round her wrist, just beside the glass. And in that light it was not faded, and it was not grey with a little pink in it. It was a colour so deep and warm and alive that she felt it more than saw it, the way you feel a kind word. You and I would have called it red — a true, glad, berry red. Wren had no word for it. Nobody had used that word in her hearing in her whole life. She only knew that her mother’s ribbon was suddenly the most beautiful thing she had ever seen, and that she had worn it for eight years without once seeing it at all. “Rot,” she whispered. It was all she could manage. Then she shoved the lamp inside her coat, did up every button over it, and went down that flue faster than any sweep in Emberwick has ever gone down anything. The Gutterlings chased her for a while, but with the lamp hidden they could not see it, and Gutterlings have short memories for what they cannot see. In the end they went back to squabbling over Mott’s brush. The last thing Wren heard as she dropped out of the great kitchen fireplace into the grey afternoon was Snib, small and far away up the chimney, squeaking sadly: “Shiny-shiny. Snib’s shiny. Snib remembers.” She went home the long way, over the roofs. All the way she could feel the lamp against her ribs, warm and steady like a hand resting there, and the warmth seemed to spread until even her bare toes on the cold slates did not feel quite so cold. And she planned. A brass lamp that burned without oil! There was not a pawnbroker in the city who would not give his eyeteeth for it. She would take it to Silas Grubb at Crookback Market first thing in the morning, and she would not let Grubb cheat her, not this time. She would sell it for silver. She would eat for a month. She would buy hot pies from the stall on Tallow Bridge, the ones with gravy in them, and eat them one after the other until she burst. She would buy Nettle a pair of stockings. By the time she climbed down into Mott’s yard at the bottom of Soot Lane, the gloaming had come — the grey of the day deepening into the grey of evening, which in Emberwick was all the difference there was — and she was very nearly smiling. “Where,” roared Gristle Mott, “is my brush?” He filled the doorway of the sweep-house: a huge man, wide and wheezing, with a face like a boiled ham, smelling as always of gin and soot. “Gutterlings had it,” said Wren. “Dozens of them.” “Gutterlings!” Mott spat. “Two shillings, that brush. That’s two shillings on your board, Ashby. And sixpence for the trouble of listening to you.” Wren did a quick sum. She would now owe Mott money until she was roughly a hundred and four. She opened her mouth to say so — and shut it again. Under her coat the lamp was warm, and Mott had a nose for anything worth money the way a dog has a nose for a bone. “Get to bed,” said Mott. “And no supper, not with two-and-six on your slate.” Wren said nothing about the lamp. She walked past him with her hands in her pockets and her chin up, which is the best way of walking past people when you want them to think you have nothing worth taking. Someone was waiting by the water-butt. It was Nettle, the smallest sweep in the yard — seven years old, so freckled you could hardly see her face for them, with two front teeth missing and arms like sticks. Nettle followed Wren everywhere. Wren pretended to mind. “You were gone ageth,” said Nettle, who could not say her s’s for the gap in her teeth. “Mott thaid you’d fallen down a chimney and he’d thell your thpare thocks.” “I haven’t got spare socks.” “That’th what I told him.” Nettle slipped her little hand into Wren’s — and looked up, surprised. “Wren. Your handth are warm.” “Must be the running,” said Wren. Nettle’s fingers were like ice, as they always were. Nettle was always cold. “Go on. Bed. I’ll see you in the morning.” “Will you have anything for breakfatht?” “Maybe,” said Wren, thinking of silver. “Maybe I will.” Wren’s room was a garret at the top of the leaning house beside Mott’s yard. It had a roof so steep you could only stand straight in the middle, a window the size of a book, a straw mattress, and one thin blanket with a hole in it. Along one side ran the chimney-breast from the rooms below; but Mott never bought coal for anybody but himself, so the bricks were always cold. If you have ever tried to sleep in a room where the fire has gone out, you will know the kind of cold I mean. It is a slow, patient cold that gets in under your blanket and sits on your chest and waits for you to give up. Wren shut the door, pushed the broken chair against it, and listened. Below, Mott was singing in the Three Wicks — badly. Then, slowly, she took out the lamp. The flame was still burning, as straight and calm as in the hidden flue. Its light filled the little garret. It was not much light, but it was golden, and Wren had never had golden light in that room before. And her ribbon — she held her wrist up close — was red again, so red that she sat down on the mattress quite suddenly and simply looked at it. “Where did you come from?” she whispered. “Who put you in that wall?” The lamp said nothing. It only burned. She wrapped it in her coat and pushed the bundle into the corner under the slope of the roof, where it glowed through the cloth like a coal through ash. Then she lay down under her blanket and waited for the cold to come and sit on her chest, the way it always did. It did not come. She noticed that her feet were warm. Then her hands, and the tip of her nose, which was always the last thing to be warm. The air in the garret was soft and still and kind; and when she reached out in the dark and touched the chimney-breast, the bricks were warm too, as though someone had lit a fire in the grate below for the first time in years. Nobody had. She knew perfectly well that nobody had. “Rot,” said Wren softly into the dark. But she did not say it as if she meant it. She meant to lie awake and plan — Grubb, and silver, and how to slip out before Mott was up. Instead, without in the least intending to, she curled up on the straw with her ribboned wrist under her cheek and the golden glow in the corner of her eye, and fell asleep. That was the first night in Wren’s life that she was warm all the way through. It was not, I am glad to say, the last.

fields.title: The Lamp That Would Not Stay Lost
fields.body_html:
Crookback Market was the noisiest place in Emberwick, and the smelliest, and Wren loved it.

It sprawled along the bank of the Soot Canal where the water bent round in a crooked elbow, and it was all stalls and barrows and awnings jammed so close together that you could walk from one end to the other across the tops of them, if you were small and quick and didn’t mind being shouted at. A woman sold eels out of a bucket; a man sold second-hand boots, every one of them odd. There were pots and pans, and rope, and rags, and tin Flame tokens on strings that the Guild said would keep your house safe from the dark, and onions that were small and grey and sour, because everything that grew in Emberwick was small and grey and sour. Over it all hung the smell of fish and smoke and canal-water, and the pale sun peering down through the haze like a sick man through a window.

Wren slipped through the crowd with her coat done up to the chin and both arms folded tight across her chest. She had left the garret before Mott was up — which was not difficult; Mott was never up before noon — and she had not stopped to look at the lamp since she woke. She had woken warm, and that was enough.

At the far end of the market, where the stalls gave way to proper shops with proper doors, there was a narrow building with a window so dirty you could not see through it, and over the door a sign that read:

GRUBB — LOANS — NO QUESTIONS

A bell jangled as Wren went in. The shop was dim and crammed to the ceiling with other people’s things: clocks that did not tick, coats that did not fit, a stuffed badger, a box of spoons, three violins with no strings. Behind the counter, on a high stool, sat Silas Grubb.

He was a thin man, so thin that he looked as if he had been folded up and put away somewhere and only lately taken out again. He had a long nose that went down and then, at the very end, went down a little further, as if it were trying to see what was in your pocket. When he saw Wren, he rubbed his hands together. He always rubbed his hands together.

“Ah,” said Silas Grubb. “The Ashby girl. Mott’s sweep. What have you brought me this time? A spoon? A very small boot? I can give you a farthing for a very small boot.”

“Not a boot,” said Wren.

She looked behind her, to make sure the door was shut. Then she unbuttoned her coat, and took out the lamp, and set it on the counter between them.

I wish you could have seen Grubb’s face. It went still all over, the way a cat goes still at a mousehole. The golden light fell on his long nose and his thin fingers and the dusty clutter all about, and wherever it fell the dust looked like something better than dust — a soft brown on the boxes, a warm glint on the brass of the dead clocks. Grubb’s eyes went small and shiny.

“Hm,” he said, very carefully, in the voice of a man trying not to sound interested. “An old lamp. Dented. Glass cracked. Not worth much. Twopence.”

“It hasn’t got any oil in it,” said Wren.

Grubb’s eyes flickered down to the base of the lamp, and then back up to the flame, and then to the base again. His hands stopped rubbing.

“It’s been burning since yesterday,” said Wren. “It doesn’t go out. I blew it out and it lit itself again.”

“Sixpence,” said Grubb, rather quickly.

“Rot.”

“A shilling. Two shillings. Two shillings and a ha’penny, and you’ll not get a better price in—“

“I’ll take it somewhere else, then,” said Wren, and she reached for the lamp.

“Wait.” Grubb leaned so far over the counter that his nose nearly went into the flame. His voice had gone high and thin. “Wait, wait, wait. A lamp that needs no oil. A lamp that burns without the Guild. Do you know what the nobs on the Hill would— never mind. Never mind. Ten shillings. A crown! Five crowns!” His fingers were twitching. “Twenty,” he said. “Twenty silver crowns. There. Twenty silver crowns, girl, and that’s robbing myself blind.”

Twenty silver crowns.

Wren had never in her life held more than four pennies at once. Twenty silver crowns was a sum so large that she could not even picture it. She tried to picture it in pies, and it was a lifetime of pies. It was — she did the sum again — enough to walk out of Mott’s yard and never come back.

“Done,” she said.

“Done!” cried Grubb, and he reached out with both hands and snatched up the lamp.

And then he screamed.

It was not a large scream, because Grubb was not a large man, but it was a very sincere one. He flung the lamp away from him as if it were a live coal. It bounced off a box of spoons, rolled along the counter, and stopped in front of Wren, still upright, still burning, as though nothing in particular had happened. Grubb was hopping round behind the counter with his hands tucked under his armpits, howling. When at last he pulled them out to look at them, Wren saw that both palms had gone an angry, blistered pink, as if he had grabbed the handle of a pan that had been sitting on the fire all day.

“It burned me!” he shrieked. “It burned me!”

Wren looked at the lamp. She looked at her own hands. Then, slowly, she picked the lamp up.

It was warm. Pleasantly warm, the way it had been all night. It did not hurt her in the least. She turned her palms over afterwards and there was not a mark on them; only the soot, and a little of yesterday’s brick-dust under her nails.

Grubb saw this, and his face, which had been pink with pain, went the colour of old paste.

“Cursed,” he whispered. He backed away from her until he hit the shelves and a violin fell off. “That thing’s cursed. That’s witch-work, that is. Burning a man for an honest bargain—“

“You were going to cheat me,” said Wren. “You’d have sold it for a hundred.”

“Get out!” Grubb grabbed a broom and flapped it at her, keeping well out of reach of the lamp. “Out! Out of my shop, you and your witch-light! Don’t you come back here! Don’t you ever come back here!”

Wren went out. The bell jangled behind her, and the door slammed, and a moment later she heard the bolt go across.

She stood for a while in the street with the lamp tucked back into her coat, feeling it warm against her ribs, and feeling extremely sorry for herself.

It was cursed. It must be. Why else would it burn Grubb and not her? And if it was cursed, then nobody would buy it — or if they did, they would burn their hands and start screaming about witches, and the next thing she knew, the guard would be knocking on the garret door. There would be no silver crowns. There would be no pies on Tallow Bridge. There would be no leaving Mott’s yard and never coming back. There would be soot, and board money, and being hungry, as always.

And she was hungry. She had not eaten since yesterday’s crust, and her stomach had begun making a noise like a cart going over cobbles. She had promised Nettle breakfast, too. “Maybe,” she had said — and Nettle, who was seven, would have heard yes.

“Everything costs,” Wren muttered. “Told you so.” She was not sure whom she was telling.

She was walking back along the edge of the market, past the eel-woman and the odd boots, wondering whether she could lift an onion without being seen, when she smelled bread.

It was not the smell of the market bread, which was grey and hard and tasted of the bottom of the bin. It was warm and rich and golden — if a smell can be golden — and it stopped her in her tracks as if she had walked into a wall. She turned round.

An old man was sitting on an upturned crate by the canal wall, with a wide basket on his knees. The basket was covered with a cloth, and from under the cloth came that smell, and a little drift of steam. He wore a long coat that had seen a good deal of weather, and he was not calling out, as the stall-holders did. He was simply sitting there, as though he had all the time in the world, watching the people go by.

As Wren stared, he looked up, and his eyes met hers.

They were kind eyes. That was the first thing she noticed, and it made her wary at once, because in Wren’s experience kind eyes generally meant somebody wanted something from you. They were deep-set, with lines at the corners from smiling, and they looked at her — at her tufty hair and her bare black feet and her sharp, suspicious chin — as if she were somebody worth looking at.

“Hungry?” he said.

“No,” said Wren.

The old man smiled, as if that were a very good joke, and lifted a corner of the cloth. He took out a loaf — a round brown loaf, with a crust that cracked when he held it — and held it out to her.

Wren did not move. “How much?”

“No charge.”

“Everything’s got a charge.”

“Not this,” said the old man. “It’s given.”

Wren looked at the loaf, and at the old man’s hand holding it out. It was a working hand, brown and broad, and across the palm there ran an old pale scar, as if long ago something had gone right through it. She only half noticed this. She was mostly noticing the loaf. Then, before he could tell her what she owed him for it, she snatched it out of his hand and stuffed it under her arm and backed away.

It was warm. It was so warm she could feel it through her sleeve.

She had gone three steps before she thought of something to say: something sharp, to show she was nobody’s fool, and that if he thought he could come asking favours later on account of one loaf of bread, he had another think coming. She turned round with her mouth already open.

The crate was there, by the canal wall. The old man was not. Nor was his basket. Wren looked up the street and down it, and along the canal both ways, and he was nowhere in sight — though there was nowhere he could have gone, not in the time it had taken her to walk three steps.

She stood with her mouth open a while longer. Then she shut it, and held the loaf a little tighter, and went to find Nettle.

She found her on the back step of the sweep-house, shivering, with her knees pulled up inside her shirt.

“You got breakfatht!” said Nettle, and her whole freckled face lit up, gap and all.

They sat on the step and ate it together. Wren tore it in half, and then, after a moment’s thought, tore a bit more off her own half and put it on Nettle’s. The inside of the loaf was soft and white and steaming, and it tasted the way it had smelled, warm and rich and somehow golden, and it went down into Wren’s empty stomach like a fire being lit in a cold grate.

“Where’d you get it?” said Nettle, with her mouth full.

“Man gave it me.”

Nettle stopped chewing. “Gave it? For nothing?”

“That’s what he said.”

Nettle thought about this very seriously. “Nobody giveth anything for nothing,” she said at last. “You thaid.”

“I know I said,” said Wren crossly. “Eat your bread.”

But all that afternoon the bread sat in her stomach, warm and puzzling, and the lamp sat against her ribs, warm and puzzling, and the two of them together made her more uncomfortable than she had been in her life. And the longer she thought about it, the more certain she became that the lamp was nothing but trouble: a cursed, burning, unsellable, witch-light sort of trouble that would bring the guard down on her head as sure as eggs. Grubb would talk. Grubb always talked. The best thing — the only thing — was to be rid of it before anybody came asking.

So she went down to the Soot Canal, to the quiet stretch behind the tanneries where nobody went if they could help it, and she took out the lamp, and she threw it in.

It went in with a dull plop. The black water closed over it. Wren stood on the edge and watched — and the lamp did not go out. It sank slowly down into the dark, turning a little, and it shone. It shone all the way down. Even when it came to rest on the bottom, among the mud and the old bottles and goodness knows what else, it lay there glowing up through the black water like a star that had fallen out of the sky and gone to sleep. Wren had never seen a star; nobody in Emberwick had, for three hundred years. But if she had, she would have thought of one then.

“Good riddance,” she said, rather loudly, and walked away without looking back.

That afternoon she swept two chimneys on Fuller Street with a borrowed brush. When she climbed up to her garret in the gloaming, the lamp was sitting on the windowsill.

It was perfectly dry. There was not a speck of canal-mud on it. It was burning away calmly in the little window as though it had been there all day, and the garret was warm.

Wren looked at it for a long time. Then she picked it up, put it under her coat, went straight back downstairs and out through the back of Mott’s yard to the tannery yard behind it. The tannery yard was a dreadful place that smelled of things you would rather not think about, and the ground there was soft and black. She dug a hole with her scraper as deep as her arm, and put the lamp at the bottom of it, and filled the hole in, and stamped on it, and put a broken barrel on top for good measure.

When she climbed back up to the garret, the lamp was sitting on the windowsill.

“Right,” said Wren, between her teeth.

This time she took it all the way to Tallow Bridge, which was a good half-mile off, in the middle of the city, where the pie stall stood. She set it down very carefully on the parapet of the bridge, in plain view, where anyone at all might pick it up and take it home — let them have the trouble of it, she thought, let them burn their fingers — and she walked away without looking round, past the pie stall, and home in the dark.

You will already have guessed where it was when she got there. Wren had guessed too. She was not surprised when she opened the door of her garret and saw the little golden flame on the sill. She was only very tired, and very cross, and — though she would not have admitted it to anybody — a little bit frightened.

She sat down on her mattress and glared at it.

“What do you want?” she said. “Eh? What do you want with me?”

The lamp burned.

“I never asked for you,” said Wren. “I never. You were stuck in a wall. I let you out, didn’t I? That’s all. That’s all I did. And I can’t sell you, and I can’t eat you, and I can’t get rid of you, and Grubb thinks I’m a witch, and he’ll tell everyone, and they’ll come for me, and it’s all your fault.” She found that her voice had gone wobbly, and she stopped, and swallowed, and went on more fiercely. “Everything costs. Everything. So what do you cost? Eh? What’s the catch? There’s always a catch. You tell me what I owe and I’ll—“

“It was given, child.”

Wren went absolutely still.

The voice had come from the chimney-breast. It was not loud. It was low and quiet and very close, as if someone were sitting just on the other side of the bricks, in the warm dark of the flue, speaking to her the way you might speak to someone you had known for a long time. It was not Mott’s voice, or any voice she knew. It was the kindest voice she had ever heard.

“Not lost,” it said. “Given.”

Then there was nothing. Only the canal, far below, sighing against its walls.

Wren did not move for a long time. Her heart was going like a hammer. She had been in a thousand dark chimneys alone and never once been frightened. She was frightened now. She could feel the fear in her fingers and the backs of her knees. And yet — this was the strange part, the part she could not make sense of afterwards — underneath the fear there was something else. Something that felt very like the warmth of the lamp, or the warmth of the bread in her stomach. As though the voice, whoever it belonged to, had not been angry with her at all. As though it had only wanted her to know.

“Who’s there?” she whispered at last.

Nobody answered. She had not really expected anybody to.

After a while she lay down on the straw, and pulled the blanket with the hole in it up to her chin, and turned on her side so that she could see the little flame on the windowsill. She did not want to look away from it. Without quite knowing why, she found that she had begun to hum.

It was a tune she did not often let herself remember. It came from a long way back, from before Mott’s yard, from before the soot — from a time she could not see at all, only feel, like a room you have been in once in the dark. Someone had sung it to her. Someone with soft arms and a voice that went up at the end of the lines. Morning comes, the song went. Morning comes, morning comes...

And then it stopped. It always stopped there. There were more words after that, she knew there were; she could feel the shape of them, the way you can feel the shape of a word on the tip of your tongue. But she had never been able to find them. She hummed the first line over again, and then again, more softly, and each time the tune ran out and left her listening to nothing.

“Morning comes,” Wren whispered to the lamp. “That’s all I’ve got.”

The lamp burned on, steady and golden. Her ribbon lay red across her wrist in its light. The garret was warm, and the bricks of the chimney-breast were warm, and the bread was still warm inside her; and somewhere in the middle of the third morning comes, without meaning to, Wren fell asleep.

And if it was cursed, then nobody would buy it — or if they did, they would burn their hands and start screaming about witches, and the next thing she knew, the guard would be knocking on the garret door. There would be no silver crowns. There would be no pies on Tallow Bridge. There would be no leaving Mott’s yard and never coming back. There would be soot, and board money, and being hungry, as always. And she was hungry. She had not eaten since yesterday’s crust, and her stomach had begun making a noise like a cart going over cobbles. She had promised Nettle breakfast, too. “Maybe,” she had said — and Nettle, who was seven, would have heard yes. “Everything costs,” Wren muttered. “Told you so.” She was not sure whom she was telling. She was walking back along the edge of the market, past the eel-woman and the odd boots, wondering whether she could lift an onion without being seen, when she smelled bread. It was not the smell of the market bread, which was grey and hard and tasted of the bottom of the bin. It was warm and rich and golden — if a smell can be golden — and it stopped her in her tracks as if she had walked into a wall. She turned round. An old man was sitting on an upturned crate by the canal wall, with a wide basket on his knees. The basket was covered with a cloth, and from under the cloth came that smell, and a little drift of steam. He wore a long coat that had seen a good deal of weather, and he was not calling out, as the stall-holders did. He was simply sitting there, as though he had all the time in the world, watching the people go by. As Wren stared, he looked up, and his eyes met hers. They were kind eyes. That was the first thing she noticed, and it made her wary at once, because in Wren’s experience kind eyes generally meant somebody wanted something from you. They were deep-set, with lines at the corners from smiling, and they looked at her — at her tufty hair and her bare black feet and her sharp, suspicious chin — as if she were somebody worth looking at. “Hungry?” he said. “No,” said Wren. The old man smiled, as if that were a very good joke, and lifted a corner of the cloth. He took out a loaf — a round brown loaf, with a crust that cracked when he held it — and held it out to her. Wren did not move. “How much?” “No charge.” “Everything’s got a charge.” “Not this,” said the old man. “It’s given.” Wren looked at the loaf, and at the old man’s hand holding it out. It was a working hand, brown and broad, and across the palm there ran an old pale scar, as if long ago something had gone right through it. She only half noticed this. She was mostly noticing the loaf. Then, before he could tell her what she owed him for it, she snatched it out of his hand and stuffed it under her arm and backed away. It was warm. It was so warm she could feel it through her sleeve. She had gone three steps before she thought of something to say: something sharp, to show she was nobody’s fool, and that if he thought he could come asking favours later on account of one loaf of bread, he had another think coming. She turned round with her mouth already open. The crate was there, by the canal wall. The old man was not. Nor was his basket. Wren looked up the street and down it, and along the canal both ways, and he was nowhere in sight — though there was nowhere he could have gone, not in the time it had taken her to walk three steps. She stood with her mouth open a while longer. Then she shut it, and held the loaf a little tighter, and went to find Nettle. She found her on the back step of the sweep-house, shivering, with her knees pulled up inside her shirt. “You got breakfatht!” said Nettle, and her whole freckled face lit up, gap and all. They sat on the step and ate it together. Wren tore it in half, and then, after a moment’s thought, tore a bit more off her own half and put it on Nettle’s. The inside of the loaf was soft and white and steaming, and it tasted the way it had smelled, warm and rich and somehow golden, and it went down into Wren’s empty stomach like a fire being lit in a cold grate. “Where’d you get it?” said Nettle, with her mouth full. “Man gave it me.” Nettle stopped chewing. “Gave it? For nothing?” “That’s what he said.” Nettle thought about this very seriously. “Nobody giveth anything for nothing,” she said at last. “You thaid.” “I know I said,” said Wren crossly. “Eat your bread.” But all that afternoon the bread sat in her stomach, warm and puzzling, and the lamp sat against her ribs, warm and puzzling, and the two of them together made her more uncomfortable than she had been in her life. And the longer she thought about it, the more certain she became that the lamp was nothing but trouble: a cursed, burning, unsellable, witch-light sort of trouble that would bring the guard down on her head as sure as eggs. Grubb would talk. Grubb always talked. The best thing — the only thing — was to be rid of it before anybody came asking. So she went down to the Soot Canal, to the quiet stretch behind the tanneries where nobody went if they could help it, and she took out the lamp, and she threw it in. It went in with a dull plop. The black water closed over it. Wren stood on the edge and watched — and the lamp did not go out. It sank slowly down into the dark, turning a little, and it shone. It shone all the way down. Even when it came to rest on the bottom, among the mud and the old bottles and goodness knows what else, it lay there glowing up through the black water like a star that had fallen out of the sky and gone to sleep. Wren had never seen a star; nobody in Emberwick had, for three hundred years. But if she had, she would have thought of one then. “Good riddance,” she said, rather loudly, and walked away without looking back. That afternoon she swept two chimneys on Fuller Street with a borrowed brush. When she climbed up to her garret in the gloaming, the lamp was sitting on the windowsill. It was perfectly dry. There was not a speck of canal-mud on it. It was burning away calmly in the little window as though it had been there all day, and the garret was warm. Wren looked at it for a long time. Then she picked it up, put it under her coat, went straight back downstairs and out through the back of Mott’s yard to the tannery yard behind it. The tannery yard was a dreadful place that smelled of things you would rather not think about, and the ground there was soft and black. She dug a hole with her scraper as deep as her arm, and put the lamp at the bottom of it, and filled the hole in, and stamped on it, and put a broken barrel on top for good measure. When she climbed back up to the garret, the lamp was sitting on the windowsill. “Right,” said Wren, between her teeth. This time she took it all the way to Tallow Bridge, which was a good half-mile off, in the middle of the city, where the pie stall stood. She set it down very carefully on the parapet of the bridge, in plain view, where anyone at all might pick it up and take it home — let them have the trouble of it, she thought, let them burn their fingers — and she walked away without looking round, past the pie stall, and home in the dark. You will already have guessed where it was when she got there. Wren had guessed too. She was not surprised when she opened the door of her garret and saw the little golden flame on the sill. She was only very tired, and very cross, and — though she would not have admitted it to anybody — a little bit frightened. She sat down on her mattress and glared at it. “What do you want?” she said. “Eh? What do you want with me?” The lamp burned. “I never asked for you,” said Wren. “I never. You were stuck in a wall. I let you out, didn’t I? That’s all. That’s all I did. And I can’t sell you, and I can’t eat you, and I can’t get rid of you, and Grubb thinks I’m a witch, and he’ll tell everyone, and they’ll come for me, and it’s all your fault.” She found that her voice had gone wobbly, and she stopped, and swallowed, and went on more fiercely. “Everything costs. Everything. So what do you cost? Eh? What’s the catch? There’s always a catch. You tell me what I owe and I’ll—“ “It was given, child.” Wren went absolutely still. The voice had come from the chimney-breast. It was not loud. It was low and quiet and very close, as if someone were sitting just on the other side of the bricks, in the warm dark of the flue, speaking to her the way you might speak to someone you had known for a long time. It was not Mott’s voice, or any voice she knew. It was the kindest voice she had ever heard. “Not lost,” it said. “Given.” Then there was nothing. Only the canal, far below, sighing against its walls. Wren did not move for a long time. Her heart was going like a hammer. She had been in a thousand dark chimneys alone and never once been frightened. She was frightened now. She could feel the fear in her fingers and the backs of her knees. And yet — this was the strange part, the part she could not make sense of afterwards — underneath the fear there was something else. Something that felt very like the warmth of the lamp, or the warmth of the bread in her stomach. As though the voice, whoever it belonged to, had not been angry with her at all. As though it had only wanted her to know. “Who’s there?” she whispered at last. Nobody answered. She had not really expected anybody to. After a while she lay down on the straw, and pulled the blanket with the hole in it up to her chin, and turned on her side so that she could see the little flame on the windowsill. She did not want to look away from it. Without quite knowing why, she found that she had begun to hum. It was a tune she did not often let herself remember. It came from a long way back, from before Mott’s yard, from before the soot — from a time she could not see at all, only feel, like a room you have been in once in the dark. Someone had sung it to her. Someone with soft arms and a voice that went up at the end of the lines. Morning comes, the song went. Morning comes, morning comes... And then it stopped. It always stopped there. There were more words after that, she knew there were; she could feel the shape of them, the way you can feel the shape of a word on the tip of your tongue. But she had never been able to find them. She hummed the first line over again, and then again, more softly, and each time the tune ran out and left her listening to nothing. “Morning comes,” Wren whispered to the lamp. “That’s all I’ve got.” The lamp burned on, steady and golden. Her ribbon lay red across her wrist in its light. The garret was warm, and the bricks of the chimney-breast were warm, and the bread was still warm inside her; and somewhere in the middle of the third morning comes, without meaning to, Wren fell asleep.

fields.title: The Warden’s Son
fields.body_html:
At the very top of the Warden’s Hall, which stood at the very top of the Hill, which was the highest part of Emberwick, there was an attic that nobody but Tobin Harrowgate ever went into if they could help it.

It was a long, low room under the slates, with beams you hit your head on and two round windows at either end, like the eyes of an owl. It was full of things. There were clocks in it, and parts of clocks; springs and cogs and coils of copper wire; jars of screws sorted by size and jars of screws not sorted at all; a telescope that had been taken to pieces and put back together with one piece left over; three half-built mechanical birds, none of which could fly; and maps. Maps were pinned to the beams and stacked on the floor and rolled up in umbrella-stands — maps of the city, maps of the canals, maps of the wall, and one very old map of the whole land of Gloamhaven, with a mountain drawn at the top of it in faded ink and the words Here the Light Began written underneath in a tiny, careful hand.

And in the middle of the room, on a round table all to itself, was the thing Tobin was proudest of in all the world.

“It’s called the Orrery of the Ring,” he was saying. “Well — I call it that. Technically speaking an orrery is a model of the sky, the sun and moons and so on, so it isn’t strictly an orrery at all. But it goes round, you see, in a way, and I couldn’t think of a better word, and Brass Model of the City Wall with Glass Beads didn’t sound nearly so—“

“Quite so, Master Tobin,” said Mr Quill.

Mr Quill was the Warden’s steward. He was a dry, upright, grey-whiskered man who had served the Harrowgates for thirty years, and he had come up the attic stairs to say that supper was served. He had been standing in the doorway for six minutes and had not yet managed to say it.

Tobin did not notice. Tobin was thirteen, and tall for it, and made almost entirely of elbows and knees; he had untidy fair hair that would not lie down, ink on every one of his fingers, and a pair of round spectacles which slid down his nose whenever he got excited, which was often. They were sliding now. He pushed them up and went on.

“It’s the whole of the city wall, you see, all the way round. Every Ring-lamp is one of these glass beads. A hundred and forty-four of them. I counted. Well — obviously I counted, I made them. And these—“ he touched a fine copper thread that ran from bead to bead, and another that ran inward from the ring across the table to a little brass cup at the very centre — “these are the flame-wires. They follow the flame-pipes exactly. The real ones, I mean. Under the city. From the Great Beacon out to every lamp on the wall. I copied the pattern from an old Lamplighter plan I found in—“ He stopped, and went a little pink, and said instead, “—in a book. And then I ran a wire all the way down the back stairs and into the cellar, where the Hall’s own old pipe comes up out of the ground, and joined it on. And the thing is, Mr Quill — the really remarkable thing is—“

“Supper, Master Tobin,” said Mr Quill.

“—that it works. When the Ring-lamps burn, the copper in the pipes gets warm, and the warmth comes up my wire, and the beads glow. Just faintly. Look.” He bent over the table. “There’s the North Wall. There’s the Grey Gate. You can see which lamps are burning well and which aren’t. That one’s nearly out — that’s the one over the tanneries — and those three there by the canal-mouth are very poor. You could stand here and see the whole Ring at once, Mr Quill, without ever going out in the—“

He stopped again.

“In the cold,” he finished.

“Indeed,” said Mr Quill. “His lordship is waiting.”

I should tell you now, before we go down to supper, the thing about Tobin that nobody in the Warden’s Hall knew — not Mr Quill, not the maids, and certainly not his father. It was this. Tobin Harrowgate was frightened of the dark.

I do not mean that he was a little nervous of it, the way most people are when they go down to the cellar for coal. I mean that when the lamps went out at night his hands began to shake, and his breath went short, and his heart thumped so hard in his ears that he could not hear anything else. It had been that way as long as he could remember. And so every night, when he went to bed in the little room off the attic, he lit a lamp beside his pillow and left it burning till morning.

It was a small lamp, made of pale glass with a little painted border, and it burned Guild oil like any other. It had been his mother’s.

Lady Elinor Harrowgate had died when Tobin was five. He did not remember very much of her, and what he remembered came in pieces, like light through leaves: her hands, which were always cool; her laugh, which was quick and surprised, as though the world kept doing funny things she had not expected; and her songs. She had known all the old Lamplighter songs, the ones nobody sang any more — songs about lamps lit on high towers, and fire carried down from mountains, and a morning that would come. She used to sing them to him at night with that little glass lamp burning beside the bed, and when he was frightened she would say, “There. You see? The dark is only the place where the light hasn’t got to yet.”

He had a thing of hers that he kept always in his waistcoat pocket: a brass compass, plain and a little worn, with a lid that snapped shut. Inside the lid, in letters so small you had to tilt them to the light, was written: Home is where the light is. He did not know what it meant, but he read it most days anyway.

His father did not like the songs. After Lady Elinor died, Lord Edric had the books of old stories taken out of the library and put away, and when Tobin, aged six, had asked to hear about the Lamplighters, his father had said in his quiet, level voice that he would not have Lamplighter nonsense spoken of in his house, and that was the end of it. Tobin had found the book with the old plan in it at the back of a cupboard, years later, with his mother’s name written in the front. He had not told anyone.

Supper in the Warden’s Hall was served in the Long Room, at a table so long that there could have been twenty people at it. There were two. Lord Edric sat at one end and Tobin sat at the other, and in between them stretched a great expanse of polished wood with a single candlestick in the middle and a great deal of silence.

The Long Room was always cold. Most of the Warden’s Hall was cold; it was built of grey stone, and it was very grand, and very old, and grand old stone houses do not warm up easily. The fire in the grate was small, because oil and coal were dear and the Warden did not believe in waste. The portraits of dead Harrowgates looked down from the walls, all in grey, all looking as if they disapproved of soup.

“Quill tells me,” said Lord Edric, “that you were not at your fencing lesson this afternoon.”

Tobin’s father was a tall man — Tobin had got his height from him, though not, it seemed, anything else — with a long stern face and hair that was going silver at the temples. He never shouted. Tobin could not remember ever hearing him shout. He did not need to. His voice had a way of going quieter and quieter until you would almost rather he did.

“No, Father. I’m sorry. I was finishing something. In the attic.”

“In the attic.” Lord Edric laid down his spoon. “Master Ravell tells me you have not held a sword properly in a month. Your riding master says you fall off. You are thirteen years old, Tobin. In five years you will be expected to take your place in this city. People will look at you, and they will see the Warden’s son. What would you have them see? A boy who plays with clockwork?”

“It isn’t playing, actually,” said Tobin. “It’s — well, technically it’s a sort of instrument. I’ve built a model of the Ring, Father, the whole wall, and it shows you which lamps are burning, from right here in the Hall, and I thought — I thought it might actually be useful, to you, I mean, with the lamps going dim, because you could see at once which ones were failing and send the Guild to—“

“Tobin.”

“—to fix them before they—“

“Tobin.”

Tobin stopped.

“The Ring,” said his father quietly, “is the business of the Guild and the Warden. Not of children. Not of toys. Eat your supper. And you will dress properly afterwards. Guild Master Prowle is coming to council this evening, and you will attend.”

Tobin looked up, startled. He had never been allowed into a council before.

“It is time,” said Lord Edric, “that you learned something of what it means to keep a city safe.” And he took up his spoon again, and said nothing more for the rest of the meal.

The council was held in the Warden’s study, which was a little warmer than the Long Room because it was smaller, and which smelled, by the time Guild Master Cuthbert Prowle had been in it for five minutes, overwhelmingly of lavender.

Prowle was a round man. He was round in the face and round in the middle and round in the voice, and he had a way of shining, as if somebody polished him every morning. Across his front, from shoulder to shoulder, hung a heavy gold chain of office, which clinked whenever he moved, and he moved a great deal. He smelled of lavender oil so strongly that Tobin’s eyes watered. And he loved long words the way some people love sweets: he could not get through a sentence without one.

“My lord Warden,” he said, bowing so low the chain swung. “I come, alas, as the bearer of regrettable — I may say lamentable — tidings.”

Besides Prowle and the Warden and Tobin, who had been put on a hard chair in a corner and told to listen, there was one other person in the room: a grizzled, tired-looking man in the grey coat of the city guard, with his helmet under his arm and mud on his boots. His name was Sergeant Bracken. He had come straight from the North Wall and had not been offered a seat.

“The Ring,” said Prowle, “is diminishing. Its luminosity is declining at an unprecedented rate. Eleven lamps on the eastern stretch have been reduced to a mere — ahem — glimmer. Four more by the tanneries. The Guild labours night and day, my lord. Night and day! But these are dark times. Dark times. The very oil seems wearied.” He spread his plump hands. “The Guild therefore most respectfully requests a further allocation of funds. For oil. A modest augmentation. Let us say — double.”

“Double,” said Lord Edric.

“These are, as I say, dark times.”

Lord Edric was silent for a while. Tobin watched him. His father’s face did not change, but his long fingers had begun, very slowly, to tap the edge of the desk.

“Sergeant,” said the Warden at last. “Your report.”

Sergeant Bracken shifted his feet. “The Greywaste watch, my lord. Last three nights.” He spoke slowly, like a man who did not want to say what he had to say. “There’s shapes out there. Past the Grey Gate. In the gloaming, mostly. Grey shapes, my lord, on the grey grass. Hard to see. You look, and you think it’s mist, and then it moves.” He paused. “There’s more of them each night. And they’re closer.”

The study seemed to get colder. Tobin found that his hands had closed tight on the edge of his chair.

“Hollows?” said Lord Edric. His voice was very quiet.

“Couldn’t swear to it, my lord. But I’ve not seen anything else move like that.”

“Nonsense,” said Guild Master Prowle, rather too loudly, and his chain clinked. “Mist and imagination, Sergeant. Mist and imagination. No Hollow has crossed the Ring of Emberwick in a hundred years. The Ring holds. The Ring will always hold — provided, of course,” he added, turning his shining face back to the Warden, “that it is properly funded.”

Lord Edric looked at the Guild Master for a long time. Then he took up his pen.

“Double,” he said, and signed.

Prowle bowed so deeply that his chain nearly touched the floor, and said a great many words of gratitude, a good number of which Tobin had never heard before, and swept out in a cloud of lavender. Sergeant Bracken put on his helmet and followed, more slowly. At the door he glanced back, and his eyes met Tobin’s in the corner, and Tobin had the odd feeling that the tired old soldier was sorry for him, though he could not think why.

His father did not look at him at all. He sat at his desk with the pen still in his hand, staring at the darkening window, and his fingers had stopped tapping.

“Go to bed, Tobin,” he said.

Tobin went up to the attic. He did not go to bed.

He lit his mother’s little glass lamp first, as he always did, and set it on the corner of the round table where its light fell on the Orrery. His hands were not quite steady. He kept thinking of the Sergeant’s voice: You look, and you think it’s mist, and then it moves.

“Mist and imagination,” he said aloud, to the empty attic, in a fair imitation of Prowle’s round voice. It did not make him feel any better.

He bent over the Orrery and looked at the Ring.

It was worse than it had been at supper. He could see that at once. All round the brass circle the little glass beads were glowing faintly — but faintly was the word, faint and dull and tired, like embers at the end of a long night. The eastern stretch was barely lit at all. The bead over the tanneries had gone quite dark. He counted the dim ones, and then counted again, and got a number he did not like.

And then he saw it.

It was not on the Ring at all. It was inside it — on one of the fine copper flame-wires that ran across the table beneath the city, through the tangle of lanes and canals of the Low Quarter. There, on the wire, where no Ring-lamp was and no bead had ever been, was a point of light.

It was very small. It was smaller than the smallest bead. But it was bright — brighter than any bead on the whole Orrery, brighter than the whole Ring put together — and it was not dull and it was not tired. It was a clear, steady, golden-white, like nothing Tobin had ever seen in his life. The copper wire around it had begun to glow too, a warm reddish shimmer he had no name for, as though the light were too strong to stay in one place and was spilling over into everything near it.

Tobin took off his spectacles, wiped them on his shirt, and put them on again. It was still there.

He had seen something like it before. Two days ago — just a flicker, high up at the edge of the Hill, near the old Thornbury place — and then last night, a little spark in the Low Quarter that came and went. He had thought it was a fault. A loose wire. A bit of dust. He had meant to take that section to pieces and find out.

This was not dust.

As he watched, the point of light moved.

It slid along the copper wire, slowly, steadily — the pace, Tobin thought with a strange prickle at the back of his neck, of somebody walking. It went down past the tanneries. It went along beside the canal. It turned a corner — a real corner, the wire bending where the real pipe bent under the real street — and Tobin ran his inky finger along his big map of the city on the beam above until he found the place, and read the name, and said it under his breath.

“Soot Lane.”

The light went on down Soot Lane. And as it went, a strange thing happened. At the end of the lane, where it met the city wall, there was a single old Ring-lamp — Tobin knew it, a poor dim one, he had been watching it fade for weeks — and as the golden point drew near it, that little bead on the Orrery flickered, and brightened, and for a moment glowed as warm and clear as if it had been lit that very hour.

Then the point of light turned again, into a tangle of houses, and stopped, and stayed where it was, burning.

Tobin stood back from the table.

There was no lamp in Soot Lane but that one old Ring-lamp on the wall. There was nothing in the Low Quarter that could burn like that. There was nothing in the whole of Emberwick — he was quite, quite sure of it — that could burn like that. Not the Ring. Not the Beacon, even, not any more. And yet there it was, a little golden point on a copper wire, as plain as print.

He thought of his father, saying not of children, not of toys. He thought of the Guild Master, shining and smelling of lavender and saying double.

He thought of the Low Quarter. In the dark.

Tobin had never been to the Low Quarter in his life. He had never been anywhere after nightfall in his life, except from one lit room to another. The thought of going out — down the Hill, through the gates, into streets with no lamps, where Hollows might be moving like mist on the grey grass — made his stomach turn over and his hands begin, quite helplessly, to shake.

He looked at the golden point on the Orrery for a long time.

Then he went and got his coat.

He put it on with trembling fingers, and did up the buttons wrong, and did them up again. He put his mother’s compass in his waistcoat pocket and laid his hand flat over it for a moment, the way some people say a word before they jump. Then he picked up the little glass night-lamp from the table — it shook in his grip, and the flame shook with it — and he went, very quietly, down the attic stairs.
