There’s the Grey Gate. You can see which lamps are burning well and which aren’t. That one’s nearly out — that’s the one over the tanneries — and those three there by the canal-mouth are very poor. You could stand here and see the whole Ring at once, Mr Quill, without ever going out in the—“ He stopped again. “In the cold,” he finished. “Indeed,” said Mr Quill. “His lordship is waiting.” I should tell you now, before we go down to supper, the thing about Tobin that nobody in the Warden’s Hall knew — not Mr Quill, not the maids, and certainly not his father. It was this. Tobin Harrowgate was frightened of the dark. I do not mean that he was a little nervous of it, the way most people are when they go down to the cellar for coal. I mean that when the lamps went out at night his hands began to shake, and his breath went short, and his heart thumped so hard in his ears that he could not hear anything else. It had been that way as long as he could remember. And so every night, when he went to bed in the little room off the attic, he lit a lamp beside his pillow and left it burning till morning. It was a small lamp, made of pale glass with a little painted border, and it burned Guild oil like any other. It had been his mother’s. Lady Elinor Harrowgate had died when Tobin was five. He did not remember very much of her, and what he remembered came in pieces, like light through leaves: her hands, which were always cool; her laugh, which was quick and surprised, as though the world kept doing funny things she had not expected; and her songs. She had known all the old Lamplighter songs, the ones nobody sang any more — songs about lamps lit on high towers, and fire carried down from mountains, and a morning that would come. She used to sing them to him at night with that little glass lamp burning beside the bed, and when he was frightened she would say, “There. You see? The dark is only the place where the light hasn’t got to yet.” He had a thing of hers that he kept always in his waistcoat pocket: a brass compass, plain and a little worn, with a lid that snapped shut. Inside the lid, in letters so small you had to tilt them to the light, was written: Home is where the light is. He did not know what it meant, but he read it most days anyway. His father did not like the songs. After Lady Elinor died, Lord Edric had the books of old stories taken out of the library and put away, and when Tobin, aged six, had asked to hear about the Lamplighters, his father had said in his quiet, level voice that he would not have Lamplighter nonsense spoken of in his house, and that was the end of it. Tobin had found the book with the old plan in it at the back of a cupboard, years later, with his mother’s name written in the front. He had not told anyone. Supper in the Warden’s Hall was served in the Long Room, at a table so long that there could have been twenty people at it. There were two. Lord Edric sat at one end and Tobin sat at the other, and in between them stretched a great expanse of polished wood with a single candlestick in the middle and a great deal of silence. The Long Room was always cold. Most of the Warden’s Hall was cold; it was built of grey stone, and it was very grand, and very old, and grand old stone houses do not warm up easily. The fire in the grate was small, because oil and coal were dear and the Warden did not believe in waste. The portraits of dead Harrowgates looked down from the walls, all in grey, all looking as if they disapproved of soup. “Quill tells me,” said Lord Edric, “that you were not at your fencing lesson this afternoon.” Tobin’s father was a tall man — Tobin had got his height from him, though not, it seemed, anything else — with a long stern face and hair that was going silver at the temples. He never shouted. Tobin could not remember ever hearing him shout. He did not need to. His voice had a way of going quieter and quieter until you would almost rather he did. “No, Father. I’m sorry. I was finishing something. In the attic.” “In the attic.” Lord Edric laid down his spoon. “Master Ravell tells me you have not held a sword properly in a month. Your riding master says you fall off. You are thirteen years old, Tobin. In five years you will be expected to take your place in this city. People will look at you, and they will see the Warden’s son. What would you have them see? A boy who plays with clockwork?” “It isn’t playing, actually,” said Tobin. “It’s — well, technically it’s a sort of instrument. I’ve built a model of the Ring, Father, the whole wall, and it shows you which lamps are burning, from right here in the Hall, and I thought — I thought it might actually be useful, to you, I mean, with the lamps going dim, because you could see at once which ones were failing and send the Guild to—“ “Tobin.” “—to fix them before they—“ “Tobin.” Tobin stopped. “The Ring,” said his father quietly, “is the business of the Guild and the Warden. Not of children. Not of toys. Eat your supper. And you will dress properly afterwards. Guild Master Prowle is coming to council this evening, and you will attend.” Tobin looked up, startled. He had never been allowed into a council before. “It is time,” said Lord Edric, “that you learned something of what it means to keep a city safe.” And he took up his spoon again, and said nothing more for the rest of the meal. The council was held in the Warden’s study, which was a little warmer than the Long Room because it was smaller, and which smelled, by the time Guild Master Cuthbert Prowle had been in it for five minutes, overwhelmingly of lavender. Prowle was a round man. He was round in the face and round in the middle and round in the voice, and he had a way of shining, as if somebody polished him every morning. Across his front, from shoulder to shoulder, hung a heavy gold chain of office, which clinked whenever he moved, and he moved a great deal. He smelled of lavender oil so strongly that Tobin’s eyes watered. And he loved long words the way some people love sweets: he could not get through a sentence without one. “My lord Warden,” he said, bowing so low the chain swung. “I come, alas, as the bearer of regrettable — I may say lamentable — tidings.” Besides Prowle and the Warden and Tobin, who had been put on a hard chair in a corner and told to listen, there was one other person in the room: a grizzled, tired-looking man in the grey coat of the city guard, with his helmet under his arm and mud on his boots. His name was Sergeant Bracken. He had come straight from the North Wall and had not been offered a seat. “The Ring,” said Prowle, “is diminishing. Its luminosity is declining at an unprecedented rate. Eleven lamps on the eastern stretch have been reduced to a mere — ahem — glimmer. Four more by the tanneries. The Guild labours night and day, my lord. Night and day! But these are dark times. Dark times. The very oil seems wearied.” He spread his plump hands. “The Guild therefore most respectfully requests a further allocation of funds. For oil. A modest augmentation. Let us say — double.” “Double,” said Lord Edric. “These are, as I say, dark times.” Lord Edric was silent for a while. Tobin watched him. His father’s face did not change, but his long fingers had begun, very slowly, to tap the edge of the desk. “Sergeant,” said the Warden at last. “Your report.” Sergeant Bracken shifted his feet. “The Greywaste watch, my lord. Last three nights.” He spoke slowly, like a man who did not want to say what he had to say. “There’s shapes out there. Past the Grey Gate. In the gloaming, mostly. Grey shapes, my lord, on the grey grass. Hard to see. You look, and you think it’s mist, and then it moves.” He paused. “There’s more of them each night. And they’re closer.” The study seemed to get colder. Tobin found that his hands had closed tight on the edge of his chair. “Hollows?” said Lord Edric. His voice was very quiet. “Couldn’t swear to it, my lord. But I’ve not seen anything else move like that.” “Nonsense,” said Guild Master Prowle, rather too loudly, and his chain clinked. “Mist and imagination, Sergeant. Mist and imagination. No Hollow has crossed the Ring of Emberwick in a hundred years. The Ring holds. The Ring will always hold — provided, of course,” he added, turning his shining face back to the Warden, “that it is properly funded.” Lord Edric looked at the Guild Master for a long time. Then he took up his pen. “Double,” he said, and signed. Prowle bowed so deeply that his chain nearly touched the floor, and said a great many words of gratitude, a good number of which Tobin had never heard before, and swept out in a cloud of lavender. Sergeant Bracken put on his helmet and followed, more slowly. At the door he glanced back, and his eyes met Tobin’s in the corner, and Tobin had the odd feeling that the tired old soldier was sorry for him, though he could not think why. His father did not look at him at all. He sat at his desk with the pen still in his hand, staring at the darkening window, and his fingers had stopped tapping. “Go to bed, Tobin,” he said. Tobin went up to the attic. He did not go to bed. He lit his mother’s little glass lamp first, as he always did, and set it on the corner of the round table where its light fell on the Orrery. His hands were not quite steady. He kept thinking of the Sergeant’s voice: You look, and you think it’s mist, and then it moves. “Mist and imagination,” he said aloud, to the empty attic, in a fair imitation of Prowle’s round voice. It did not make him feel any better. He bent over the Orrery and looked at the Ring. It was worse than it had been at supper. He could see that at once. All round the brass circle the little glass beads were glowing faintly — but faintly was the word, faint and dull and tired, like embers at the end of a long night. The eastern stretch was barely lit at all. The bead over the tanneries had gone quite dark. He counted the dim ones, and then counted again, and got a number he did not like. And then he saw it. It was not on the Ring at all. It was inside it — on one of the fine copper flame-wires that ran across the table beneath the city, through the tangle of lanes and canals of the Low Quarter. There, on the wire, where no Ring-lamp was and no bead had ever been, was a point of light. It was very small. It was smaller than the smallest bead. But it was bright — brighter than any bead on the whole Orrery, brighter than the whole Ring put together — and it was not dull and it was not tired. It was a clear, steady, golden-white, like nothing Tobin had ever seen in his life. The copper wire around it had begun to glow too, a warm reddish shimmer he had no name for, as though the light were too strong to stay in one place and was spilling over into everything near it. Tobin took off his spectacles, wiped them on his shirt, and put them on again. It was still there. He had seen something like it before. Two days ago — just a flicker, high up at the edge of the Hill, near the old Thornbury place — and then last night, a little spark in the Low Quarter that came and went. He had thought it was a fault. A loose wire. A bit of dust. He had meant to take that section to pieces and find out. This was not dust. As he watched, the point of light moved. It slid along the copper wire, slowly, steadily — the pace, Tobin thought with a strange prickle at the back of his neck, of somebody walking. It went down past the tanneries. It went along beside the canal. It turned a corner — a real corner, the wire bending where the real pipe bent under the real street — and Tobin ran his inky finger along his big map of the city on the beam above until he found the place, and read the name, and said it under his breath. “Soot Lane.” The light went on down Soot Lane. And as it went, a strange thing happened. At the end of the lane, where it met the city wall, there was a single old Ring-lamp — Tobin knew it, a poor dim one, he had been watching it fade for weeks — and as the golden point drew near it, that little bead on the Orrery flickered, and brightened, and for a moment glowed as warm and clear as if it had been lit that very hour. Then the point of light turned again, into a tangle of houses, and stopped, and stayed where it was, burning. Tobin stood back from the table. There was no lamp in Soot Lane but that one old Ring-lamp on the wall. There was nothing in the Low Quarter that could burn like that. There was nothing in the whole of Emberwick — he was quite, quite sure of it — that could burn like that. Not the Ring. Not the Beacon, even, not any more. And yet there it was, a little golden point on a copper wire, as plain as print. He thought of his father, saying not of children, not of toys. He thought of the Guild Master, shining and smelling of lavender and saying double. He thought of the Low Quarter. In the dark. Tobin had never been to the Low Quarter in his life. He had never been anywhere after nightfall in his life, except from one lit room to another. The thought of going out — down the Hill, through the gates, into streets with no lamps, where Hollows might be moving like mist on the grey grass — made his stomach turn over and his hands begin, quite helplessly, to shake. He looked at the golden point on the Orrery for a long time. Then he went and got his coat. He put it on with trembling fingers, and did up the buttons wrong, and did them up again. He put his mother’s compass in his waistcoat pocket and laid his hand flat over it for a moment, the way some people say a word before they jump. Then he picked up the little glass night-lamp from the table — it shook in his grip, and the flame shook with it — and he went, very quietly, down the attic stairs.

fields.title: Flicker
fields.body_html:
Some people look as if they could belong anywhere. Others look as if they belong in exactly one place and nowhere else at all. Tobin Harrowgate was the second sort, and if you had seen him that evening, picking his way down off the Hill and into the Low Quarter, you would have known at once that he had come from somewhere with carpets.

It was not his clothes. He had put on his oldest coat, the brown one with the darned elbow, and had even rubbed a smear of soot onto one cheek, because he had read that this was what one did to pass unnoticed. It was everything else. It was the way he walked, as if the cobbles might be counted later and he wanted to be sure of the number. It was his spectacles, which flashed at every lit window. It was the way he said “I beg your pardon” to a dog.

And it was the thing in his hand.

It was a pocket-watch case with the watch taken out of it. Where the hands and numbers should have been, a single copper needle balanced on a pin, and on the tip of the needle sat a glass bead no bigger than a lentil, taken from the box of spares he kept under the Orrery. He had spent a feverish quarter of an hour making it before he left, and the whole of the back stairs trying to think of a name for it, and in the end he had scratched FLICKER on the lid, because PORTABLE THERMO-SYMPATHETIC LOCATING INDICATOR would not fit.

The principle, as Tobin would have been very glad to tell you, was simple. The beads on the Orrery warmed in sympathy with the Ring-lamps they stood for. A bead cut loose and set on a pivot ought, therefore, to swing towards whatever burned brightest nearby, the way a sunflower was said to turn towards the sun. Nobody in Emberwick had seen a sunflower for a very long time. But the theory was sound.

The theory had felt a great deal sounder in his warm attic than it did now.

In Gloamhaven, of course, the whole day is a kind of evening. But there is a time, after the pale sun has given up altogether and before the real dark comes, when the light goes thin and blue and everything looks as though it is standing a long way off. The old word for it is the gloaming. It was the gloaming now, and in the gloaming the Low Quarter looked very low indeed.

The houses leaned towards each other over the crooked lanes like old women sharing a secret. Washing lines zigzagged overhead, hung with shirts the colour of dishwater. The air smelled of tanneries and cabbage and soot. Two girls on a doorstep stopped their clapping game to stare. A woman with a basket of turnips looked him up and down, slowly, from his clean boots to his combed hair.

“Lost, are we, your lordship?” she said.

“Oh, no,” said Tobin. “Well, yes, in a geographical sense, but not in the sense you mean. And technically I’m not a lordship. My father is the Warden, which is an appointed office, not a hereditary—“

The two girls on the doorstep burst out laughing. Tobin went red to the tips of his ears and hurried on.

In his other coat pocket, the one that did not hold his mother’s compass, was his mother’s little night-lamp. He had blown it out at the foot of the Hill, so as not to be stared at, and promised himself that he would only light it again if it became truly dark. It was not truly dark yet. He kept one hand on it all the same, and felt the cool glass under his fingers, and told himself firmly that he was not frightened, he was merely gathering data.

Flicker’s needle trembled. Then it swung, slowly but quite definitely, down a lane to his left. A crooked sign on the corner said SOOT LANE.

“There you are,” Tobin whispered. The bead at the needle’s tip had begun, very faintly, to glow.

He was so busy staring at it that he did not see the small figure coming the other way until it bumped hard into his elbow.

“Oi! Mind yourself, mister!”

It was a girl, a sweep by the look of her, small and thin and black with soot from head to heel. Her hair was cut short and ragged, as if somebody had done it with a knife in the dark. She had a sharp chin and quick eyes, and for half a moment those eyes looked straight into his. Then she was gone round the corner.

“I do beg your pardon,” Tobin called after her, because he had been brought up properly.

Then he put his hand in his pocket, and the compass was not there.

Now, I would like to tell you that Wren Ashby had not meant to rob him. But this is a true story, and so I had better tell you instead that she had meant it very much indeed.

She had seen him coming: a proper Hill nob, with clean ears and a shiny thing in his hand. She had wanted the shiny thing. But the shiny thing was in his hand, and his other pocket was hanging open like a mouth, and inside it something gleamed gold. Wren had not stopped to think. She never did. Thinking was for people who could afford to wait.

It was a fine piece, heavy and smooth and round. Gold, maybe. Grubb would give her five crowns for it, or he would have, if he had not thrown her out of his shop, the old weasel. Somebody else would, then. A week of suppers, for her and Nettle both. Two weeks if she was clever.

“Stop! Thief! Stop!”

Wren grinned. Nobs always shouted “Stop!”, as though anybody ever had.

She went up a water-butt, over a lean-to, and onto the long slate roof of the rope-maker’s, and there she slowed, because there was no need to hurry now. No nob alive could follow her across the roofs of Soot Lane. These were her roads. She knew every loose slate and rotten gutter, every chimney-stack you could hide behind and every gap you could jump. She turned at the ridge to have a last look at him, and her mouth fell open.

He was coming up the water-butt.

He did it badly, with a sound like a sack of pans falling down a stair, and he very nearly fell off twice. But he did it. He hauled himself onto the lean-to and stood there wobbling with his arms out, and then he looked straight up at her and pointed.

“That,” he called, “is mine. And it is not gold, if that’s what you’re thinking. It’s brass. Gilded brass. It would barely fetch—“

“Rot!” shouted Wren, and ran.

She leapt the gap to the cooper’s roof, slid down his slates, dropped onto the flat top of the old wash-house and ran again. Behind her she heard a clatter and a yelp. She went up a drainpipe and round two chimney-stacks, and only then did she stop and listen.

Nothing. Only the wind in the flues, and somebody’s baby crying in a room below.

“Great lump,” she said, pleased with herself, and went on more slowly towards the Nest.

What Wren did not know, and what Tobin himself only half believed, was that she had a light in her coat that could be followed through the dark like a bonfire on a hill.

Tobin had fallen off the rope-maker’s roof into a cart of wet sacking. He lay there a moment, thinking that his father would certainly have something to say about this. Then he remembered Flicker, and found it still in his fist, its glass unbroken.

The needle was pointing up and to the left. Not along the lane, where any sensible person would run. Up. Over the roofs. And the little bead was brighter than before.

“Oh,” said Tobin slowly. “Oh. That’s interesting.”

He did not go back up the water-butt; he had learned that he was not much good at water-butts. Instead he looked about him, the way he looked at a broken clock before he opened it, and he saw what Wren had never had to notice, because she had always had her own feet to trust: the washing lines. They ran across the lane from window to window and roof to roof, dozens of them, tied off to iron hooks and chimney-pots, sagging under their loads of shirts.

“Tension,” murmured Tobin, “and the coefficient of — no. No, don’t think about it. Just do it.”

He found an outside stair, climbed it to a first-floor landing, took hold of the stoutest line he could see, and swung himself out over the lane hand over hand. The line dipped alarmingly. A wet stocking slapped him in the face. A shirt wrapped itself lovingly round his head, so that for several terrible seconds he was hanging in mid-air in the dark with no idea which way was up. Then his boots struck slate, and he let go, and sat down very hard on the far roof in a heap of somebody’s sheets.

He was not hurt. He was, he realised, almost laughing. He checked Flicker again, and went on.

The Nest was a hollow between two chimney-stacks on the oldest house in Soot Lane. The stacks kept it a little warm, and from it you could see the whole Low Quarter while nobody in the Low Quarter could see you. Nettle was waiting there, as she always was at this hour, curled up like a cat in a nest of old sacks.

“Wren!” Nettle sat up. She was seven, and small for seven, with a face so freckled it looked as if somebody had flicked a paintbrush at it, and two gaps where her front teeth had been. “You’re late. I’ve been waiting ageth.”

“Ages,” said Wren. “Budge up.”

She sat down, and pulled from inside her coat a heel of bread, which was all the supper there was going to be tonight. It was not a large heel. Wren looked at it. Then she broke it in two, very carefully, and gave Nettle the bigger half.

“Ith that the betht bit?”

“It’s the bit you’re getting. Eat it before I change my mind.”

Nettle ate it. Wren ate the smaller half, slowly, to make it last. She had just put the last crumb into her mouth when a voice behind her said, rather breathlessly, “Excuse me.”

Wren went up like a scalded cat. She was on her feet in an instant with her back to the chimney-stack and Nettle pushed behind her, and there was the nob, standing on the ridge-tiles not three yards away. He had a sheet over one shoulder and a stocking caught on one ear. His spectacles were crooked. In one hand he held his shiny watch-thing, and its little glass eye was glowing like a coal.

“How?” said Wren. “How did you — nobody follows me. Nobody can.”

“I wasn’t following you, exactly,” said the nob. “Well. I was. But I couldn’t have, actually, if you’d kept running. You’d have lost me in another two roofs. I only caught up because you stopped.” He looked at Nettle, and then at the empty place in Wren’s hand where the bread had been, and something in his face changed. “You stopped to give her your supper.”

Wren felt her face go hot under the soot, which made her angrier than anything.

“Mind your own business,” she said.

“I’m sorry. I didn’t mean — it’s only that you gave her the bigger piece. I saw you.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “My name is Tobin Harrowgate. I would like my compass back, please.”

“What compass?”

“The one in your pocket, Wren,” said Nettle helpfully, from behind her.

Wren closed her eyes. “Thank you, Nettle.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Harrowgate,” said Wren, opening them again. “Harrowgate like the Warden?”

“He’s my father.”

“Then you can buy yourself another one, can’t you? Your dad’s got a whole Hall full of gold. I’ve seen it. Well. I’ve seen the outside of it.”

“It’s not about the gold.” The boy’s voice wobbled, very slightly, and he steadied it. “It was my mother’s. She gave it to me. It has words inside the lid. Look, if you like. It says Home is where the light is.”

Wren did not look. Words like that got inside you, and then you could not sell a thing at all. She kept her hand clamped round the compass and said nothing, and the wind came round the stack and made them both shiver.

Then the boy took out a second thing from his coat, a small glass night-lamp with a little painted border, and lit it with a match. His hands were shaking so badly that it took him three matches. The flame that came up was small and yellowish and smelled of Guild oil.

“Scared of the dark, are you?” said Wren. “A big lump like you?”

“I am not scared,” said Tobin. “I’m being practical. It’s getting dark. Light is practical.” Then, because he was an honest boy even when it was inconvenient: “Also, yes. A bit.”

And that was when he saw it.

Next to his night-lamp, something else was shining. It came through the girl’s coat, through the rough cloth over her ribs, a soft golden glow that made his own little flame look grey and sickly beside it. In that glow, he saw that she had a ribbon tied round her left wrist. And the ribbon was not grey. It was not brown. It was a colour Tobin had seen in only one place in his whole life: in a single faded picture in his mother’s old songbook, a picture of a rose.

“What,” he said, “have you got in your coat?”

“Nothing.”

“You have. It’s glowing. I can see it glowing.” He held up Flicker. The needle was no longer trembling. It pointed at her, steady as a finger, and the bead at its tip blazed. “That’s it. That’s what I followed. Not you. That.”

“There’s nothing in my coat but me,” said Wren, and stepped back, and her heel came up against the low brick lip at the edge of the Nest.

Beyond the Nest, past the last roofs of Soot Lane, rose the great dark line of the city wall. And on the wall, perhaps a hundred yards away, stood one of the old Ring-lamps of the Low Quarter. It was an iron cage on a stone post, and inside it, for as long as Wren could remember, a smoky little flame had burned, dimmer every winter. Nobody ever looked at it. It was just there, like the canal and the cold.

As Wren stepped to the edge, it flared.

It was only the sort of brightening a candle gives when you open a door. But Tobin saw it, and Wren saw it too. The old lamp jumped up bright and yellow, brighter than it had been in years, and stayed bright as long as she stood there. When she stepped back, uneasily, into the shelter of the stack, it sank down again.

Tobin’s mouth was open.

“It’s you,” he said. “The bright bead. It’s you.”

“What bead? What are you on about?”

“I’ve got a — well, it’s a sort of model. Of the Ring. Of the whole wall, all hundred and forty-four lamps, in brass, with a bead for each one, joined by copper wires, and the beads warm up when the lamps burn, it’s a matter of sympathetic resonance, I’ll explain it properly another time — and then there was a new bead. A bright one. Brighter than any of the others. Only there isn’t a Ring-lamp in Soot Lane. And it was moving.” He was talking faster and faster. “I watched it wander about the Low Quarter. I watched it go down to the canal and back. And I thought it must be a fault in the wiring, but it isn’t, is it? It’s whatever you’ve got in your coat. And whatever it is, it makes the Ring burn brighter.”

Wren stared at him. “Do you always talk like a book falling down the stairs?”

“Mostly,” Tobin admitted. “Especially when I’m nervous. Can I see it?”

“No.”

“Please?”

“No. And you’re not having your compass back neither.”

“Neither — well, technically, that’s a double negative, which means I am —“

“Rot!” said Wren. “Look. Things cost. Everything costs. You want your compass, what’s it worth to you?”

Tobin felt in his pockets. He had a pencil, a screwdriver, two matches and half a page of calculations. It had never once occurred to him that he might need money.

“I haven’t got anything,” he said.

“Then you haven’t got a compass.” Wren folded her arms. “Bring me a sausage. A proper one, a Hill one, with meat in it. Bring one for Nettle and all. Then maybe we’ll talk.”

“That’s extortion.”

“I don’t know what that is, so I can’t be doing it. Finders keepers.”

“You didn’t find it! You took it out of my pocket!”

“Took it, found it.” Wren shrugged. “Same thing in Soot Lane.”

Tobin opened his mouth to argue, and closed it again, and opened it, and then he stopped, because Nettle had stood up in her nest of sacks and was looking past both of them, out over the wall.

“Wren,” she said, in a very small voice. “Wren, look.”

The wind had dropped. That was the first thing Wren noticed: the wind had dropped, all at once, as if a door had been shut somewhere. And in its place came a cold. Not the ordinary cold of a Soot Lane evening, which she had known all her life and could put up with. This was a different cold. It came over the top of the wall the way water comes over the lip of a basin, slow and heavy, and it made her teeth ache.

From the Nest you could just see over the wall to a grey strip of the Greywaste, with its dead grass and black trees. There was never anything there.

There was something there now.

There were shapes out on the plain. Grey shapes, a little paler than the grey dark around them, so that at first you could not be sure you were seeing them at all. They were shaped something like people. But they did not walk like people. They drifted, the way smoke drifts when there is no wind to push it, and they had no faces that Wren could see — only a smoothness where faces ought to be. There were five. No, there were more than five. There were twenty. There were more than she could count, and they were all moving the same way, slowly, silently, across the dead grass.

Towards the wall. Towards the Ring.

Towards the Low Quarter.

On the wall, the old Ring-lamp shuddered in its iron cage, though there was no wind to shake it.

Tobin’s night-lamp rattled in his hand. He did not even notice. Inside Wren’s coat, against her ribs, the brass lamp she had found in the flue grew warm, and then warmer, as though it, too, had seen.

Nobody spoke. Every child in Emberwick had heard the stories grown-ups told to make you come home before dark — and had been told, in the same breath, that nothing had come over the Ring for a hundred years.

It was Nettle who said it in the end. She said it in a whisper, with her cold little hand wrapped tight round Wren’s.

“Hollowth.”
fields.body_text: Some people look as if they could belong anywhere. Others look as if they belong in exactly one place and nowhere else at all. Tobin Harrowgate was the second sort, and if you had seen him that evening, picking his way down off the Hill and into the Low Quarter, you would have known at once that he had come from somewhere with carpets. It was not his clothes. He had put on his oldest coat, the brown one with the darned elbow, and had even rubbed a smear of soot onto one cheek, because he had read that this was what one did to pass unnoticed. It was everything else. It was the way he walked, as if the cobbles might be counted later and he wanted to be sure of the number. It was his spectacles, which flashed at every lit window. It was the way he said “I beg your pardon” to a dog. And it was the thing in his hand. It was a pocket-watch case with the watch taken out of it. Where the hands and numbers should have been, a single copper needle balanced on a pin, and on the tip of the needle sat a glass bead no bigger than a lentil, taken from the box of spares he kept under the Orrery. He had spent a feverish quarter of an hour making it before he left, and the whole of the back stairs trying to think of a name for it, and in the end he had scratched FLICKER on the lid, because PORTABLE THERMO-SYMPATHETIC LOCATING INDICATOR would not fit. The principle, as Tobin would have been very glad to tell you, was simple. The beads on the Orrery warmed in sympathy with the Ring-lamps they stood for. A bead cut loose and set on a pivot ought, therefore, to swing towards whatever burned brightest nearby, the way a sunflower was said to turn towards the sun. Nobody in Emberwick had seen a sunflower for a very long time. But the theory was sound. The theory had felt a great deal sounder in his warm attic than it did now. In Gloamhaven, of course, the whole day is a kind of evening. But there is a time, after the pale sun has given up altogether and before the real dark comes, when the light goes thin and blue and everything looks as though it is standing a long way off. The old word for it is the gloaming. It was the gloaming now, and in the gloaming the Low Quarter looked very low indeed. The houses leaned towards each other over the crooked lanes like old women sharing a secret. Washing lines zigzagged overhead, hung with shirts the colour of dishwater. The air smelled of tanneries and cabbage and soot. Two girls on a doorstep stopped their clapping game to stare. A woman with a basket of turnips looked him up and down, slowly, from his clean boots to his combed hair. “Lost, are we, your lordship?” she said. “Oh, no,” said Tobin. “Well, yes, in a geographical sense, but not in the sense you mean. And technically I’m not a lordship. My father is the Warden, which is an appointed office, not a hereditary—“ The two girls on the doorstep burst out laughing. Tobin went red to the tips of his ears and hurried on. In his other coat pocket, the one that did not hold his mother’s compass, was his mother’s little night-lamp. He had blown it out at the foot of the Hill, so as not to be stared at, and promised himself that he would only light it again if it became truly dark. It was not truly dark yet. He kept one hand on it all the same, and felt the cool glass under his fingers, and told himself firmly that he was not frightened, he was merely gathering data. Flicker’s needle trembled. Then it swung, slowly but quite definitely, down a lane to his left. A crooked sign on the corner said SOOT LANE. “There you are,” Tobin whispered. The bead at the needle’s tip had begun, very faintly, to glow. He was so busy staring at it that he did not see the small figure coming the other way until it bumped hard into his elbow. “Oi! Mind yourself, mister!” It was a girl, a sweep by the look of her, small and thin and black with soot from head to heel. Her hair was cut short and ragged, as if somebody had done it with a knife in the dark. She had a sharp chin and quick eyes, and for half a moment those eyes looked straight into his. Then she was gone round the corner. “I do beg your pardon,” Tobin called after her, because he had been brought up properly. Then he put his hand in his pocket, and the compass was not there. Now, I would like to tell you that Wren Ashby had not meant to rob him. But this is a true story, and so I had better tell you instead that she had meant it very much indeed. She had seen him coming: a proper Hill nob, with clean ears and a shiny thing in his hand. She had wanted the shiny thing. But the shiny thing was in his hand, and his other pocket was hanging open like a mouth, and inside it something gleamed gold. Wren had not stopped to think. She never did. Thinking was for people who could afford to wait. It was a fine piece, heavy and smooth and round. Gold, maybe. Grubb would give her five crowns for it, or he would have, if he had not thrown her out of his shop, the old weasel. Somebody else would, then. A week of suppers, for her and Nettle both. Two weeks if she was clever. “Stop! Thief! Stop!” Wren grinned. Nobs always shouted “Stop!”, as though anybody ever had. She went up a water-butt, over a lean-to, and onto the long slate roof of the rope-maker’s, and there she slowed, because there was no need to hurry now. No nob alive could follow her across the roofs of Soot Lane. These were her roads. She knew every loose slate and rotten gutter, every chimney-stack you could hide behind and every gap you could jump. She turned at the ridge to have a last look at him, and her mouth fell open. He was coming up the water-butt. He did it badly, with a sound like a sack of pans falling down a stair, and he very nearly fell off twice. But he did it. He hauled himself onto the lean-to and stood there wobbling with his arms out, and then he looked straight up at her and pointed. “That,” he called, “is mine. And it is not gold, if that’s what you’re thinking. It’s brass. Gilded brass. It would barely fetch—“ “Rot!” shouted Wren, and ran. She leapt the gap to the cooper’s roof, slid down his slates, dropped onto the flat top of the old wash-house and ran again. Behind her she heard a clatter and a yelp. She went up a drainpipe and round two chimney-stacks, and only then did she stop and listen. Nothing. Only the wind in the flues, and somebody’s baby crying in a room below. “Great lump,” she said, pleased with herself, and went on more slowly towards the Nest. What Wren did not know, and what Tobin himself only half believed, was that she had a light in her coat that could be followed through the dark like a bonfire on a hill. Tobin had fallen off the rope-maker’s roof into a cart of wet sacking. He lay there a moment, thinking that his father would certainly have something to say about this. Then he remembered Flicker, and found it still in his fist, its glass unbroken. The needle was pointing up and to the left. Not along the lane, where any sensible person would run. Up. Over the roofs. And the little bead was brighter than before. “Oh,” said Tobin slowly. “Oh. That’s interesting.” He did not go back up the water-butt; he had learned that he was not much good at water-butts. Instead he looked about him, the way he looked at a broken clock before he opened it, and he saw what Wren had never had to notice, because she had always had her own feet to trust: the washing lines. They ran across the lane from window to window and roof to roof, dozens of them, tied off to iron hooks and chimney-pots, sagging under their loads of shirts. “Tension,” murmured Tobin, “and the coefficient of — no. No, don’t think about it. Just do it.” He found an outside stair, climbed it to a first-floor landing, took hold of the stoutest line he could see, and swung himself out over the lane hand over hand. The line dipped alarmingly. A wet stocking slapped him in the face. A shirt wrapped itself lovingly round his head, so that for several terrible seconds he was hanging in mid-air in the dark with no idea which way was up. Then his boots struck slate, and he let go, and sat down very hard on the far roof in a heap of somebody’s sheets. He was not hurt. He was, he realised, almost laughing. He checked Flicker again, and went on. The Nest was a hollow between two chimney-stacks on the oldest house in Soot Lane. The stacks kept it a little warm, and from it you could see the whole Low Quarter while nobody in the Low Quarter could see you. Nettle was waiting there, as she always was at this hour, curled up like a cat in a nest of old sacks. “Wren!” Nettle sat up. She was seven, and small for seven, with a face so freckled it looked as if somebody had flicked a paintbrush at it, and two gaps where her front teeth had been. “You’re late. I’ve been waiting ageth.” “Ages,” said Wren. “Budge up.” She sat down, and pulled from inside her coat a heel of bread, which was all the supper there was going to be tonight. It was not a large heel. Wren looked at it. Then she broke it in two, very carefully, and gave Nettle the bigger half. “Ith that the betht bit?” “It’s the bit you’re getting. Eat it before I change my mind.” Nettle ate it. Wren ate the smaller half, slowly, to make it last. She had just put the last crumb into her mouth when a voice behind her said, rather breathlessly, “Excuse me.” Wren went up like a scalded cat. She was on her feet in an instant with her back to the chimney-stack and Nettle pushed behind her, and there was the nob, standing on the ridge-tiles not three yards away. He had a sheet over one shoulder and a stocking caught on one ear. His spectacles were crooked. In one hand he held his shiny watch-thing, and its little glass eye was glowing like a coal. “How?” said Wren. “How did you — nobody follows me. Nobody can.” “I wasn’t following you, exactly,” said the nob. “Well. I was. But I couldn’t have, actually, if you’d kept running. You’d have lost me in another two roofs. I only caught up because you stopped.” He looked at Nettle, and then at the empty place in Wren’s hand where the bread had been, and something in his face changed. “You stopped to give her your supper.” Wren felt her face go hot under the soot, which made her angrier than anything. “Mind your own business,” she said. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean — it’s only that you gave her the bigger piece. I saw you.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “My name is Tobin Harrowgate. I would like my compass back, please.” “What compass?” “The one in your pocket, Wren,” said Nettle helpfully, from behind her. Wren closed her eyes. “Thank you, Nettle.” “You’re welcome.” “Harrowgate,” said Wren, opening them again. “Harrowgate like the Warden?” “He’s my father.” “Then you can buy yourself another one, can’t you? Your dad’s got a whole Hall full of gold. I’ve seen it. Well. I’ve seen the outside of it.” “It’s not about the gold.” The boy’s voice wobbled, very slightly, and he steadied it. “It was my mother’s. She gave it to me. It has words inside the lid. Look, if you like. It says Home is where the light is.” Wren did not look. Words like that got inside you, and then you could not sell a thing at all. She kept her hand clamped round the compass and said nothing, and the wind came round the stack and made them both shiver. Then the boy took out a second thing from his coat, a small glass night-lamp with a little painted border, and lit it with a match. His hands were shaking so badly that it took him three matches. The flame that came up was small and yellowish and smelled of Guild oil. “Scared of the dark, are you?” said Wren. “A big lump like you?” “I am not scared,” said Tobin. “I’m being practical. It’s getting dark. Light is practical.” Then, because he was an honest boy even when it was inconvenient: “Also, yes. A bit.” And that was when he saw it. Next to his night-lamp, something else was shining. It came through the girl’s coat, through the rough cloth over her ribs, a soft golden glow that made his own little flame look grey and sickly beside it. In that glow, he saw that she had a ribbon tied round her left wrist. And the ribbon was not grey. It was not brown. It was a colour Tobin had seen in only one place in his whole life: in a single faded picture in his mother’s old songbook, a picture of a rose. “What,” he said, “have you got in your coat?” “Nothing.” “You have. It’s glowing. I can see it glowing.” He held up Flicker. The needle was no longer trembling. It pointed at her, steady as a finger, and the bead at its tip blazed. “That’s it. That’s what I followed. Not you. That.” “There’s nothing in my coat but me,” said Wren, and stepped back, and her heel came up against the low brick lip at the edge of the Nest. Beyond the Nest, past the last roofs of Soot Lane, rose the great dark line of the city wall. And on the wall, perhaps a hundred yards away, stood one of the old Ring-lamps of the Low Quarter. It was an iron cage on a stone post, and inside it, for as long as Wren could remember, a smoky little flame had burned, dimmer every winter. Nobody ever looked at it. It was just there, like the canal and the cold. As Wren stepped to the edge, it flared. It was only the sort of brightening a candle gives when you open a door. But Tobin saw it, and Wren saw it too. The old lamp jumped up bright and yellow, brighter than it had been in years, and stayed bright as long as she stood there. When she stepped back, uneasily, into the shelter of the stack, it sank down again. Tobin’s mouth was open. “It’s you,” he said. “The bright bead. It’s you.” “What bead? What are you on about?” “I’ve got a — well, it’s a sort of model. Of the Ring. Of the whole wall, all hundred and forty-four lamps, in brass, with a bead for each one, joined by copper wires, and the beads warm up when the lamps burn, it’s a matter of sympathetic resonance, I’ll explain it properly another time — and then there was a new bead. A bright one. Brighter than any of the others. Only there isn’t a Ring-lamp in Soot Lane. And it was moving.” He was talking faster and faster. “I watched it wander about the Low Quarter. I watched it go down to the canal and back. And I thought it must be a fault in the wiring, but it isn’t, is it? It’s whatever you’ve got in your coat. And whatever it is, it makes the Ring burn brighter.” Wren stared at him. “Do you always talk like a book falling down the stairs?” “Mostly,” Tobin admitted. “Especially when I’m nervous. Can I see it?” “No.” “Please?” “No. And you’re not having your compass back neither.” “Neither — well, technically, that’s a double negative, which means I am —“ “Rot!” said Wren. “Look. Things cost. Everything costs. You want your compass, what’s it worth to you?” Tobin felt in his pockets. He had a pencil, a screwdriver, two matches and half a page of calculations. It had never once occurred to him that he might need money. “I haven’t got anything,” he said. “Then you haven’t got a compass.” Wren folded her arms. “Bring me a sausage. A proper one, a Hill one, with meat in it. Bring one for Nettle and all. Then maybe we’ll talk.” “That’s extortion.” “I don’t know what that is, so I can’t be doing it. Finders keepers.” “You didn’t find it! You took it out of my pocket!” “Took it, found it.” Wren shrugged. “Same thing in Soot Lane.” Tobin opened his mouth to argue, and closed it again, and opened it, and then he stopped, because Nettle had stood up in her nest of sacks and was looking past both of them, out over the wall. “Wren,” she said, in a very small voice. “Wren, look.” The wind had dropped. That was the first thing Wren noticed: the wind had dropped, all at once, as if a door had been shut somewhere. And in its place came a cold. Not the ordinary cold of a Soot Lane evening, which she had known all her life and could put up with. This was a different cold. It came over the top of the wall the way water comes over the lip of a basin, slow and heavy, and it made her teeth ache. From the Nest you could just see over the wall to a grey strip of the Greywaste, with its dead grass and black trees. There was never anything there. There was something there now. There were shapes out on the plain. Grey shapes, a little paler than the grey dark around them, so that at first you could not be sure you were seeing them at all. They were shaped something like people. But they did not walk like people. They drifted, the way smoke drifts when there is no wind to push it, and they had no faces that Wren could see — only a smoothness where faces ought to be. There were five. No, there were more than five. There were twenty. There were more than she could count, and they were all moving the same way, slowly, silently, across the dead grass. Towards the wall. Towards the Ring. Towards the Low Quarter. On the wall, the old Ring-lamp shuddered in its iron cage, though there was no wind to shake it. Tobin’s night-lamp rattled in his hand. He did not even notice. Inside Wren’s coat, against her ribs, the brass lamp she had found in the flue grew warm, and then warmer, as though it, too, had seen. Nobody spoke. Every child in Emberwick had heard the stories grown-ups told to make you come home before dark — and had been told, in the same breath, that nothing had come over the Ring for a hundred years. It was Nettle who said it in the end. She said it in a whisper, with her cold little hand wrapped tight round Wren’s. “Hollowth.”

fields.title: Over the Wall
fields.body_html:
Market day in Soot Lane happened every Thursday, and it was the only day of the week when the Low Quarter was loud for a good reason.

By the middle of the morning the lane was packed from wall to wall. There were barrows of small hard apples, a man selling second-hand boots that were really only one boot, and a woman with a cage of hens who all looked as if they had been told bad news. There was a knife-grinder whose wheel threw out sparks, a fiddler with three strings, and a Guild oil-cart with a little painted sign on the side that said GUILD OIL — ONE PENNY THE MEASURE — FLAME TOKENS TWO A PENNY, BLESSED AT THE BEACON. The oil-man, whose name was Tallis, had a voice like a rusty gate and sold a great many tokens, for people in the Low Quarter were frightened of the dark and two a penny is cheap for courage.

And in the middle of it all, with its door propped open and its window steamed up, stood Mrs Fenn’s bakery.

You could smell Mrs Fenn’s bakery from the canal. It was the only good smell in Soot Lane, and people walking past would stop and close their eyes and breathe it in, as if it were a sort of breakfast. For most of them it was the only kind they got.

Wren and Nettle were sitting on the step, which was where they always sat on market days, because Mrs Fenn always came out sooner or later.

“Now then,” said Mrs Fenn, coming out. She was a wide, soft, floury woman with arms like bread rolls and a face as round and kind as a loaf. There was flour in her hair and flour on her apron and, somehow, flour on the tip of her nose. “Now then, you two sparrows. I’ve some crusts here going begging. Burnt, mind. Can’t sell ‘em. You’d be doing me a favour.”

They were not burnt. They were never burnt. Wren knew that, and Mrs Fenn knew that Wren knew it, and neither of them ever said so.

“Ta, Mrs Fenn,” said Wren, and took them.

“Thank you, Mithith Fenn,” said Nettle.

“Bless you, duck.” Mrs Fenn turned to shout into the shop. “Pip! Hettie! Mind that oven! Sam, put your sister down, she’s not a sack of flour — Molly, where’s your brother? Where’s the baby? Who’s got Jem?”

“I’ve got Jem, Mum!”

“Well, don’t drop him!”

There were five Fenn children, always everywhere at once. Pip was ten and very serious about bread. Hettie was eight and sang all day. Sam was six and liked to carry things that did not want to be carried, such as his sisters. Molly was four, and Jem was a baby, and Wren sometimes thought the bakery must be the warmest place in Emberwick.

Wren was halfway through her second crust when a shadow fell across the step, and she looked up, and groaned.

“Good morning,” said Tobin Harrowgate.

He had clearly tried to make his hair untidy and had only managed to comb it in a slightly different direction. He was holding something wrapped in a white linen napkin. People were staring at the napkin. Nobody in Soot Lane had ever owned a napkin.

“You again,” said Wren. “Haven’t you got a Hall to go and sit in?”

“I’ve brought the sausages,” said Tobin.

He unfolded the napkin. There lay two fat brown sausages, still faintly warm, smelling of pepper and onions and a great deal of meat. Nettle made a small noise like a kettle starting to boil.

Wren looked at the sausages for a long moment. Then she looked at Tobin.

“You actually brought them.”

“You said to. A proper one, a Hill one, with meat in it, and one for Nettle. I took them off the breakfast sideboard. I hope that’s all right. It isn’t stealing, technically, because they’re my father’s sausages, and I’m his son, so in a sense they’re partly mine, and anyway I didn’t eat my own breakfast, so the household is exactly level—“

“Give,” said Wren.

He gave. She handed one to Nettle and bit into the other, and for a moment the whole world was sausage. It was the best thing she had ever tasted. She would never have said so.

“So,” said Tobin hopefully. “My compass?”

Wren swallowed. “That,” she said, “was the down payment.”

“The what?”

“The first bit. Sausages, that’s the first bit. Now we talk about the rest.”

“You said bring sausages and then maybe we’ll talk. This is talking!”

“Then we’re getting on lovely,” said Wren, and licked her fingers.

Tobin opened his mouth. Then he did something she had not expected. He laughed. It was a short, surprised laugh, as if it had come out without asking, and he looked rather startled by it himself.

“You are,” he said, “the most unreasonable person I have ever met.”

“You should get out more,” said Wren. But she found, a little to her annoyance, that she was almost smiling.

He stayed. He followed her up and down the market asking questions — where had she found it, did it ever go out, what did it burn, had she weighed it — and at last, in the alley behind the bakery, mostly to make him stop talking, she opened her coat for half a second and let him look.

The lamp lay against her ribs, small and dented, its glass chimney cracked, its golden flame no bigger than a fingernail. And in its light the grey alley changed. The bricks were not grey. They were a deep dusty colour, warm as a fox. The moss between them was not grey either. And Tobin’s own hands, held up in front of him, were pink.

Wren shut her coat. The alley went grey again.

Tobin did not say anything at all. It was the first time she had known him not to.

It happened in the late afternoon, when the market was packing up.

The first thing Wren noticed was the dogs. All at once every dog in Soot Lane stopped nosing for scraps and stood stiff, staring at the wall. Then one by one they put their tails between their legs and slunk away under the carts.

The second thing she noticed was the lamps.

Along the stretch of city wall that ran behind Soot Lane stood five of the old Ring-lamps, the same tired iron cages she had seen from the Nest the night before. As she watched, the nearest one dipped. Its flame shrank down to a blue bead, then rose again, smoky and thin. Then the next lamp did the same, and the next. It looked as if something were blowing on them, very softly, from the other side. But there was no wind at all.

“Wren,” said Tobin, behind her. His voice had gone high. “Wren, the lamps.”

“I see them.”

Then came the cold.

It came over the wall as it had the evening before, only this time it poured down. It rolled over the battlements in a long white-grey wave, like fog off the canal on a winter morning, but heavier and slower than any fog, and it slid down the stones and spread along the ground and came creeping in between the market stalls. Where it touched, frost bloomed on the cobbles. A puddle went white with a small, hard crack. The fiddler’s last note died away in the middle, and he did not start another.

And then everything was quiet.

If you have ever been in a crowded place that has suddenly gone silent — a schoolroom when the master walks in, or a kitchen when somebody has dropped the best dish — you will know that kind of quiet, the kind where everybody is holding their breath at the same moment. This was like that, except that it went on and on. Nobody moved. Nobody spoke. A whole street full of people stood in the cold fog with their breath smoking, and looked up at the wall.

The Hollows came over it.

They did not climb. They poured over the top like smoke poured into a jug, ran down the stones, and at the bottom gathered themselves up into shapes. Tall shapes, grey shapes, shaped like men and women and yet not like them, because where their faces should have been there was nothing at all, only a dim smooth greyness, like the inside of a cloud. They made no sound. Their feet, if they had feet, did not touch the ground. They drifted forward into the market, one and then three and then a dozen, and the cold came with them, so bitter that Wren’s eyes watered and the water froze on her lashes.

Then somebody screamed, and everybody ran.

This is the part of the story that Wren never liked to tell. She told it once, years later, and stopped halfway, and would not go on. So I shall tell it for her, as gently as I can.

Barrows went over. Apples bounced across the frosted cobbles. The hen-woman’s cage burst open and hens went flapping in every direction. Mothers snatched up children, and doors slammed all along Soot Lane.

And through it all the Hollows drifted, slowly, never hurrying, as if they had all the time in the world.

Wren saw the knife-grinder, who had stayed too long by his wheel, turn round and find one standing right behind him. It did not strike him. It only reached out one long grey hand and laid it on his shoulder, almost kindly, the way a friend might. And the colour went out of him. There had not been much colour in the knife-grinder to begin with — a little brown in his coat, a little ruddiness in his cheeks — but what there was drained out of him the way water drains out of a basin, and he went grey all over, grey face, grey hands, grey hair. He did not cry out. He sat down, quite slowly, on his own upturned wheel, and folded his hands in his lap, and looked at nothing.

Everywhere the Hollows passed, the colour went. The faded awnings went grey. The few small apples went grey. The bread in the bakery window, which had been the brown of good crust, went the colour of old stone.

“Inside!” Mrs Fenn was in her doorway, shooing children like hens. “Pip, inside! Hettie, Sam, in, in, in! Molly — Jem — where’s —“

“I’ve got Jem, Mum!”

“Then get him in!”

Wren had Nettle by the hand. She was dragging her towards the bakery, because the bakery was close and the bakery had a door, and Tobin was stumbling along beside them with his little night-lamp held out in front of him in both hands. He had lit it. Wren did not know when. Its small yellow flame shook as if it were as frightened as he was.

A Hollow drifted out of the fog to their left. It turned its blank face towards them.

Tobin stopped. Wren saw his knees shake. She saw his teeth chattering, and his spectacles misting over with cold. And she saw him step sideways, not away from the Hollow but towards it, so that he was standing between it and little Molly Fenn, who had tripped on the step and was sitting there in the frost, too frightened to cry.

“G-go away,” said Tobin. “P-please. G-g-go away.”

He held up the night-lamp. The Hollow paused. The oil-light did not hurt it; Wren could see that. But it did not like the light. It hung there in the fog, swaying, and did not come closer, and Pip darted out, scooped up his little sister and bolted inside with her.

Mrs Fenn was still in the doorway, counting. Wren could see her lips moving. One, two, three, four —

She did not see the Hollow come up behind her out of the alley.

“Mrs Fenn!” Wren shouted. “Behind you —“

Mrs Fenn turned round. And the Hollow put out its long grey hand and touched her, very gently, on the cheek.

That was all. It was such a small thing. And then the Hollow drifted on past, as if it had done nothing much, and was gone into the fog.

Mrs Fenn stood quite still in her doorway. The flour on her apron, which had been white, went grey. Her round pink face went grey. Even her eyes, which had been a soft kind brown, faded until they were the colour of rain on a window. Then she sat down on her own step, quite slowly, the way the knife-grinder had, and put her grey hands in her grey lap.

“Mum?” Pip had come back to the door. He had Jem in his arms. “Mum, come inside. Mum?”

Mrs Fenn looked up at him. Her face was not frightened. That was the worst of it. It was polite and puzzled and gentle, the face of someone who has been asked the way by a stranger and does not know the town.

“Hello, dear,” she said. “Are you lost?”

Pip stared at her.

“It’s me,” he said. “Mum. It’s me. It’s Pip.”

“Pip,” said Mrs Fenn. She said it carefully, as though it were a word in a foreign language, and she was not sure she had it right. “Pip. That’s a nice name.” She frowned a little, and looked down at her hands. “I think I had some children. Didn’t I? I’m sure I had some children. I can’t think what I called them.”

Behind Pip, in the doorway, Hettie began to cry. Mrs Fenn did not turn round. She only sat on her step, in the cold, looking at nothing, and smiled a small, faint, faraway smile.

Wren had seen a great many bad things in her twelve years. She had never seen anything like this. It went into her like a nail.

And while she was standing there, a cold breath touched the back of her neck.

She turned. Nettle had let go of her hand. Nettle had run to Mrs Fenn — of course she had, Nettle always ran to anybody who was sad — and was patting her grey arm and saying, “Mithith Fenn? Mithith Fenn, it’th all right,” in her small lisping voice. And behind Nettle, rising up out of the fog, taller than the bakery door, was a Hollow.

It bent over her. It reached out one long grey hand towards the top of her freckled head.

Wren did not think. Afterwards, she could never remember deciding anything at all. She only knew that her hand was inside her coat, and then her hand was out of her coat, and there was the lamp in it, held out at arm’s length, and she was shouting something — she never knew what — at the top of her voice.

The lamp flared.

It was not the small warm glow she knew. It was white. It was white-gold, blazing, as if somebody had opened the door of a great furnace in the middle of Soot Lane, and it threw her shadow and Nettle’s and Mrs Fenn’s far down the street behind them. The fog went up in a great rushing billow like steam off a kettle. The frost on the cobbles ran to water. And for one long moment, in a circle all round her, the colour came back into the world: the bricks warm as a fox, the spilled apples suddenly, impossibly, red as her ribbon, and Nettle’s freckles a bright and glorious gold.

The Hollow screamed.

It was the only sound Wren ever heard a Hollow make, and she never forgot it: a high, thin, tearing shriek, like wind through a broken window, that came out of no mouth at all. It reeled back from the light with its grey hands thrown up over its blank face. And all down Soot Lane, the other Hollows shrieked too, every one of them, a dreadful rising chorus, and they turned and fled. They fled back the way they had come, pouring up the wall like smoke going backwards up a chimney, and over the top, and away into the Greywaste.

All but one.

The last of them stopped at the top of the wall. It turned. It did not have eyes, so it could not look at her. But Wren knew, the way you know when somebody behind you in a crowd is staring, that it was looking at her. At the lamp. It held there, a grey shape against the grey sky, for one long, cold moment.

Then it was gone.

Slowly the lamp sank back to its small golden glow. Slowly the colour went out of the apples again, and the bricks went grey. The fog was gone. The cold was going. Wren’s arm was shaking so much she could hardly hold the lamp up.

It was very quiet again in Soot Lane. But it was a different quiet now.

Wren looked up at the wall. Behind Soot Lane the five old Ring-lamps had all gone out. And not only those five. Along the wall in both directions, as far as she could see, the Ring was dark: a long black gap in the circle of lights, like a missing row of teeth.

Then she looked round, and saw the people.

They were coming out of doorways and from under carts, and standing in a wide, ragged ring all round her, at a careful distance, staring. Not at the dark wall. Not at the greyed knife-grinder, or at Mrs Fenn on her step. At her. At the girl with soot on her face and a blazing lamp in her hand.

Nobody said thank you.

“I saw it,” somebody said. “I saw it flare up. Like a furnace.”

“What’s she got there?”

“That’s no Guild lamp. Where’s the oil? There’s no oil in it.”

“The Ring went out when she lit it. Did you see? The whole Ring went dark.”

“That’s not true!” said Tobin. “That’s — the Ring went out before — it’s a question of sequence, you see, the lamps were already guttering when —“

Nobody was listening to him. Tallis the oil-man had climbed up onto the step of his cart. His face was grey with fright, not with Hollows, and he was pointing at Wren with a shaking finger.

“Witch-light,” somebody else said. And then somebody else, and somebody else, and the word went round the ring of people like a cold wind. Witch-light. Witch-light. Somebody picked up a frozen turnip from the gutter.

fields.body_text: Market day in Soot Lane happened every Thursday, and it was the only day of the week when the Low Quarter was loud for a good reason. By the middle of the morning the lane was packed from wall to wall. There were barrows of small hard apples, a man selling second-hand boots that were really only one boot, and a woman with a cage of hens who all looked as if they had been told bad news. There was a knife-grinder whose wheel threw out sparks, a fiddler with three strings, and a Guild oil-cart with a little painted sign on the side that said GUILD OIL — ONE PENNY THE MEASURE — FLAME TOKENS TWO A PENNY, BLESSED AT THE BEACON. The oil-man, whose name was Tallis, had a voice like a rusty gate and sold a great many tokens, for people in the Low Quarter were frightened of the dark and two a penny is cheap for courage. And in the middle of it all, with its door propped open and its window steamed up, stood Mrs Fenn’s bakery. You could smell Mrs Fenn’s bakery from the canal. It was the only good smell in Soot Lane, and people walking past would stop and close their eyes and breathe it in, as if it were a sort of breakfast. For most of them it was the only kind they got. Wren and Nettle were sitting on the step, which was where they always sat on market days, because Mrs Fenn always came out sooner or later. “Now then,” said Mrs Fenn, coming out. She was a wide, soft, floury woman with arms like bread rolls and a face as round and kind as a loaf. There was flour in her hair and flour on her apron and, somehow, flour on the tip of her nose. “Now then, you two sparrows. I’ve some crusts here going begging. Burnt, mind. Can’t sell ‘em. You’d be doing me a favour.” They were not burnt. They were never burnt. Hettie! Mind that oven! Sam, put your sister down, she’s not a sack of flour — Molly, where’s your brother? Where’s the baby? fields.title: The Guild’s Verdict
fields.body_html:
The Guild Hall of Emberwick had been built by people who wanted you to know they had money. It had a gilded door and gilded window-frames and a gilded weathercock on its gilded dome, and all that gilding gleamed faintly through the gloom like the inside of an old purse. Wide stone steps ran down from the door to the square. It was on these steps, early the next morning, that the Guild delivered its verdict.

Tobin stood at the bottom of them beside his father, and wished he were anywhere else.

He had not slept. He had followed Wren across three roofs the evening before, until she had turned on him on a slippery ridge and hissed, “Go home, nob, before you fall off and they blame me for that too,” and vanished into the dark as if she had been rubbed out. He had walked home with his night-lamp held out in front of him, flinching at every shadow. And all night, lying in bed with the little flame burning beside him, he had seen Mrs Fenn’s face. I think I had some children. I can’t think what I called them.

Now a crowd filled the square, rich folk at the front and poor folk at the back, and a crier in a Guild tabard rang a bell for silence.

“Hear ye! Hear ye! Pray silence for the Master of the Worshipful Guild of the Lamp, Cuthbert Prowle!”

Guild Master Prowle came out through the gilded door as though he were coming on to a stage. He was a round, glossy man in a round, glossy coat, and round his neck hung a gold chain of office so heavy that Tobin had always wondered how he kept his chin up. Even from the bottom of the steps you could smell him: lavender oil, a great deal of it.

“Citizens of Emberwick,” said Prowle, spreading his soft white hands. “We live in dark times. Dark and perilous times. Yesterday, for the first time in a hundred years, the creatures of the Greywaste breached our blessed Ring. And why?” He paused. He liked pausing. “I shall tell you why. Because a pernicious, malignant and wholly unsanctioned witch-light has been carried into our city, and has poisoned the Ring-lamps of the Low Quarter, and drawn the Hollows down upon us like moths to a — like flies to a — like moths.”

A murmur went through the crowd.

“The Guild has deliberated,” Prowle went on. “The Guild has consulted the most ancient authorities. And the Guild’s verdict is this: the said witch-light is to be seized and surrendered to the Guild, that it may be safely extinguished. And the creature who carries it” — he unrolled a paper with a flourish — “a sweep-girl of the Low Quarter, small, dark-haired, about twelve years of age, answering to the name of Wren — is to be arrested and held. A reward of fifty silver crowns is offered for her capture.”

Tobin heard the back of the crowd draw in its breath. In the Low Quarter, fifty crowns was a whole life.

“The order,” said Prowle, “awaits only the Warden’s seal.”

Lord Edric Harrowgate went up the steps. He did not hurry and he did not hesitate. A little table had been set out with a quill and a stick of grey sealing-wax, and he signed the paper in his neat, tall hand, and pressed his ring into the wax. His face showed nothing at all. It never did.

Tobin watched his father’s hand, and wanted to shout. She saved them. The lamps were going out before she ever touched that lamp. But the words stuck in his throat, the way they always did when his father was near, and he said nothing. I am sorry to say that is very often what happens to the things we most ought to say.

They walked back up to the Warden’s Hall together, in silence. At the door, his father stopped.

“Sergeant Bracken tells me you were seen in Soot Lane yesterday,” he said. He did not raise his voice. He never raised his voice. “In the middle of the disturbance. With a lamp.”

Tobin’s mouth went dry. “I — yes, Father. I was — conducting an experiment.”

“An experiment.” Lord Edric looked at him for a long moment, the way he might have looked at a clock that kept bad time. “Well. It seems that you know the Low Quarter, which is more than can be said for most of my guard. You will make yourself useful for once. You will go with Bracken’s men this morning and show them the girl’s haunts.”

“But Father, she isn’t —“

“That will be all, Tobin.”

So Tobin went down the Hill again with six of the Warden’s guardsmen, and Sergeant Bracken walking beside him. Bracken was a grizzled, heavy-footed man with a grey moustache and tired eyes, and he did not seem to be enjoying himself either.

“Just point, lad,” he said quietly, as they came into the Low Quarter. “Point and keep your head down. Nobody’s asking you to like it.”

Soot Lane was very quiet that morning. Up on the wall two Guild workmen on ladders were poking at the dead Ring-lamps and shaking their heads. People watched the guardsmen go by with hard faces. Mrs Fenn’s door was shut, and there was no smell of bread.

Tobin pointed at things. He pointed at the rope-maker’s roof, and the wash-house, and the tannery, all of which were quite truthfully places he had seen Wren, and none of which, he was fairly sure, she would be anywhere near. While the guards were poking with their halberds under the tannery steps, something tugged at his sleeve.

He looked down. A freckled face looked up at him. It had two teeth missing.

“You’re the thauthage boy,” said Nettle.

“Shh!” Tobin glanced at the guards. Nobody was looking. “Nettle. Where is she? Is she all right?”

Nettle considered him very seriously for a moment, with her head on one side, the way a bird considers a worm.

“Wren thayth you’re a great lump,” she said at last. “But you thtood in front of Molly. I thaw.” She took hold of two of his fingers in her small cold hand. “Come on.”

Wren was in a dead chimney behind the old glue-works, folded up in the dark of the flue like a bat. She came down when Nettle whistled, and when she saw Tobin behind Nettle her face went hard as a stone.

“You brought him?”

“He’th all right,” said Nettle. “He’th nithe.”

“He’s the Warden’s son. His dad just signed a paper saying I’m to be locked up. I heard the crier. Half of Soot Lane heard the crier.” Wren glared at Tobin. “Go on, then. Shout for your soldiers. Fifty crowns. Your dad’ll be proud of you.”

“I’m not going to shout for anybody,” said Tobin. “I came to help.”

“Rot. Nobody helps. Not for nothing.”

“I can hide you.”

“Where? Under your hat?”

Tobin took a breath. “In the Warden’s Hall,” he said. “In my workshop. It’s right at the top, under the roof, and nobody ever comes up there, not even the maids, because they say it ticks. Nobody will search the Warden’s own house for a girl the Warden wants arrested. It’s the last place in the city anyone would look. Statistically speaking,” he added, “it’s the safest room in Emberwick.”

Wren stared at him as if he had gone mad. Then, slowly, a very small and wicked grin spread across her sooty face.

“Under your dad’s nose,” she said. “In his own house. Oh, that’s good. That’s rotten. I like it.”

They sent Nettle to the Fenns’. “Go and help Pip with the little ones,” Wren told her, crouching down. “Nobody’s after you. Keep your head down and your mouth shut, and if anybody asks, you haven’t seen me for a week.” Nettle hugged her hard round the neck, and then, after a moment’s thought, hugged Tobin round the knees, and ran.

Wren did not walk up the Hill. She went over it, by chimneys and garden walls, while Tobin walked up the street below like a respectable person. Once she dropped a pebble on his head to show him where she was. When he reached the Hall, he went in through the kitchens and up the back stairs, five flights, to his attic, and opened the skylight, and there she was, sitting on the roof-leads outside with her chin on her knees.

“Took your time,” she said, and dropped in.

Tobin’s workshop ran the whole length of the roof. It was full of benches, and the benches were full of cogs and springs and lenses, coils of copper wire, a half-built clock with its insides showing, and in the far corner, propped against the wall, a tall tin figure shaped like a man, with a round head and two round glass eyes and a door in its chest.

“What,” said Wren, “is that?”

“The Mechanical Footman. It’s going to carry trays. Eventually. At the moment it mostly falls over.” Tobin pushed his spectacles up. “Don’t touch the left arm, it’s sprung.”

Wren walked round the room slowly, touching everything but the left arm, and Tobin, who had never let anybody into his workshop, found he did not mind.

Then she stopped in front of the Orrery.

It stood in the middle of the room on its own round table: a great circle of brass, the city wall in miniature, with a hundred and forty-four little glass beads set along it, all joined by threads of copper wire. Most of the beads glowed a dim, sleepy yellow. But along one side, the Low Quarter side, a long run of them had gone quite dark, like a gap in a smile.

“That’s where they came in,” said Wren quietly.

“Yes.”

She was silent for a moment. Then she saw it. Not on the wall of the Orrery at all, but here, in the room, in the middle of the circle, where nothing should have been: one tiny spark of light on the brass map of the Hill, burning brighter than all the others put together.

“That’s me,” she said. “That’s — that’s here. That’s this room.”

“That’s the lamp,” said Tobin. “Yes.”

Wren looked at the Orrery for a long time. Then, as if it cost her something, she said, “It’s dead clever. I’ll give you that.” And at once, as if to pay herself back, she put her hand in her coat and pulled out the compass and held it out to him.

“Here. Have it. It’s not even gold.”

Tobin took it. He turned it over in his hands. It was warm from her pocket.

“Why?” he said.

“Because you didn’t shout for the soldiers.” She shrugged, and looked away. “Don’t make a thing of it.”

“I’m not making a thing of it. I only want to know why. I want to know why about everything. Why does the lamp burn without oil? Why does it make the colours come back? Why did the Ring-lamp flare when you walked past it? Why did the Hollows run?” He spread his ink-stained hands. “That’s all I want. I just want to understand it.”

“Everyone wants something,” said Wren. “That’s what I’m saying. You want to understand it. Grubb wanted to sell it. The Guild wants to put it out. Everyone wants something, and in the end they’ll all take it, one way or another. That’s how it goes. Nothing’s free.”

“That isn’t true.”

“Isn’t it? What do you want, then? Really?”

Tobin opened his mouth, and then shut it again, because the honest answer was I want not to be frightened of the dark, and he could not possibly say that.

“I don’t want to take it off you,” he said at last. “That’s all I know.”

Wren looked at him narrowly.
