fields.title: Old Ash
fields.body_html:
The Leaning Tower did not so much stand on the North Wall as lounge against it, like a tired old man resting his shoulder on a friend. It was built of grey stone furred with moss, and it tipped so far towards the city that Tobin, looking up at it in the last of the gloaming, worked out the angle in his head and did not like the answer.

“Eleven degrees,” he whispered. “At least. Technically speaking, it ought to have fallen down a century ago.”

“Then it’s had a good run,” said Wren. “Stop measuring it and climb.”

On one side lay Emberwick, chimneys and lamp-towers smudged together in the smoke, with the Ring of great lamps along the wall burning their tired yellow. On the other side there was nothing at all but the Greywaste going away into the dusk, flat and still.

Only one window in the tower was lit: a round one, high up, like an eye.

Wren had her hand inside her coat, round the lamp. Everyone in Soot Lane knew about mad old Ash. He kept a demon that looked like a fox. He boiled cats in his kettle, or, according to Nettle, who had it from a boy who had it from his cousin, he boiled boys, which was worse. Wren did not believe a word of it. But she was not sorry to have Tobin, with all his elbows, standing between her and the door.

The door was low and round-topped and studded with black nails. Tobin lifted his hand to knock.

Before his knuckles touched the wood, it swung open.

“Hm,” said a voice from inside. “You took your time.”

The man in the doorway was so tall that he had to stoop under his own lintel, and so old that Wren could not have guessed his age if you had paid her. His beard was long and white, except on the left side, where it was singed a toasty brown, as if he had once leaned too close to something hot and had not bothered to mind. He wore a coat so patched that it was more patch than coat, all of it the dull blue-grey of a puddle under a cloudy sky, and he held a long pole with a brass hook at the top.

He looked at them, slowly, from under eyebrows like two white hedges.

“You’ll be the sweep,” he said to Wren. “And you’ll be the Warden’s boy. Come in before you let the cold in. Mind the owl.”

“How did you know we—“ Tobin began.

“I have a window,” said Old Ash, and went inside, and that seemed to be all the answer anyone was getting.

The room at the bottom of the tower was round, and every inch of it was full. There were maps on the walls and maps used as tablecloths, and lamp-parts everywhere: glass chimneys, brass collars, coils of wick. A staircase wound up round the wall and vanished into the ceiling, and on every step of it sat something: a teacup, a candle-end, a boot, another teacup. By the door stood a stuffed owl with one glass eye missing, which gave it a look of permanent disapproval.

A fire burned in a small iron stove, and beside it, in a basket, something lifted its head.

It was a fox, smaller than a dog, with a coat the grey of old ashes in a cold grate. But at the very tip of its brush there was a spark — a real spark, a little live coal of light — that winked and wavered like a candle in a draught. When it saw the children, the spark brightened.

“That’s the demon,” whispered Wren.

“That,” said Old Ash, “is Cinder. She is not a demon. She is a great deal worse. She is a fox with opinions.”

Cinder trotted across to inspect the visitors. She sniffed Wren’s boots, which smelled of soot, and seemed to approve. Then she sniffed Tobin’s shoes, which were polished, and the hem of his good wool coat, which smelled of the Warden’s Hall.

Her nose wrinkled.

“Hello,” said Tobin politely, bending down. “I’ve read that foxes are actually more closely related to—“

Cinder sneezed. A little burst of sparks flew out of her nose like sparks from a blacksmith’s hammer, and three of them landed on Tobin’s coat and made three tiny smoking holes.

“She doesn’t care what you’ve read,” said Old Ash. “Sit down.”

Wren laughed so suddenly that she had to pretend it was a cough. Tobin patted out his coat with an injured air while Old Ash lifted a kettle off the stove.

“Tea,” he announced.

If you have ever been given a cup of something by a person who is very proud of it, you will know there is only one thing to do, and that is to drink it and say it is lovely. Tobin, who had been brought up properly, knew this. Wren knew that you never turn down anything hot. So they both took the chipped cups, and said thank you, and drank.

Tobin’s face did something complicated. Wren’s did not; she had swallowed worse. But afterwards, telling the story to Nettle, she said it had tasted like a boot that had been boiled in a puddle, and then she said that this was unfair to boots.

“It’s very —“ Tobin swallowed. “It’s very distinctive.”

“My own blend,” said Old Ash, settling into an armchair that sighed under him. “Nettle leaves. Pine bark. A little dried mushroom. Smoke.”

“Smoke?” said Wren.

“It gets in,” said Old Ash. “I’ve stopped arguing with it. Have a biscuit.”

The biscuits lived in a tin with a lighthouse on the lid. They were square and grey and so hard that when Wren knocked one on the table it sounded like a door-knocker. She was working out how to get her teeth into it when a grey shape poured over the arm of the bench like water, a mouth closed on the biscuit, and the biscuit was gone.

Cinder lay down by the stove with it, her spark glowing with triumph, and began to crunch.

“Oi!” said Wren. “That was mine, you thieving—“

“Yes,” said Old Ash, “she does that. She has never paid for a biscuit in her life. I find it best to regard every biscuit in this tower as being on loan from Cinder.”

Wren glared. The fox looked back with its mouth full, quite unashamed, and Wren, who had stolen a great many things herself, found she could not stay cross with anything that thieved so well. When the biscuit was finished, Cinder climbed onto the bench, turned round three times, and lay down in Wren’s lap as though she had been doing it for years. She smelled of woodsmoke.

Nobody had ever lain down on Wren before, except Nettle on cold nights. After a while, very carefully, she put one hand on the fox’s back.

Old Ash watched this. He said nothing, but he said “Hm,” and drank his tea as though it were delicious.

“Well,” he said at last, putting down his cup. “I know why the Warden’s boy is here. He hasn’t anywhere else to go, which is the best reason there is. And I know why the city is shouting your name, child, because they’ve been shouting it under my window all day. Witch-light, they call it. Show me.”

Wren’s hand went to her coat, and stopped.

All her life she had kept her few good things hidden. You did not show a coin in Soot Lane, or a warm scarf, or a whole loaf, because the moment you showed it someone wanted it, and the moment someone wanted it, you had lost it. Half Emberwick wanted the lamp. And this old man had a room full of lamps.

“Why?” she said. “What’ll you give me for a look?”

Old Ash did not seem offended. If anything, he seemed a little sad.

“Nothing,” he said. “I haven’t anything you want. I won’t touch it; you have my word. I only want to see it, child. I have been waiting a long time to see it.”

There was something in the way he said it — not greedy, the way Grubb had said twenty silver crowns, but quiet and tired and hungry in a different way, like a man in a desert talking about rain — that made Wren take the lamp out before she had quite decided to.

She set it on the table among the teacups: a little brass lamp, dented on one side, with a hook on top and a crack in its chimney fine as a hair. And in the middle of it burned a small flame, golden-white, steady as a held breath, that smelled faintly of new bread and of something Wren had no name for, because she had never in her life smelled a summer.

The room changed.

The stove-light seemed to step back, the way a servant steps back when the master comes in. The shadows went soft and far off, as if they were listening. And the colours came.

Tobin saw it first in the old man’s coat. The patches that had been the colour of a puddle were not the colour of a puddle any longer. They were blue: not grey-blue, not dun-blue, but a deep clear blue that Tobin had never seen anywhere except, perhaps, in a dream. The maps woke up, and their forests were a colour Tobin did not know the name of. On Wren’s wrist the faded ribbon glowed red, red as a robin’s breast in a picture-book, and Wren looked down at it and did not even pretend not to.

Cinder’s spark blazed up like a little star.

And Old Ash went very still.

He kept his word and did not reach for the lamp. But Tobin, sitting nearest, saw the old man’s great knotted hands begin to shake on his knees: first a little, then so much that he pressed them flat to keep them quiet. His eyes, which had been sharp and dry and amused all evening, were not dry now.

For a long moment the only sounds were Cinder’s breathing and the small tick-tick of the stove.

“Where,” said Old Ash, and his voice came out rough, and he cleared it and tried again. “Where did you find this?”

“Thornbury House,” said Wren. “In a sealed flue.”

“Thornbury House.” He shut his eyes. “Hm. Of course it was. Fifty years I’ve walked past that chimney.” He opened them again and looked at the lamp as if it were a face he had not seen since he was a boy. “And it waited for a sweep.”

“Do you know what it is?” said Tobin, his spectacles sliding down his nose. “Because there’s no reservoir, and no wick I can see, and—“

“I know what it is,” said Old Ash. “And I’ll tell you. But not all at once, and not tonight. A thing like this has to be told in the right order, or it comes out wrong, like a clock put together backwards. Do you know why the sun is pale?”

“It just is,” said Wren. “It’s the sun.”

“It’s the dark times,” said Tobin uncertainly. “That’s what Master Prowle says.”

“Master Prowle,” said Old Ash, “would call a hole in his own boat the wet times. No. The sun is pale because a man made it so. Listen.”

He told it simply, the way you would tell a thing that had happened in your own street, and the lamp burned on the table, and the colours stayed.

Three hundred years ago, he said, there was a king in Gloamhaven called Ardric, who was clever and handsome and brave and afraid of exactly one thing, which was dying. Far in the north rose the Bright Mountain, where, it was said, the sun’s own fire came to rest in the evenings like a bird coming home to its nest.

Ardric climbed the Bright Mountain. It took him a year. And at the top, in a cleft in the rock where the light did not reach, he found someone waiting for him.

“Morvaine,” said Old Ash, and the stove-fire ducked for a moment as if a door had opened. “The Umbral Queen. She is very old, and very cold, and she never shouts. She does not need to. She asked Ardric what he wanted, and he told her: a crown he would never have to take off. A life that would never end. And she smiled and said, Easily done. I ask only one small thing in return. I ask for the sun’s fire.”

“What did she want it for?” whispered Tobin.

“Not to use,” said Old Ash. “To put out. She hates light the way you hate a stone in your shoe. So Ardric reached up — oh, he was brave, I’ll give him that, though bravery isn’t worth much when it’s going the wrong way — Ardric reached into the sun’s fire with his two bare hands and took it. He put it into his crown, and gave the rest to her, and she folded it up in the dark and kept it. And from that day to this the sun has risen pale, and the colours have gone out of the world one by one, and the Hollows have come out of the Greywaste, and every city has had to build a wall and a ring of lamps to keep the cold away.”

“And Ardric?” said Wren. Her voice came out smaller than she meant.

“Some say he wears his crown still,” said Old Ash, “somewhere in her grey halls, and cannot take it off, and cannot die. Hm. That is what undying means, child, when it is the Queen who gives it.”

Nobody said anything for a while.

Wren looked at the round window. In the morning the sky over the Greywaste would be grey, and at noon, as on every noon of her life, the sun would hang in it like a coin seen through dirty water. You did not think about the sun, any more than you thought about the cobbles.

“What colour was it?” she said. “Before.”

Old Ash looked at the lamp, and its light lay on his face, and Wren saw that his face was not grey but brown and pink and weathered, like a face in a story.

“Gold,” he said. “Like that.”

Wren stared at the little flame. It was not the yellow of the Guild’s oil, and not the dull brass of a coin. It was something warm and alive and glad, something that made you want to hold out your hands to it. And she thought: the whole sky. Every morning. The whole sky, that colour. And somebody took it.

She found she was angry, and could not have said why, and it was a much bigger anger than she was used to.

Tobin had taken off his spectacles and was polishing them on his shirt, which was what he did when he did not want anyone to see his face.

“My mother used to sing about it,” he said. “A song about the gold morning, and the green hills, and the blue water. I asked my father once what green was, and he said it was a word in old songs, and I should stop asking about Lamplighter nonsense.” He put his spectacles back on. “I thought she’d made them up. The colours. I thought they were just pretty words.”

“They are pretty words,” said Old Ash gently. “But they were not made up. Your mother knew that, lad. A good many mothers used to.”

Then he got up, with a creak of knees, and went to the window.

The children could see what he saw over his shoulder. Out on the Greywaste, beyond the reach of the Ring-lamps, shapes were moving, only a little paler than the dark. They did not walk. They drifted, the way smoke drifts on a still day, slowly and all together, towards the wall. Tobin stopped counting at forty.

Cinder, in Wren’s lap, lifted her head and growled, a low steady sound like a kettle beginning to think about boiling.

“Hm,” said Old Ash. “Yes. I see them.” He turned round. “You’ll stay here, both of you. The guard won’t come near this tower; they think I’m mad, and they’re quite right, and it’s very convenient. There’s a room at the top with two beds and a good deal of dust. The fox will want to sleep with one of you. I advise you to let her.”

“We can’t pay,” said Wren at once.

Old Ash looked at her for a moment, the way he had looked at the lamp.

“No,” he said. “I know. Go to bed, child.”

The beds in the top room sloped, so that Wren had to sleep with one foot braced against the wall to keep from rolling out. Tobin was asleep almost at once, with his mother’s little night-lamp burning low on the floor beside him. Wren noticed that he checked it twice before he shut his eyes, and noticed that he did not know she had noticed. She decided not to say anything. You never spent a secret before you needed to.

The lamp she kept under her blanket, against her ribs. Cinder lay across her feet like a warm stole.

She could not sleep. She lay thinking about a gold sky, and a king reaching into the sun with his bare hands, and a smiling queen in a crack of rock. She thought about Mrs Fenn sitting grey on her doorstep, and Nettle, back in Soot Lane, alone.

Somewhere outside there was a sound: a scrape, a step, a soft metal click.

Wren slid out from under the blanket, Cinder grumbling, and went to the little window under the eaves.

Below her the North Wall ran away east and west, a broad stone walk with a parapet on the Greywaste side, and every forty paces one of the great Ring-lamps stood on its iron post like a sentry. One of them, a little way along, had guttered nearly out; it was only a smudge of brown light, and the dark was leaning in around it.

And beneath it stood Old Ash.

He reached up with his long pole, the brass hook glinting, and opened the lamp’s little door, and trimmed the wick, and touched it with a taper. The Ring-lamp coughed and caught and burned up again, brighter than its neighbours.

Old Ash lowered his pole and stood with his white head bowed, looking out at the dark. And then, so softly that if the night had not been so still she would never have heard it, he began to hum.

It was only a few notes. They rose, and fell, and rose again, gentle as a hand on a sleeping child’s hair.

Morning comes, morning comes…

Wren’s fingers closed on the window-ledge so hard that the stone bit into them.

She knew that tune. She had known it longer than she had known her own name. It was the only thing she had left that had never been sold or lost or stolen: a woman’s voice, very close, very warm, singing in the dark, and two words, and then nothing. She had never heard anyone else in the whole of Emberwick sing it.

The old man on the wall hummed on, and the tune went past the place where Wren’s memory always broke off, and kept going, into the part she did not have.

She stood frozen at the window, the cold creeping up through her bare feet, and did not breathe, and listened.

Go to bed, child.” The beds in the top room sloped, so that Wren had to sleep with one foot braced against the wall to keep from rolling out. Tobin was asleep almost at once, with his mother’s little night-lamp burning low on the floor beside him. Wren noticed that he checked it twice before he shut his eyes, and noticed that he did not know she had noticed. She decided not to say anything. You never spent a secret before you needed to. The lamp she kept under her blanket, against her ribs. Cinder lay across her feet like a warm stole. She could not sleep. She lay thinking about a gold sky, and a king reaching into the sun with his bare hands, and a smiling queen in a crack of rock. She thought about Mrs Fenn sitting grey on her doorstep, and Nettle, back in Soot Lane, alone. Somewhere outside there was a sound: a scrape, a step, a soft metal click. Wren slid out from under the blanket, Cinder grumbling, and went to the little window under the eaves. Below her the North Wall ran away east and west, a broad stone walk with a parapet on the Greywaste side, and every forty paces one of the great Ring-lamps stood on its iron post like a sentry. One of them, a little way along, had guttered nearly out; it was only a smudge of brown light, and the dark was leaning in around it. And beneath it stood Old Ash. He reached up with his long pole, the brass hook glinting, and opened the lamp’s little door, and trimmed the wick, and touched it with a taper. The Ring-lamp coughed and caught and burned up again, brighter than its neighbours. Old Ash lowered his pole and stood with his white head bowed, looking out at the dark. And then, so softly that if the night had not been so still she would never have heard it, he began to hum. It was only a few notes. They rose, and fell, and rose again, gentle as a hand on a sleeping child’s hair. Morning comes, morning comes… Wren’s fingers closed on the window-ledge so hard that the stone bit into them. She knew that tune. She had known it longer than she had known her own name. It was the only thing she had left that had never been sold or lost or stolen: a woman’s voice, very close, very warm, singing in the dark, and two words, and then nothing. She had never heard anyone else in the whole of Emberwick sing it. The old man on the wall hummed on, and the tune went past the place where Wren’s memory always broke off, and kept going, into the part she did not have. She stood frozen at the window, the cold creeping up through her bare feet, and did not breathe, and listened.

fields.title: The Tale of the Lampwright
fields.body_html:
Wren came down the crooked stair next morning with her boots in her hand and a question in her mouth, and she did not wait to put either of them on.

Old Ash was at the table, trimming wicks with a pair of tiny scissors. Cinder was under the table, watching the scissors in case they turned out to be edible.

“That song,” said Wren. “Last night. On the wall.”

Ash did not look up. Snip. “Good morning, child.”

“You were humming it. Morning comes. Where did you get it?”

Snip. Snip. He set down the scissors and looked at her then, and Wren had the feeling, which she did not like, that he had been waiting for her to ask.

“It’s an old Lamplighter song,” he said. “Very old. We used to sing it on the wall at the turning of the night, when the dark is thickest and the lamps want minding. It was sung by a good many people, once.” He paused. “And by more than one mother.”

Wren’s hand went to the ribbon on her wrist. She did not know she had done it until she saw him look at it.

“Then you know the words,” she said. “All of them. The rest of it.”

“I know the words I was taught.”

“Then tell me.”

Old Ash was quiet for so long that Tobin, coming down the stair behind her with his hair standing up like a hayrick, stopped on the bottom step and did not dare come further.

“No,” said the old man at last, quite gently. “Not yet. I think somebody sang those words to you first, child, and they were hers to give, and I won’t take them out of her mouth. Not this morning.”

“That’s rot,” said Wren. “She’s not here. She’s not anywhere. You can’t take anything from somebody who’s not anywhere.”

“Hm,” said Old Ash, and picked up his scissors again. “You’d be surprised.”

Wren sat in the round window with her back to him and her arms folded, and stayed there most of the morning. This lasted until Cinder brought her a biscuit, put it down on the bench beside her, looked at it, looked at Wren, and then — because she was a fox, and had her limits — picked it up again and ate it herself. Wren laughed in spite of herself, and after that it was hard to go on sulking.

It was a long, grey, waiting sort of day. Old Ash slept most of it in his armchair with his mouth open, because, he said, a man who walks the wall all night must sleep somewhere, and the bed was too far up. Tobin took apart three broken lamps and put two of them back together. Wren kept watch from the window. Twice she saw guardsmen tramping below the wall, look up at the Leaning Tower, mutter to each other, and walk the other way.

When the gloaming came down and the Ring-lamps along the wall coughed into their poor yellow life, Old Ash woke, stretched, made a pot of tea which nobody drank, and said:

“Now. I promised you the beginning.”

He went to a chest under the stair and came back with a bedsheet. It was patched in the middle with a darn shaped, Tobin said, almost exactly like a duck. He strung a cord from the banister to a nail in the wall, hung the sheet over it, and set a three-legged stool behind it. Then he held out his hand.

“The lamp, child. I’ll not touch it. Put it on the stool yourself.”

Wren did. The light came through the sheet warm and gold, and the whole sheet glowed like a page held up to a window, and the duck-shaped darn showed dark in the middle of it.

Old Ash fetched the biscuit tin with the lighthouse on the lid, emptied the last three biscuits onto the table (Cinder had two of them before they stopped rolling), and tipped out of it a heap of shapes cut from stiff black paper: a mountain, some rooftops, a crown, a long thin hand with too many fingers, a little figure of a man holding up a lamp.

Wren looked at them, and at the sheet, and at the old man kneeling behind it with his white beard full of light.

“Shadow puppets,” she said. “I’m twelve.”

“Then you’re old enough to sit still,” said Old Ash. “Sit.”

He began with his bare hands. He laid them together behind the sheet, and on the bright cloth a mountain rose, steep and black, and on its peak — he did something quick with his thumb — a tiny point of brightness that was the gap between two knuckles.

“After the king’s bargain,” he said, “the world went grey. Not all at once. Colours went the way names go when you are old: one, and then another, and then you can’t remember what you’ve lost. Cities built walls. People forgot what warm meant. And then, one evening, a shepherd on the lower slopes of the Bright Mountain looked up and saw a light coming down.”

The point of brightness began to move down the mountain’s side, slowly, as his knuckles slid apart.

“Excuse me,” said Tobin. “Sorry. But actually, if your hands are that close to the source, the shadow ought to be enormous, and if they’re further away—“

“Thank you,” said Old Ash, without stopping. “The light came down the mountain, and it was a man. And he was carrying—“

Cinder strolled out from behind the stool, and her shadow fell across the sheet: a fox the size of a carthorse, with a brush like a bonfire, padding across the mountain and sitting down on top of it.

“—and in those days,” said Old Ash, perfectly calmly, “there were very large foxes. Cinder, get out of it.”

Cinder yawned, and her shadow yawned, a great black cave of a mouth with teeth like fence-posts. Wren snorted so hard she had to put her face in her knees.

Old Ash took the little paper figure of the man with the lamp, and held it up to the light, and on the sheet the stranger walked down out of the mountains and into a town of black rooftops.

“He was quite ordinary to look at,” he said. “That was the first surprise. No crown. No sword. A traveller’s coat, and boots that had been mended, and in his hand a small brass lamp with a flame in it that was not yellow, and not grey, but gold. And he went to the first door he came to, and knocked, and when they opened it he said, Your lamp’s gone out. May I light it?”

“And then he charged them,” said Wren.

“No.”

“Then he charged them later. That’s how it goes. They give you a bit for nothing, and then when you’re used to it they want it back with something on top. Everyone knows that.”

“He lit it,” said Old Ash, “and went to the next door, and lit that. He went down the whole street, and the next street, and through the whole town, and on to the next one. Anyone who asked. Rich and poor. Kind and unkind. The ones who thanked him and the ones who slammed the door afterwards. He never asked a penny, and he never once asked anyone whether they deserved it. In the end people stopped asking his name, and simply called him the Lampwright.”

“He’d have been robbed in Soot Lane in a minute,” said Wren.

“Oh, he was robbed,” said Old Ash. “Often. People tried to take the lamp from him in every city in Gloamhaven.” He paused. “They found they couldn’t keep it.”

Wren opened her mouth and shut it again. She was thinking of Grubb’s long nose, and Grubb shaking his burned fingers, and the way he had howled.

“How did one lamp light all of them?” said Tobin. He had stopped fidgeting. “If he lit a thousand lamps from one flame, it would have to — I mean, by the end there’d be nothing left. That’s just arithmetic.”

“Is it?” said Old Ash. “Hm. Hold that question, lad. Keep it in your pocket. It’s a good one.”

Now the paper man came to a house where a figure sat in a doorway, bent and still. Ash’s fingers made it: a head bowed, hands in the lap.

“There were people,” he said, “whom the Hollows had touched. You’ve seen them now. You know.” Wren thought of Mrs Fenn on her step, and her stomach went cold. “Grey all through. Forgetting their own children. And there were people who were blind, who had never seen even the grey. And he came to them, and he did not light a lamp. He knelt down, and put his hand on them, and held the Flame near.”

The bowed figure on the sheet lifted its head.

That was all. It was only a shadow lifting its head. But something about the way Ash did it — slowly, as if waking, as if surprised — made the hair stand up along Wren’s arms. And at that same moment, as though it had been listening, the lamp on the stool flared a little brighter, and the sheet turned from gold to a colour that was almost the colour of a sunrise, and on Wren’s wrist the ribbon blazed red.

“The grey went out of their faces,” said Old Ash softly. “Their cheeks came back pink. The blind ones looked up and saw the light, and the light was the first thing they ever saw, and they wept. And they remembered names they had forgotten for twenty years.”

Nobody said anything. Even Tobin.

Then Cinder got up again, trotted to the table, stood on her hind legs, and took the little paper man out of the old man’s fingers with her teeth — very delicately, as if she had done it before. Then she walked across in front of the lamp with him, and on the sheet the stranger with his lamp went walking on through the towns, from one side to the other, bobbing a little, with a large fox’s head attached to the back of him.

“Yes,” said Old Ash, a little hoarsely. “Thank you, Cinder. That’s exactly right. He went on.”

“Some of the people he lit lamps for followed him,” Ash went on, when Cinder had been persuaded to give the paper man back. “He taught them to carry the Flame and to tend the lamps of every city, and they made a promise, and the promise was this: to give light freely, to all who ask, and to take nothing for it. They called themselves Lamplighters. They wore blue, because blue was the colour of the sky when the sun was gold.”

Tobin looked at the old man’s patched coat, and said nothing.

“And the Queen,” said Old Ash, and he picked up the long-fingered paper hand, “hated him.”

The hand came onto the sheet from the edge, enormous, reaching. It was only black paper. But it was cut so that the fingers were a little too long and a little too thin, and they did not grab. They hovered. They seemed to wait.

“She did not shout,” said Old Ash. “She never does. First she offered him things. She offered him a crown, like Ardric’s, and a city of his own, and a sun that would shine on him alone. And he said no. Then she offered to leave the cities in peace, every one, if he would only put out his lamp and go home. And he said no to that too, because he knew what her peace is worth. So she sent her darkness after him. And his friends, the Lamplighters, who had promised so much — hm. Most of them ran.”

The paper hand closed slowly round the little man with the lamp.

“There is a hill,” said Old Ash, “a long way from here, called Cinder Hill. Nothing grows on it now. They say the ground there is still warm. And on that hill the Queen’s darkness came up round him like a tide coming in over the sand, and it was cold, and it was all the cold there has ever been, and it covered him. And it put out his light.”

He reached for the tea-cosy, lifted it off the pot, and set it over the lamp.

The room went dark.

It was not the ordinary dark of a room at night, with grey at the window and shapes you can half see. It was black, black as the inside of a sealed flue, so black that Wren could not see her own hand. Somewhere to her left she heard Tobin’s breath catch and go quick and shallow, the way a small animal breathes when it is caught. Without quite deciding to, she reached out in the dark and found his sleeve, and took hold of it. His arm was shaking.

“Rot,” she whispered. “It’s only a tea-cosy.”

“I know,” whispered Tobin. “I know it’s only a tea-cosy.”

But neither of them let go.

“His friends wept,” said Old Ash’s voice out of the blackness. It sounded very old now, and very tired, and very near. “They said: it’s over. They said: we were fools to hope. They said: she was right, the grey is easier. They went home and shut their doors. And it was dark on the first day.”

Silence. Cinder, invisible, gave a small whine.

“And it was dark on the second day.”

Wren found that she was holding her breath. She was twelve, and it was a story, and it was only a tea-cosy. She knew all that perfectly well. She held her breath anyway.

“And on the third day,” said Old Ash—

“Get on with it,” whispered Wren, and her voice cracked in the middle.

“—on the third morning, very early, before even the pale sun was up, a shepherd on the slopes of the Bright Mountain looked up. And on the top of the mountain, where nobody had climbed, there was a fire burning.”

He lifted the tea-cosy.

The light came back into the room all at once, the way a wave comes over a rock — gold and warm and smelling of bread — and the sheet blazed with it, so bright after the dark that Wren had to screw her eyes shut, and when she opened them they were wet, and she told herself it was the brightness. Cinder’s spark was burning like a star. The patches on Old Ash’s coat were blue, blue, blue. Tobin’s face beside her was pink and astonished and had a tear running down it behind his spectacles, which he did not wipe away.

“They ran up the mountain,” said Old Ash quietly. “His friends. All the ones who had gone home. They ran all the way up. And when they got there, there was the Flame, burning on the bare rock, burning without oil and without wick, warmer than anything they had ever felt. And he was gone.”

“Gone?” said Tobin. “Gone where?”

“Hm,” said Old Ash.

“That’s not an answer,” said Wren. “That’s a noise.”

“It is the answer I have,” said the old man.

He took down the sheet and folded it, and while he did it he told them the rest, plainly, without any shadows at all. How the Lamplighters had carried the Flame from the mountain to every city in Gloamhaven, and lit the great Rings from it, and the Rings had held back the Hollows for three hundred years. How, little by little, the Lamplighters had grown fewer and the Guild had grown larger. How someone had first said, Surely it is only fair to charge a little, for the oil. How the oil had been easier than the Flame, because oil could be weighed and counted and sold. How the lamps had grown dimmer every year, and the Guild had grown richer, and the price had gone up, and up.

“And the Flame,” said Tobin. “The real one. From the mountain.”

Old Ash sat down in his armchair. He looked at the little brass lamp on the stool, dented and cracked and burning, and the gold light lay on his face.

“You’re looking at it,” he said.

Nobody moved.

“That is his lamp,” said Old Ash. “His own. The one he carried down the mountain. When he was gone, his friends kept it, and passed it from hand to hand, from one Lamplighter to the next, for three hundred years. The last who kept it were the Thornburys, up on the Hill. And when the last of the Thornburys died, fifty years ago, the lamp could not be found. We searched that house from cellar to roof. I searched it myself, when I was a young man.” He shook his head. “And all the while it was sitting in a sealed flue behind a row of bricks, waiting for a sweep.”

Wren looked at the lamp, and then at her own hands, black under the nails with soot that never quite came out.

“Why me?” she said. “I’m nobody. I’m a thief. I’d have sold it the first morning if Grubb hadn’t—“ She stopped.

“I know,” said Old Ash.

“So why didn’t it burn me? It burned him.”

“Because Grubb tried to buy it,” said Old Ash, “and you were given it. That’s its law, child, and it’s the oldest law there is. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given.”

Wren felt something go cold and then hot at the back of her neck. She was in the market again, with her stomach aching, and a warm loaf being put into her hands by an old man with kind eyes. No charge. It’s given. She had meant to say something cheeky. And when she turned round, he had not been there.

She pushed the thought away hard, the way you push a door shut on a draught.

“Well, that’s rot,” she said, louder than she needed to. “That’s just rot. Nothing in the world is free. Everything costs. If it doesn’t cost you now, it’ll cost you later. I’ve known that since I was four.”

Old Ash looked at her for a long moment. He did not look cross. He looked, if anything, as though he were sorry for her, and also as though he knew something that would one day make her very glad.

“Then you’ve never met him,” he said.

The silence after that was so complete that they could hear the Ring-lamps hissing on the wall outside.

“There is a second half to the law,” said Old Ash at last. “What is given, grows. Remember that, both of you, though you won’t understand it yet. I didn’t, for years.” He laced his long fingers together. “And there’s more to the story than I’ve told you tonight. A good deal more. But it is not mine to tell. Not yet.”

Tobin had taken his spectacles off again. He held them in his lap and looked at the lamp without them, so that it must have been only a gold blur to him.

“Mr Ash,” he said. “Sir. The Lampwright. The man in the story.” He swallowed. “Could he come back?”

Old Ash did not answer. He said, “Hm,” very quietly, the way you might say it to yourself in an empty room.

Then he sat in his armchair, with Cinder’s chin on his boot, and looked at the little brass lamp for a long, long time, and did not say anything else at all.

And on that hill the Queen’s darkness came up round him like a tide coming in over the sand, and it was cold, and it was all the cold there has ever been, and it covered him. And it put out his light.” He reached for the tea-cosy, lifted it off the pot, and set it over the lamp. The room went dark. It was not the ordinary dark of a room at night, with grey at the window and shapes you can half see. It was black, black as the inside of a sealed flue, so black that Wren could not see her own hand. Somewhere to her left she heard Tobin’s breath catch and go quick and shallow, the way a small animal breathes when it is caught. Without quite deciding to, she reached out in the dark and found his sleeve, and took hold of it. His arm was shaking. “Rot,” she whispered. “It’s only a tea-cosy.” “I know,” whispered Tobin. “I know it’s only a tea-cosy.” But neither of them let go. “His friends wept,” said Old Ash’s voice out of the blackness. It sounded very old now, and very tired, and very near. “They said: it’s over. They said: we were fools to hope. They said: she was right, the grey is easier. They went home and shut their doors. And it was dark on the first day.” Silence. Cinder, invisible, gave a small whine. “And it was dark on the second day.” Wren found that she was holding her breath. She was twelve, and it was a story, and it was only a tea-cosy. She knew all that perfectly well. She held her breath anyway. “And on the third day,” said Old Ash— “Get on with it,” whispered Wren, and her voice cracked in the middle. “—on the third morning, very early, before even the pale sun was up, a shepherd on the slopes of the Bright Mountain looked up. And on the top of the mountain, where nobody had climbed, there was a fire burning.” He lifted the tea-cosy. The light came back into the room all at once, the way a wave comes over a rock — gold and warm and smelling of bread — and the sheet blazed with it, so bright after the dark that Wren had to screw her eyes shut, and when she opened them they were wet, and she told herself it was the brightness. Cinder’s spark was burning like a star. The patches on Old Ash’s coat were blue, blue, blue. Tobin’s face beside her was pink and astonished and had a tear running down it behind his spectacles, which he did not wipe away. “They ran up the mountain,” said Old Ash quietly. “His friends. All the ones who had gone home. They ran all the way up. And when they got there, there was the Flame, burning on the bare rock, burning without oil and without wick, warmer than anything they had ever felt. And he was gone.” “Gone?” said Tobin. “Gone where?” “Hm,” said Old Ash. “That’s not an answer,” said Wren. “That’s a noise.” “It is the answer I have,” said the old man. He took down the sheet and folded it, and while he did it he told them the rest, plainly, without any shadows at all. How the Lamplighters had carried the Flame from the mountain to every city in Gloamhaven, and lit the great Rings from it, and the Rings had held back the Hollows for three hundred years. How, little by little, the Lamplighters had grown fewer and the Guild had grown larger. How someone had first said, Surely it is only fair to charge a little, for the oil. How the oil had been easier than the Flame, because oil could be weighed and counted and sold. How the lamps had grown dimmer every year, and the Guild had grown richer, and the price had gone up, and up. “And the Flame,” said Tobin. “The real one. From the mountain.” Old Ash sat down in his armchair. He looked at the little brass lamp on the stool, dented and cracked and burning, and the gold light lay on his face. “You’re looking at it,” he said. Nobody moved. “That is his lamp,” said Old Ash. “His own. The one he carried down the mountain. When he was gone, his friends kept it, and passed it from hand to hand, from one Lamplighter to the next, for three hundred years. The last who kept it were the Thornburys, up on the Hill. And when the last of the Thornburys died, fifty years ago, the lamp could not be found. We searched that house from cellar to roof. I searched it myself, when I was a young man.” He shook his head. “And all the while it was sitting in a sealed flue behind a row of bricks, waiting for a sweep.” Wren looked at the lamp, and then at her own hands, black under the nails with soot that never quite came out. “Why me?” she said. “I’m nobody. I’m a thief. I’d have sold it the first morning if Grubb hadn’t—“ She stopped. “I know,” said Old Ash. “So why didn’t it burn me? It burned him.” “Because Grubb tried to buy it,” said Old Ash, “and you were given it. That’s its law, child, and it’s the oldest law there is. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given.” Wren felt something go cold and then hot at the back of her neck. She was in the market again, with her stomach aching, and a warm loaf being put into her hands by an old man with kind eyes. No charge. It’s given. She had meant to say something cheeky. And when she turned round, he had not been there. She pushed the thought away hard, the way you push a door shut on a draught. “Well, that’s rot,” she said, louder than she needed to. “That’s just rot. Nothing in the world is free. Everything costs. If it doesn’t cost you now, it’ll cost you later. I’ve known that since I was four.” Old Ash looked at her for a long moment. He did not look cross. He looked, if anything, as though he were sorry for her, and also as though he knew something that would one day make her very glad. “Then you’ve never met him,” he said. The silence after that was so complete that they could hear the Ring-lamps hissing on the wall outside. “There is a second half to the law,” said Old Ash at last. “What is given, grows. Remember that, both of you, though you won’t understand it yet. I didn’t, for years.” He laced his long fingers together. “And there’s more to the story than I’ve told you tonight. A good deal more. But it is not mine to tell. Not yet.” Tobin had taken his spectacles off again. He held them in his lap and looked at the lamp without them, so that it must have been only a gold blur to him. “Mr Ash,” he said. “Sir. The Lampwright. The man in the story.” He swallowed. “Could he come back?” Old Ash did not answer. He said, “Hm,” very quietly, the way you might say it to yourself in an empty room. Then he sat in his armchair, with Cinder’s chin on his boot, and looked at the little brass lamp for a long, long time, and did not say anything else at all.

fields.title: The Captain in Grey
fields.body_html:
“I have to go home,” said Tobin.

He said it at breakfast, which was porridge the colour and texture of wet cement. Wren put her spoon down.

“Course you do,” she said.

“Not like that. Not for good.” Tobin pushed his spectacles up his nose. “Look. If I’m missing for a third night, my father will turn the whole city upside down, and the first place anyone sensible looks for a missing boy is wherever the missing girl is. But if I’m at supper, and I’m sulky, and I’ve been out ‘sketching the canal locks’, then I’m just being peculiar again, and nobody will think twice. And if I’m in the Hall, I can find out what he’s planning.”

“Nobs always go home,” said Wren. “That’s what home’s for.”

Tobin went red, and opened his mouth, and shut it again. Old Ash, behind his teacup, said, “Hm,” which might have meant anything.

“I’ll be back by dark,” said Tobin. “I promise.”

Wren shrugged, and picked up her spoon, and did not look at him. But when he was halfway down the wall-stair, she called after him — “Mind the guard on Tallow Bridge, he looks under everyone’s hat” — and Tobin, who did not own a hat, found that he was smiling all the way to the bottom.

He was not smiling an hour later.

He had come up through the Low Quarter and over the canal, and was climbing the long cobbled street to the Hill, when he found that everybody else was going the other way. Apprentices, washerwomen, clerks with ink on their cuffs, all hurrying north, all talking in low voices. Tobin turned and went with them, and that is how he came to be standing on the steps of a chandler’s shop in Gate Street, craning over the heads of the crowd, when the Grey Gate opened.

It had not opened in Tobin’s lifetime. But now its great iron leaves swung inward, groaning, and the cold came in with them — not wind, but cold, the way cold comes off a block of ice — and the crowd went quiet as a cellar.

A rider came through.

He was tall and pale, and he sat his horse as if he had been born on it. His armour was grey, and his long cloak was grey, and his horse was grey, and when he turned his head to look along the street Tobin saw that his eyes were grey too, a light, clear, polished grey, like water in a pewter jug. He was rather handsome. He did not look cruel. He looked, Tobin thought, like a man who had never once in his life been in a hurry.

Behind him, on foot, came six more.

They were men, or they had been. They wore grey armour like their captain, but their faces were not like his. Their faces were the colour of ash, and smooth, and empty, and their eyes did not look at anything. They walked in step, like clockwork. And as they passed, the paint on the chandler’s sign above Tobin’s head — it had been a sort of brownish not-quite-red — faded, very slowly, to the colour of dust.

A herald in the Warden’s livery, white-faced, stepped out from the gatehouse and cried in a voice that wobbled: “Make way! Make way for Captain Varrick, envoy of the Queen’s peace, who comes to treat with the Lord Warden of Emberwick!”

The Queen’s peace. Tobin heard the words go through the crowd like a draught going through a house. The Queen. The Queen’s peace. Peace, he said. Some people sounded frightened. Some — and this made Tobin’s stomach turn over — sounded hopeful.

The grey rider rode up Gate Street at a walk, nodding pleasantly to the people on either side, and the crowd parted in front of him like a field of barley parting for the wind. As he passed the chandler’s steps his eyes moved, without any hurry, over the faces there, and for one half of a second they rested on Tobin’s.

Then they moved on.

Tobin found that he had stopped breathing. He started again. Then he jumped off the steps and ran by the back lanes, all elbows and knees, towards the Warden’s Hall.

There was a way into the Hall that nobody knew about except Tobin, the coal-man and possibly the cat: through the coal-cellar and up the servants’ back stair. Tobin went up it three steps at a time. He came out into his workshop, where the Orrery of the Ring stood on its round table with its hundred and forty-four glass beads glowing faintly, and he did not even stop to look at it.

He went instead to the corner, where a wooden panel was screwed to the wall, took out the four screws with the little screwdriver he kept in his top pocket, and lifted the panel away.

Behind it was dark.

Tobin had found the crawlway when he was eight years old, hiding from his fencing master. It ran between the attic floor and the ceilings of the rooms below, a long low gap full of dust and old beams and the bones of mice, and if you crawled along the third beam on the left for forty-one lengths of your own body, you came out above his father’s study, where a crack beside the plaster rose in the ceiling let you look straight down onto the desk. He had spent a great many afternoons there when he was small, watching his father write, wishing he would look up.

He had forgotten how dark it was.

He knelt at the opening with his heart going like a hammer, and thought about going back for his night-lamp, and knew that he could not: a light in the crawlway would show through every crack in every ceiling between here and the study. He thought about Wren in the flue at Thornbury House, not minding the dark at all. He thought: she’d laugh at me. And then, oddly: no. She wouldn’t. Not about this.

He took a breath of dust and crawled in.

The dark closed over him like water. He could not see his hands. He could feel the beam under his knees and the cobwebs on his face, and every few lengths something small scuffled away from him. He counted lengths out loud, under his breath, the way his mother had taught him to count stairs when he was frightened of the cellar — “fourteen, fifteen, sixteen” — and his voice shook, and he kept counting. At thirty he heard voices. At forty-one he lay flat along the beam, put his eye to the crack beside the plaster rose, and looked down.

His father was standing by the window.

Lord Edric Harrowgate stood with his hands behind his back and his chin up, as he always did when there were visitors, and the grey light from the window made the silver at his temples shine like frost. He looked very calm. Only Tobin, who had spent his whole life watching that back, could see that the hands behind it were holding each other far too tightly.

The door opened. The steward announced, in a voice that was trying hard not to squeak, “Captain Varrick, my lord.”

And the captain in grey came in, and took off his gloves, and bowed.

“Lord Warden,” he said.

His voice was the most pleasant voice Tobin had ever heard. It was low, and smooth, and unhurried, and it went into your ears as easily as oil goes into a lock.

“You keep a fine city,” said Captain Varrick, “in very poor light. It cannot be easy, with the lamps as they are, and the Guild as it is.” He smiled a little. “I have met Master Prowle.”

“You did not come here to discuss Master Prowle,” said Lord Edric.

“No.” Varrick sat down, uninvited, in the chair before the desk, and crossed one long grey leg over the other. “I came to make you an offer. My mistress has no quarrel with Emberwick. None at all. The Hollows that came over your wall the other day — that was a misunderstanding. They were drawn by something. A light that did not belong in your city.” He turned his gloves over in his hands. “Give me that light, Lord Warden, and they will go away. Your Ring will hold. Your people will sleep. You will have peace, for as long as you like.”

“What light?” said Lord Edric, though Tobin could tell from his voice that he knew.

“A certain lamp. A small thing. Brass, rather battered. Not worth a great deal to look at.” Varrick’s grey eyes rested on the Warden’s face. “It is a dangerous object in the hands of a child. And it does, if I may say so, belong to my mistress. It was taken from her a long time ago.”

Up on the beam, Tobin’s fingers dug into the wood. That’s a lie, he thought. That’s a lie, that’s a lie. Tell him it’s a lie.

“The Guild calls it witch-light,” said his father slowly.

“The Guild,” said Varrick, “is wiser than it knows.”

There was a silence. Lord Edric turned from the window and walked to his desk, and stood there, looking down at nothing. On the wall behind the desk hung a portrait of a woman with fair hair and a laughing mouth. Tobin saw his father’s eyes go to it, and stay there for a moment, and then come away, as if it had been too hot to touch.

“And the girl?” said Lord Edric. “The sweep who carries it?”

“Children are no concern of mine,” said Varrick lightly. “Do as you please with her.”

“And if I refuse?”

Varrick looked almost sorry. “Then I am afraid your lamps will go on being — unreliable. And the misunderstandings will go on happening. And one night there may be a misunderstanding that does not stop at the Low Quarter.” He leaned forward a little. “But I do not think you will refuse. You are a sensible man, Lord Warden. You have a great deal to keep. And for a man of your quality — perhaps there could be more. My mistress is generous to her friends. A seat at a larger table than this one.”

He said it as gently as if he were offering a cup of tea.

And as he said it, Tobin saw him do a strange thing. He laid his gloves on his knee, and with the thumb of his left hand he began to rub the palm of his right, slowly, round and round, the way you might rub a sore place without knowing you were doing it. From up in the ceiling Tobin could see the palm quite clearly. There was a scar across it: a long, pale, shiny scar, puckered at the edges, like an old burn.

His father was quiet for a long time. Tobin, lying on the beam in the dark, wished with his whole body, as hard as he had ever wished anything: Say no. Please. Say no. Be the man she married. Say no.

“Very well,” said Lord Edric Harrowgate. “You shall have it.”

Varrick stood up and bowed. “I knew we would understand each other.”

He drew on his gloves and went to the door. And at the door he stopped, and turned his head, and looked up — not quickly, not as if he had heard anything, but quite slowly and pleasantly — at the ceiling. At the plaster rose. At the crack beside it.

Tobin lay without breathing, his eye an inch from the gap, a single thread of dust drifting down from the beam beneath his chin.

“You have mice, my lord,” said Captain Varrick.

Then he went out.

Tobin did not remember crawling back. He remembered only that he was suddenly kneeling on his own workshop floor in the grey afternoon light, with cobwebs in his hair, and that he was shaking so hard he could not fit the screws back into the panel. He gave up and sat with his back against the bench.

Above him, on the Orrery, the glass beads along the north stretch of the wall flickered, faint and tired.

His father had said yes.

He had always known, in the way you know a thing without letting yourself look at it, that his father was afraid. Afraid of the dark beyond the wall, and of losing his place. But he had never thought — he had never once in his life thought — that his father would look at a lie, and know it was a lie, and say very well.

And now he had to go back to the Leaning Tower, and look at Wren, and decide.

Everyone wants something, she had said, in this very attic, with her chin up. She would think he had known all along. She would think he had been sent. And why should she trust the Warden’s son, when the Warden had just sold her?

He could say nothing. He could say his father was making plans, and leave it there. It would not even be a lie. Not exactly.

Tobin sat on the floor until the light at the window began to go. Then he got up, left the panel lying where it was, and ran.

The lamp in the round window was lit when he came up the wall-stair, and the door opened before he could knock. But it was Wren who opened it this time, not Old Ash.

“You came back,” she said. Just for a moment she sounded surprised. “You look like something the cat sicked up. What happened?”

Tobin opened his mouth. But before he could say anything, Old Ash, who was standing at the round window with his pole in his hand, said in a voice none of them had heard him use before:

“Come here. Both of you. Quietly.”

They went to the window.

Below the North Wall, on the inside, there ran a road, and along the road, in the last of the gloaming, a grey horse was walking. The rider on its back rode easily, looking up at the Ring-lamps as he passed them, one after another, the way a man might look at the locks on a house he meant to buy. Six grey shapes walked behind him. As they went by, each Ring-lamp dimmed a little, and did not quite come back.

Under the Leaning Tower, the rider stopped. He lifted his pale face, and looked up at the round window, and smiled.

Old Ash did not move. But Tobin, standing beside him, saw his face, and never forgot it. It was not angry. It was not afraid. It was the face of a man who has been told, all at once, that someone he loved has died — except that the someone was alive, and sitting on a grey horse below the window, smiling at him.

“Hm,” said Old Ash, very low. “So it’s you they sent, lad.”

Down on the road, the rider touched two fingers to his brow, like a salute, and rode on into the dusk.

“You know him,” said Wren.

“I taught him.” The old man let the curtain fall. His hands were not quite steady. “He was a Lamplighter once. The best I ever had. Quick and brave and clever, and kind — oh, he was kind, then. He could light a Ring-lamp in a gale at the full stretch of his pole. He took the oath at the Beacon with his hand held over the oath-flame, the way we all did, and it marked him, the way it marked us all.” He turned his own right hand over, and on the palm, faint and old, there was a pale mark across it, like a burn.

Tobin felt cold all over. “He’s got a scar,” he said. “There. Just like that. He rubs it. I saw him.”

Old Ash closed his eyes. “Does he,” he said. “Does he, now.”

“What happened to him?” said Wren.

“He fell,” said Old Ash. “Bargains will do that.” And he went out of the door onto the wall, into the dark, with his pole on his shoulder, and did not say anything more.

So then there was nobody in the tower but Tobin and Wren and the fox.

Tobin sat down on the bench. He took off his spectacles, and put them on again. And then, because he found that he could not bear to sit there for one more minute with the thing inside him, he told her. All of it. The gate, the beam, the dark, the voice like oil, the portrait on the wall. And very well. You shall have it.

Wren did not interrupt him once. When he had finished she was standing quite still in the middle of the room with her arms folded, and her face had gone the way he had known it would: closed, like a shop with the shutters down.

“So,” she said. “Your dad’s going to sell me.”

“Yes.”

“And you’ve come to tell me.” Her voice was very flat. “Why? So I’ll run, and you can tell him which way? Or so I’ll hand it over nicely, so nobody gets hurt? Go on. Which one is it? Everybody wants something.”

“Neither,” said Tobin. His voice came out wobbly, and he made it steady. “I came to tell you because it’s true. And because he’s wrong. And because Captain Varrick is a liar, and I heard him lie, and my father heard it too, and said yes anyway.” He swallowed. “He’s my father. I’m not going to pretend he isn’t. But I’m not on his side. Not about this.”

Wren looked at him for a long time. In her lap — she had sat down without noticing — Cinder’s spark was burning brighter than it had all day.

“You’d pick a sweep,” she said slowly, “over the Warden.”

“I’d pick—“ Tobin stopped. He did not know how to say it without sounding like a book. “I’d pick you not being sold,” he said at last. “That’s all.”

Wren turned her face away, very quickly, and looked hard at the stuffed owl.

“That night-lamp of yours,” she said, after a while, to the owl. “The little one. You sleep with it.”

Tobin’s ears went hot. “How did you—“

“I’m not blind.” She still did not look at him. “I won’t tell. That’s all. I won’t tell anyone.”

It was not much. It was, Tobin thought afterwards, perhaps the most anyone in Soot Lane had ever given anyone for nothing. His throat was too tight to say thank you, so he just nodded, and Wren nodded at the owl, and that was that.

The door opened, and Old Ash came in with the cold on his coat.

“Well,” he said, looking from one to the other. “Hm. Good.” He hung up his pole. “We can’t stay. Not now. There’s only one place in Gloamhaven where that lamp will be safe, and only one place where whatever’s broken might be mended, and that’s the Bright Mountain, where the Flame began. But it’s a long way, and the road isn’t on any map you can buy. I’ll need my charter, and my old map, the one the Lamplighters kept. The Guild took both when they turned me out.” He sat down heavily. “They’re in the vault under the Guild Hall.”

Wren’s head came up. For the first time since Tobin had walked through the door, something lit in her eyes.

“A vault,” she said. “Now that’s something I know about.”
