And Cinder would get them out again, if it came to that, because Cinder could smell a watchman through three floors and a door. “Step one,” breathed Tobin, reading his paper by the red glow of Cinder’s tail. “Enter by the north flue of the great hall fireplace, which, according to the builder’s drawings—“ “I know what a flue is.” Wren was already prising the iron cap off the nearest chimney. A breath of cold, sooty air rose out of the dark. “Not lit. They never light this one. Too mean to buy the coal. Feet against one side, back against the other, and if you get stuck, don’t shout.” Tobin looked into the black hole and swallowed so loudly that she heard it. Then he lit his mother’s little night-lamp with fingers that shook only slightly, hooked it to his collar, and followed her down. If you have never been down a chimney, I can tell you that it is worse than going up one. You cannot see your feet. Soot gets into your ears and up your nose and somehow, mysteriously, into your socks. Wren went down that flue the way other girls go down a staircase. Tobin went down it the way a sack of potatoes goes down a well, with a great deal of bumping and one long, muffled squeak, and came out at the bottom in such a cloud of soot that for a moment he looked like a chimney himself. They stood in a fireplace big enough to park a cart in. Before them lay the great hall of the Lamp Guild: gilded pillars marching away into the gloom, portraits of past Guild Masters frowning down from the walls, each one rounder and glossier than the last. The air smelled of lavender and floor polish. Cinder dropped out of the chimney behind them, shook herself, and sneezed. A little spray of sparks danced across the polished floor. “Shh!” said both children at once. Cinder gave them a look that said she would sneeze when she pleased, thank you, and trotted off between the pillars with her nose down. The vault lay at the bottom of a short stone stair behind a door marked GUILD OFFICERS ONLY in gold letters. The door was not even locked. (“Why would it be?” said Wren. “Everyone’s too frightened of the Guild to try it.”) But the vault door itself was another matter. It was iron, painted dark green, with brass hinges as thick as Wren’s arm. In the middle was a round brass plate set with five little dials, each marked round its edge with tiny numbers. Behind the plate, if you put your ear to it, you could hear a faint, steady ticking, like a clock in another room. Tobin put his ear to it, and his whole face changed. Wren had seen that look before, in his attic, when he showed her the Orrery. It was the look of a boy who has forgotten to be afraid because something more interesting has come along. “Oh,” he breathed. “It’s a Pellingham. A Pellingham Patent Five-Tumbler. I’ve only ever seen the drawings. Listen — every time a dial passes the right number, a tumbler drops, but the clock keeps turning, so if you don’t set the next dial before the tick comes round again, it resets all of them, which means—“ “Which means can you open it or not?” “Which means you have to listen for the drop between the ticks. It’s actually rather beautiful. Mister Pellingham was a—“ “Tobin.” “Yes. Sorry. Hold the lamp closer.” He laid his long ink-stained fingers on the first dial and turned it, very slowly, with his ear pressed flat to the brass. Tick, went the lock. Tick. Tick. And then, so small that Wren almost missed it, a tiny tock, like a pebble dropping into a cup. “One,” whispered Tobin. On the fourth dial he went wrong, and the lock gave a soft, disappointed whirr, and all the tumblers clicked back up again. Wren said “Rot!” under her breath, and he said “Sorry, sorry,” and his fingers began to tremble. She did not say anything else. She only held the lamp steadier. The second time, he got all five. The last tumbler dropped with a heavy, satisfied clunk, and the great green door swung inward an inch on its own weight. Tobin sat back on his heels, grinning all over his sooty face. “Not bad,” said Wren, “for a nob.” It was the nicest thing she had ever said to him, and they both knew it. The vault was a long low room lined with shelves of strongboxes, tin tubes and leather ledgers with the years stamped on their spines in gold. Wren slipped the lamp from her coat, just enough to see by, and its warm golden glow ran along the shelves like honey. She found Ash’s things almost at once, because they were the only things there that did not look as if they belonged. They had been shoved on a bottom shelf behind a crate: a tin tube with a cracked blue seal, and a bundle in oilcloth, with a label in the Guild’s spiky handwriting — CONFISCATED. PROPERTY OF THE EXPELLED MASTER LAMPLIGHTER. NOT TO BE RETURNED. The tube held a sheet of thick creamy paper with a little painted lamp at the top and a great many signatures at the bottom. The oilcloth held a map, folded so many times that it had gone soft as cloth. “Got them,” said Wren. “Come on.” But Tobin had taken a ledger off the shelf, because Tobin could never walk past a book without opening it, and his mouth was slowly coming open. “Wren. Listen to this. Ring oil, purchased, four thousand gallons. Canal water added, one thousand two hundred gallons. Sold to the Ring account at full price, five thousand two hundred gallons.” He turned the page. “They’re watering the oil. They’ve been doing it for years. And here — Flame tokens, struck, twenty thousand, at one farthing each. Sold in the Low Quarter at tuppence, blessed at the Beacon. Blessed! They’re bits of tin, Wren! They sell bits of tin to people who can’t afford bread and tell them it’ll keep the Hollows off, and all the while they’re watering the oil that actually does keep the Hollows off, and that’s why the Ring’s failing, it’s not the dark times at all, it’s — it’s them!” His voice had climbed higher and higher. Cinder flattened her ears at him. Wren only shrugged. She had a Flame token herself, somewhere in the bottom of her coat. Mott had sold it to her for a week of her bread money. “Course it’s them,” she said. “It’s always them. What did you think it was?” “But it’s wrong.” “Lots of things are wrong. Doesn’t stop them. Put it in my bag, if you want it. Ash’ll like it.” He was still putting it in her bag when the first Gutterling dropped out of the ceiling. High in the vault wall was a small round grating, where an air-flue came in from above. Something was squeezing out between its bars — something about the size of a cat, black as the inside of a chimney, with long spidery fingers and two enormous round white eyes. It dropped onto the top shelf with a soft plop, sat up, and stared at the gilt lettering on the ledgers. “Shiny,” it whispered, in a voice like a squeaky hinge. A second one squeezed through behind it. Then a dozen more, in a sort of black trickle. “Gold on the books and gold on the box!” “Gilt on the lid and gilt on the locks!” “Oh, rot,” said Wren. The Gutterlings poured down the shelves like spilled ink. They scratched at the gilded corners of the strongboxes. They pulled the ledgers half out to lick the gold letters on the spines. One of them found a crate of Flame tokens, and the lid came off, and a great shining avalanche of tin went jingling and clattering across the stone floor, rolling into every corner, ringing like a hundred tiny bells. Far above them, up the stair, a voice said, “Eh? What was that?” “Out,” hissed Wren. “Out, out, out—“ But one Gutterling had dropped right in front of her, and it was not looking at the ledgers. It was looking at the front of her coat, where three brass buttons gleamed in the lamplight. It had a bent ear, a nose like a candle-snuffer and a sly, crooked face, and Wren knew it at once. It was the very Gutterling that had stolen her brush in the flues of Thornbury House, the day all this began. “Sweepy-girl!” it squeaked, delighted. “Sweepy-girl’s come again! Sweepy-girl’s got the shiny-shine!” “Snib,” said Wren grimly. “Shiny-shiny, mine-mine!” sang Snib, and reached for her buttons with both hands. She slapped his fingers away. He hopped back, offended, and opened his mouth very wide, and Wren had the horrible certainty that he was going to set up such a squealing that every watchman in the building would come running. So she did the only thing she could think of. She twisted the top button off her coat, thread and all, and held it up. Snib’s mouth shut with a snap. “Yours,” said Wren, “if you’re quiet.” “Quiet-quiet,” whispered Snib. “Quiet as mice.” He snatched the button, bit it, and hugged it to his narrow black chest. Then his bent ear twitched, and his eyes went wide in a new way. “Boots on the stair! Boots on the stair! Two big men with a lantern there!” Cinder was already growling. Wren heard it too — heavy boots, a jingle of keys, a man saying “Probably rats, Dobbs,” and another answering “Rats don’t jingle, Hobb.” Wren stuffed the lamp into her coat. “That’s the only stair!” squeaked Tobin. “Snib knows a way,” said Snib unexpectedly. “Up the flue and over the top, round the glass and never stop!” And he was off up the shelves like a spider, and through the grating, and gone. The grating was far too small for a person. But beside it Wren saw now a wider square of darkness — an old coal-chute, the kind of thing no grown-up ever noticed and every sweep knew. She shoved Tobin at the shelves. “Climb!” He climbed faster than she would have believed possible. Cinder went up past them both in two bounds. Wren went last, and as she pulled her feet into the chute, the two watchmen arrived at the bottom of the stair and stopped, and stared at the open vault, the floor shining with a thousand tin tokens, and a dozen Gutterlings sitting on the shelves licking the gilt off the ledgers. “Gutterlings!” roared one. “Get out of it, you thieving little smuts!” I am sorry to say that the Gutterlings did not get out of it. They threw tokens at him instead. It made a very great deal of noise, and it was the best thing that could have happened, because nobody thought to look up the coal-chute at all. The chute came out on a ledge just under the rim of the dome, where a small iron hatch stood open to the night. They squeezed out onto the roof — and stopped. The way to the drainpipe at the far corner was blocked by a gilded parapet too high to climb, and the only way round it was across the dome. Not over the top. Across its lower slope, along one of the iron ribs that held the glass in place — a narrow black rail running round the great curve like a line on a map. On either side of it was glass. And under the glass, a long, long way down, was the floor of the great hall, where lanterns were now bobbing about and voices were shouting, because the watchmen had woken the whole building. “No,” said Tobin. “Wren, I can’t. The thing is, technically, I’m not very good with heights either. I didn’t put that in the plan. I should have put that in the plan.” His face, in the glow of Cinder’s tail, had gone the colour of old porridge. He was clinging to the hatch-frame with both hands, and the night-lamp at his collar was shaking so hard its little flame danced. Wren thought of all the things she could say — you great lump, and get on with it, and we haven’t got time. And then, without quite knowing why, she said none of them. “Look at me,” she said instead. “Not down. Me. You put your foot where mine was. That’s all. That’s all a roof is.” “That’s not all a roof is.” “It is tonight.” She stepped out onto the rib. Under her feet the glass creaked — a long, thin, terrible sound, like ice on a pond. “Now you.” Tobin let go of the frame. He put one foot on the rib, and then the other. The glass creaked again, and he made a noise like a kettle just before it boils. “Me,” said Wren. “Look at me.” He looked at her. He put his foot where hers had been, and then the next, and the next. Cinder came behind him, light as a leaf, and once, when he wobbled, she pressed her small warm body against the backs of his legs and held him there. Halfway across, a man below lifted his lantern and looked straight up, and for one dreadful heartbeat Wren was certain he had seen them — but the dome was dark, and they were dark, and all he saw was the night. Three more steps. Two. One. Wren seized Tobin’s wrist and pulled him onto the solid leads, and they both sat down very suddenly with their backs against a chimney. “I,” said Tobin, and breathed for a while. “I did that.” “You did,” said Wren. And then, because she did not want him getting ideas: “Slowest I ever saw, mind.” On the parapet above them, something small and black sat admiring a brass button in the gloom. “Sweepy-girl owes Snib,” it remarked. “Button for quiet. Not for the way.” “Sweepy-girl’s out of buttons she can spare,” said Wren. Snib considered this, his big white eyes blinking slowly, as though some strange new thought had wandered into his head and he did not know what to do with it. Then he shook himself, squeaked “Buttons later! Buttons later!” and dropped away into a chimney-pot. It was nearly three in the morning when they came up the last crooked step of the Leaning Tower, black from head to foot, with soot in their hair and soot in their eyebrows and soot, Tobin discovered, in places he did not wish to discuss. Old Ash was waiting in his armchair by the round window, the stuffed owl watching over his shoulder. He did not say anything. He only held out his hands. Wren gave him the tin tube. He drew out the charter and spread it on his knees and touched the little painted lamp at the top with one long finger, very gently, the way you might touch the face of someone you had not seen in thirty years. Then he unwrapped the map, and something in his face that had been tight for a long time seemed to loosen. “Hm,” he said roughly. “Well. Well, well.” “And this,” said Tobin, and laid the ledger on top, open at the page about the canal water. Old Ash read it in silence. Cinder, who had already found the biscuit tin, crunched loudly in the corner. “Proof,” said Ash at last. “Hm. Proof of what every poor soul in the Low Quarter has known in their bones for twenty years.” He looked at the two black-faced children over the top of the ledger, and there was something in his eyes that might have been pride and might have been worry and was probably both. “The Guild will hate you now, you know. Not just the witch-girl and the Warden’s boy. The ones who know.” “They hated me already,” said Wren. “They didn’t know my name,” said Tobin, a little faintly. “They will.” Ash heaved himself up and reached for the teapot. “Tea. You’ve earned it. No — forgive me — you’ve had it coming, which is quite a different thing.” Wren, who had tasted Ash’s tea before, opened her mouth to say she was not thirsty, thank you, not in the least. But she never said it. Cinder had stopped crunching. The fox had gone stiff all over, her nose to the round window, her tail-spark flaring white, and a low growl was rolling in her throat like distant thunder. Wren turned to the window. Out across the dark city, the long curve of the Ring-lamps stood along the wall like a string of dim yellow beads. As she watched, the one nearest the tanneries flickered — and went out. Then the one beside it. Then the next, and the next, one after another, quite steadily, the way you might pinch out candles at the end of a long evening — marching along the wall towards Soot Lane, and the canal, and the bakery, and the loft over Mott’s yard where Nettle slept. And behind each one, where the light had been, the dark came over the wall like a tide.

fields.title: The Long Dark of Soot Lane
fields.body_html:
Wren was out of the door before anyone could stop her.

She did not remember the stairs of the Leaning Tower afterwards, nor the drop from the wall to the roofs below. She only remembered running, and the cold, and the sound her own breath made. Behind her she heard Old Ash call her name once, sharply, and then Tobin’s boots clattering after her, and the soft quick patter of Cinder overtaking them both.

“Wren! Wait — Wren, you don’t even know—“

“Nettle’s in the loft,” she flung over her shoulder. “Nettle’s always in the loft. She’ll be on her own.”

Up on the wall behind them a light was moving. Wren glanced back once and saw it — a tall stooped shape with a long pole, striding along the battlements towards the nearest dead Ring-lamp, the brass hook at the end of the pole held up like a question. Ash had not followed them. He had gone the other way, towards the lamps, to do the thing he had done every night for thirty years while the city laughed at him. Wren had no time to wonder whether one old man could relight a whole wall before the dark got in. She already knew the answer.

If you have ever walked into a house where the fire has been out for a week, you will know the particular cold that met them at the edge of the Low Quarter. It was not the clean cold of a winter morning. It was a stale, heavy, hopeless cold that seemed to come up out of the ground and settle on your shoulders like a wet coat, and it made you want, very badly, to sit down.

“Don’t,” said Wren, when she saw Tobin slow. “Don’t stop. That’s how it gets you.”

“How do you know?”

“I don’t. Keep running.”

The Low Quarter had never been bright. But it had always been noisy — dogs and babies and arguments, the clank of the tannery, someone singing badly in a gin-shop. Tonight there was nothing. Their own footsteps sounded far too loud. The washing-lines strung between the leaning houses hung perfectly still, and the shirts and sheets pegged on them had gone the same flat grey as the walls, so that it was hard to tell where the washing ended and the street began.

And there were people. That was the worst of it.

They were sitting in the doorways. A man on a step with a broom across his knees, staring at nothing. A woman at an open window with a teacup halfway to her mouth, not moving. Two boys Wren knew from the tannery, sitting back to back in the gutter, as quiet as stones. All of them grey. Grey faces, grey hands, grey hair. Not hurt — Wren could see them breathing — but emptied, as if someone had come along with a cloth and wiped away everything that made them who they were.

“Mister Crabbe,” said Wren, stopping in front of the man with the broom. “Mister Crabbe, it’s Wren. You chased me off your step last week, remember? For sitting on it?”

The man looked at her. His eyes were the colour of dishwater.

“Who?” he said politely.

Wren backed away from him. Tobin had his hand over his mouth. His night-lamp, hooked to his collar, was burning steadily, and in its little circle of yellow light the colour of the cobbles came back very faintly — a hint of brown, a smudge of moss-green between the stones — and then faded again at the edge, like the tide going out.

Cinder growled.

At the end of the lane, where it opened onto the canal, the Hollows were drifting.

There were five of them, or six — it was hard to count, because they did not quite keep their edges. They were like smoke poured into the outline of a person, tall and thin and faceless, and they did not walk so much as lean forward and let the dark carry them. They made no sound at all. Where they passed, a front door that had been painted some colour once was suddenly no colour whatever. A cat on a wall went grey from nose to tail and sat down, quite still, and did not wash itself.

Wren did not wait to see more. She ducked under a washing-line, round the back of the chandler’s, and in through the broken gate of Gristle Mott’s sweep yard.

The yard was empty. The brushes stood against the wall in their racks. Mott’s own window above the coal store was shuttered tight — he had a Flame token nailed to the shutter, Wren noticed, a little tin disc winking in the gloom, and it was doing exactly as much good as Tobin had said it would. She scrambled up the ladder to the loft where the little sweeps slept, and put her head through the hatch.

“Nettle?”

Four small faces looked back at her out of the straw, white and terrified, but not grey. Not yet. Tam and the two Hallet boys and little Sal, huddled in a heap under one blanket.

“Where’s Nettle?”

“She went out,” whispered Sal. “When the lamps went. She said you’d be out there in the dark and you’d want someone with you. She said—“ Sal’s lip wobbled. “She said Wren’s not scared of anything but Wren still ought to have someone.”

Wren stood quite still on the ladder.

“Which way?”

“Bakery,” said Tam. “She said she’d look at the bakery first. You always go there.”

“Stay here. Don’t open the hatch for anyone but me. Not even Mott. Especially not Mott.”

She slid down the ladder without using the rungs.

They found her outside Mrs Fenn’s.

The bakery stood near the bottom of Soot Lane, with its bow window and its sign of a wheatsheaf, and on any other night it would have smelled of tomorrow’s loaves rising. Tonight the window was dark. Mrs Fenn herself was sitting just inside the open door, in her chair, where she had sat every day since the Hollows came the first time — grey, quiet, her floury hands folded in her lap — and her five children were crowded round her knees, the youngest asleep against her. The children had not been touched. They were simply too frightened to leave their mother, and too small to know what else to do.

And on the step outside, with her back against the doorpost, sat Nettle.

She was very small. She always had been, but she looked smaller now, with her knees drawn up and her arms round them. And she was grey. Her freckles were gone — not faded, gone, as if they had been rubbed out. Her hair was the colour of ash. Her lips were the colour of ash. Her eyes were open and looking at the street, but they were not looking at anything in it.

Three Hollows stood over her. They were bending down, slowly, the way a person bends to look into a well.

Wren did not think. She tore the lamp out of her coat and ran at them.

“Get off her! Get away from her, you — you filthy great — get off!”

She swung the lamp at the nearest Hollow like a club. She had seen it flare white-gold in this very lane, on the day the Hollows first came over the wall. She had seen them shriek and run. She wanted that now. She wanted them burned. She wanted them to hurt the way she hurt.

The lamp barely glowed.

It was as though she were swinging a cold coal. The little flame inside the cracked chimney shrank down to a bead, a pin-point, a dull orange smudge. The Hollow she had swung at did not even flinch. It turned its blank no-face towards her, and the cold coming off it was so bitter that it made her teeth ache.

“Burn!” shouted Wren. “Go on! Burn them!”

She swung again. The light grew dimmer. Behind her she heard Tobin shout something, and the small steady glow of his night-lamp came up beside her — ordinary Guild oil, watered oil, but it was something, and the Hollows leaned back from it a little, the way you lean back from a draught. Cinder darted in among them, snapping, her tail-spark blazing, and sneezed a shower of sparks into the nearest grey shape. It drifted back a pace. Only a pace. Then all three began, very slowly, to lean in again.

“It’s not working,” gasped Tobin. “Wren, it’s not working, why isn’t it—“

“I know it’s not working!”

She shoved past the Hollows — it was like shoving through freezing fog, and for a moment the whole world went grey at the edges and she could not remember why she was there — and dropped to her knees on the step in front of Nettle.

“Nettle. Nettle, it’s me.”

Nettle turned her head. She looked at Wren for a long moment, with polite, empty eyes.

“Who are you?” she said.

She did not lisp. That was the thing Wren could not bear, afterwards, when she thought about it. Nettle had always lisped, ever since her two front teeth fell out — Wren, you’re the betht — and now her voice was smooth and flat and perfectly correct, as though the lisp had been part of her and had been wiped away with all the rest.

“It’s Wren,” said Wren. Her voice cracked in the middle. “You know me. I’m Wren. I give you my crusts. I taught you to climb a stack. You said I was the best. You said it about a hundred times, you said it till I told you to shut up—“

“I don’t know anyone called that,” said Nettle, and turned back to look at the street.

Wren did not tell this part of the story often, and when she did, she told it quickly. She knelt on the step of Mrs Fenn’s bakery with the cold lamp in her hand and the Hollows leaning over her, and something inside her that had held on all her life — through Mott and the debts and the cold garret and the empty belly and all the years of knowing that nobody gives anybody anything — simply let go. She was too tired to swing the lamp again. She was too tired to shout. She had nothing left to fight with and nothing to bargain with. She had no buttons and no money, no plan and no clever lie. There was nothing she could do.

So she stopped trying to do anything.

She did not raise the lamp. She did not aim it at the Hollows. She only turned to Nettle and held it out to her in both hands, low down, the way you might hold out a cup of milk to a very small child.

“Here,” she said. “Here, Nettle. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything. You don’t have to pay. It’s just for you.”

And the lamp blazed.

It did not flicker up. It did not slowly brighten. It blazed, all at once, as if it had only been waiting to be asked properly — a great soft burst of golden-white light that filled the doorway and spilled into the lane and ran up the fronts of the leaning houses like sunrise running up a hill. It was warm. It was so warm that Wren felt it on her face like a hand. It smelled of bread, and of summer, and of something else she had no name for.

And in that light, Nettle’s freckles came back.

They came back one at a time, like stars coming out — first one on her nose, then three across her cheek, then all of them at once, a whole spattered handful. Then the pink came into her cheeks, faint and then deeper, the way colour comes into a cold hand when you hold it to the fire. Then her hair, not grey but mousy-brown and tangled. Then her eyes — and they were not dishwater-coloured at all, Wren saw. They were blue. She had never in her life known that Nettle’s eyes were blue.

Nettle blinked. She looked at the lamp. Then she looked up at Wren, and her whole small face crumpled with relief.

“Wren?” she said. “Wren, I wath looking for you. I wath looking for you everywhere.”

Behind them the Hollows screamed.

It was the same high, thin, tearing shriek Wren had heard on market day, like a nail drawn slowly down a slate. They reeled back out of the light. Where its edge touched them, they seemed to fray, like smoke in a gust, and then they were fleeing — not drifting now, but fleeing, streaming away down Soot Lane and over the canal and back towards the dark gap in the wall, and the cold went with them.

The lane was silent. Then, somewhere up the street, a dog barked. It was the first ordinary sound Soot Lane had made all night.

Wren did not hear it. She had her arms round Nettle, and the lamp was squashed between them, and it did not burn either of them in the least.

“You great lump,” she said into Nettle’s hair. “You great, stupid lump. What did you go out for?”

“For you,” said Nettle, muffled. “Thomebody had to.”

They went into the bakery, because it was the nearest door and because Mrs Fenn’s children were crying. Tobin shut the door behind them and wedged a chair under the handle, and Cinder sat down in front of it with her tail-spark glowing and her ears up. The lamp stood on the counter between the empty bread trays, and its light filled the little shop to every corner. In it, Hettie Fenn’s dress turned out to be green.

“Green,” she whispered, holding out the skirt. “Is that what green is?”

Tobin was walking up and down, which was what he did instead of being afraid.

“It’s the law,” he said. “It must be. What Ash told us. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given. When you used it to get something — even something good, even getting them away from her — it wouldn’t. Because that was taking. Using it. But when you just gave it—“ He pushed his spectacles up his nose with a sooty finger. “It’s not a weapon at all, is it? It’s a — it’s a present. It only works as a present. That’s extraordinary. Technically, that’s the most extraordinary—“

“Stop it,” said Wren.

He stopped.

She was sitting on the floor against the counter with Nettle half asleep in her lap. She did not look at the lamp. She did not want to look at it. For the first time since she had found it in the flue at Thornbury House, it frightened her — more than the Hollows had, more than Mott ever had. Because she understood it now, a little, and she did not like what she understood.

All her life Wren had known how the world worked. Everything costs. You want bread, you pay for it or you nick it. You want a roof, you work it off. You want somebody to look after you, you’d better be useful, or they’ll stop. It was a hard way to live, but at least you knew where you were. You knew the rules. You could be clever about them.

But you could not be clever about this. You could not trick it, or bargain with it, or make it do anything. It only did what it did when you let go. When you gave it away. And Wren had never in her life given anything away without a reason, and she did not know how to do it twice, and she did not know what it would cost her in the end.

“It’s not fair,” she said in a low voice.

“What isn’t?”

“That it won’t fight. That it’s got to be given.” She glared at the lamp. “What use is that? What use is a thing you can’t keep hold of?”

Tobin opened his mouth, and then, for once in his life, shut it again without saying anything.

In the corner Mrs Fenn sat in her chair with her floury hands in her lap, grey and quiet, her five children round her knees. Wren looked at her for a long moment. Then she lifted Nettle gently off her lap, and got up, and picked up the lamp. Her hands were not quite steady.

She had taken one step towards Mrs Fenn’s chair when Cinder began to growl.

It was not her Hollow-growl. It was lower, angrier. Tobin went to the window and lifted a corner of the blind.

“Lights,” he said. “Lanterns. Lots of them. Coming up the lane.”

Wren came and looked. Up from the canal end of Soot Lane came a procession of lanterns, swinging, a dozen at least, and in their yellow glow she could see the dark coats and brass buttons of the Warden’s guard, and the glint of their pikes. And walking in front of them all, puffing and wheezing, his big red knuckles wrapped round a lantern of his own, was a man she would have known anywhere, by his shape alone, by the way he walked, by the smell of gin she could almost smell from here.

Gristle Mott stopped in the middle of the lane. He lifted his lantern high. And then he turned to the guards behind him and pointed straight at the bakery window.

“In there,” he said. “That’s her. That’s the witch-girl. Now where’s my reward?”
fields.body_text: Wren was out of the door before anyone could stop her. She did not remember the stairs of the Leaning Tower afterwards, nor the drop from the wall to the roofs below. She only remembered running, and the cold, and the sound her own breath made. Behind her she heard Old Ash call her name once, sharply, and then Tobin’s boots clattering after her, and the soft quick patter of Cinder overtaking them both. “Wren! Wait — Wren, you don’t even know—“ “Nettle’s in the loft,” she flung over her shoulder. “Nettle’s always in the loft. She’ll be on her own.” Up on the wall behind them a light was moving. Wren glanced back once and saw it — a tall stooped shape with a long pole, striding along the battlements towards the nearest dead Ring-lamp, the brass hook at the end of the pole held up like a question. Ash had not followed them. He had gone the other way, towards the lamps, to do the thing he had done every night for thirty years while the city laughed at him. Wren had no time to wonder whether one old man could relight a whole wall before the dark got in. She already knew the answer. If you have ever walked into a house where the fire has been out for a week, you will know the particular cold that met them at the edge of the Low Quarter. It was not the clean cold of a winter morning. It was a stale, heavy, hopeless cold that seemed to come up out of the ground and settle on your shoulders like a wet coat, and it made you want, very badly, to sit down. “Don’t,” said Wren, when she saw Tobin slow. “Don’t stop. That’s how it gets you.” “How do you know?” “I don’t. Keep running.” The Low Quarter had never been bright. But it had always been noisy — dogs and babies and arguments, the clank of the tannery, someone singing badly in a gin-shop. Tonight there was nothing. Their own footsteps sounded far too loud. The washing-lines strung between the leaning houses hung perfectly still, and the shirts and sheets pegged on them had gone the same flat grey as the walls, so that it was hard to tell where the washing ended and the street began. And there were people. That was the worst of it. They were sitting in the doorways. A man on a step with a broom across his knees, staring at nothing. A woman at an open window with a teacup halfway to her mouth, not moving. Two boys Wren knew from the tannery, sitting back to back in the gutter, as quiet as stones. All of them grey. Grey faces, grey hands, grey hair. Not hurt — Wren could see them breathing — but emptied, as if someone had come along with a cloth and wiped away everything that made them who they were. “Mister Crabbe,” said Wren, stopping in front of the man with the broom. “Mister Crabbe, it’s Wren. You chased me off your step last week, remember? For sitting on it?” The man looked at her. His eyes were the colour of dishwater. “Who?” he said politely. Wren backed away from him. Tobin had his hand over his mouth. His night-lamp, hooked to his collar, was burning steadily, and in its little circle of yellow light the colour of the cobbles came back very faintly — a hint of brown, a smudge of moss-green between the stones — and then faded again at the edge, like the tide going out. Cinder growled. At the end of the lane, where it opened onto the canal, the Hollows were drifting. There were five of them, or six — it was hard to count, because they did not quite keep their edges. They were like smoke poured into the outline of a person, tall and thin and faceless, and they did not walk so much as lean forward and let the dark carry them. They made no sound at all. Where they passed, a front door that had been painted some colour once was suddenly no colour whatever. A cat on a wall went grey from nose to tail and sat down, quite still, and did not wash itself. Wren did not wait to see more. She ducked under a washing-line, round the back of the chandler’s, and in through the broken gate of Gristle Mott’s sweep yard. The yard was empty. The brushes stood against the wall in their racks. Mott’s own window above the coal store was shuttered tight — he had a Flame token nailed to the shutter, Wren noticed, a little tin disc winking in the gloom, and it was doing exactly as much good as Tobin had said it would. She scrambled up the ladder to the loft where the little sweeps slept, and put her head through the hatch. “Nettle?” Four small faces looked back at her out of the straw, white and terrified, but not grey. Not yet. Tam and the two Hallet boys and little Sal, huddled in a heap under one blanket. “Where’s Nettle?” “She went out,” whispered Sal. “When the lamps went. She said you’d be out there in the dark and you’d want someone with you. She said—“ Sal’s lip wobbled. “She said Wren’s not scared of anything but Wren still ought to have someone.” Wren stood quite still on the ladder. “Which way?” “Bakery,” said Tam. “She said she’d look at the bakery first. You always go there.” “Stay here. Don’t open the hatch for anyone but me. Not even Mott. Especially not Mott.” She slid down the ladder without using the rungs. They found her outside Mrs Fenn’s. The bakery stood near the bottom of Soot Lane, with its bow window and its sign of a wheatsheaf, and on any other night it would have smelled of tomorrow’s loaves rising. Tonight the window was dark. Mrs Fenn herself was sitting just inside the open door, in her chair, where she had sat every day since the Hollows came the first time — grey, quiet, her floury hands folded in her lap — and her five children were crowded round her knees, the youngest asleep against her. The children had not been touched. They were simply too frightened to leave their mother, and too small to know what else to do. And on the step outside, with her back against the doorpost, sat Nettle. She was very small. She always had been, but she looked smaller now, with her knees drawn up and her arms round them. And she was grey. Her freckles were gone — not faded, gone, as if they had been rubbed out. Her hair was the colour of ash. Her lips were the colour of ash. Her eyes were open and looking at the street, but they were not looking at anything in it. Three Hollows stood over her. They were bending down, slowly, the way a person bends to look into a well. Wren did not think. She tore the lamp out of her coat and ran at them. “Get off her! Get away from her, you — you filthy great — get off!” She swung the lamp at the nearest Hollow like a club. She had seen it flare white-gold in this very lane, on the day the Hollows first came over the wall. She had seen them shriek and run. She wanted that now. She wanted them burned. She wanted them to hurt the way she hurt. The lamp barely glowed. It was as though she were swinging a cold coal. The little flame inside the cracked chimney shrank down to a bead, a pin-point, a dull orange smudge. The Hollow she had swung at did not even flinch. It turned its blank no-face towards her, and the cold coming off it was so bitter that it made her teeth ache. “Burn!” shouted Wren. “Go on! Burn them!” She swung again. The light grew dimmer. Behind her she heard Tobin shout something, and the small steady glow of his night-lamp came up beside her — ordinary Guild oil, watered oil, but it was something, and the Hollows leaned back from it a little, the way you lean back from a draught. Cinder darted in among them, snapping, her tail-spark blazing, and sneezed a shower of sparks into the nearest grey shape. It drifted back a pace. Only a pace. Then all three began, very slowly, to lean in again. “It’s not working,” gasped Tobin. “Wren, it’s not working, why isn’t it—“ “I know it’s not working!” She shoved past the Hollows — it was like shoving through freezing fog, and for a moment the whole world went grey at the edges and she could not remember why she was there — and dropped to her knees on the step in front of Nettle. “Nettle. Nettle, it’s me.” Nettle turned her head. She looked at Wren for a long moment, with polite, empty eyes. “Who are you?” she said. She did not lisp. That was the thing Wren could not bear, afterwards, when she thought about it. Nettle had always lisped, ever since her two front teeth fell out — Wren, you’re the betht — and now her voice was smooth and flat and perfectly correct, as though the lisp had been part of her and had been wiped away with all the rest. “It’s Wren,” said Wren. Her voice cracked in the middle. “You know me. I’m Wren. I give you my crusts. I taught you to climb a stack. You said I was the best. You said it about a hundred times, you said it till I told you to shut up—“ “I don’t know anyone called that,” said Nettle, and turned back to look at the street. Wren did not tell this part of the story often, and when she did, she told it quickly. She knelt on the step of Mrs Fenn’s bakery with the cold lamp in her hand and the Hollows leaning over her, and something inside her that had held on all her life — through Mott and the debts and the cold garret and the empty belly and all the years of knowing that nobody gives anybody anything — simply let go. She was too tired to swing the lamp again. She was too tired to shout. She had nothing left to fight with and nothing to bargain with. She had no buttons and no money, no plan and no clever lie. There was nothing she could do. So she stopped trying to do anything. She did not raise the lamp. She did not aim it at the Hollows. She only turned to Nettle and held it out to her in both hands, low down, the way you might hold out a cup of milk to a very small child. “Here,” she said. “Here, Nettle. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything. You don’t have to pay. It’s just for you.” And the lamp blazed. It did not flicker up. It did not slowly brighten. It blazed, all at once, as if it had only been waiting to be asked properly — a great soft burst of golden-white light that filled the doorway and spilled into the lane and ran up the fronts of the leaning houses like sunrise running up a hill. It was warm. It was so warm that Wren felt it on her face like a hand. It smelled of bread, and of summer, and of something else she had no name for. And in that light, Nettle’s freckles came back. They came back one at a time, like stars coming out — first one on her nose, then three across her cheek, then all of them at once, a whole spattered handful. Then the pink came into her cheeks, faint and then deeper, the way colour comes into a cold hand when you hold it to the fire. Then her hair, not grey but mousy-brown and tangled. Then her eyes — and they were not dishwater-coloured at all, Wren saw. They were blue. She had never in her life known that Nettle’s eyes were blue. Nettle blinked. She looked at the lamp. Then she looked up at Wren, and her whole small face crumpled with relief. “Wren?” she said. “Wren, I wath looking for you. I wath looking for you everywhere.” Behind them the Hollows screamed. It was the same high, thin, tearing shriek Wren had heard on market day, like a nail drawn slowly down a slate. They reeled back out of the light. Where its edge touched them, they seemed to fray, like smoke in a gust, and then they were fleeing — not drifting now, but fleeing, streaming away down Soot Lane and over the canal and back towards the dark gap in the wall, and the cold went with them. The lane was silent. Then, somewhere up the street, a dog barked. It was the first ordinary sound Soot Lane had made all night. Wren did not hear it. She had her arms round Nettle, and the lamp was squashed between them, and it did not burn either of them in the least. “You great lump,” she said into Nettle’s hair. “You great, stupid lump. What did you go out for?” “For you,” said Nettle, muffled. “Thomebody had to.” They went into the bakery, because it was the nearest door and because Mrs Fenn’s children were crying. Tobin shut the door behind them and wedged a chair under the handle, and Cinder sat down in front of it with her tail-spark glowing and her ears up. The lamp stood on the counter between the empty bread trays, and its light filled the little shop to every corner. In it, Hettie Fenn’s dress turned out to be green. “Green,” she whispered, holding out the skirt. “Is that what green is?” Tobin was walking up and down, which was what he did instead of being afraid. “It’s the law,” he said. “It must be. What Ash told us. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given. When you used it to get something — even something good, even getting them away from her — it wouldn’t. Because that was taking. Using it. But when you just gave it—“ He pushed his spectacles up his nose with a sooty finger. “It’s not a weapon at all, is it? It’s a — it’s a present. It only works as a present. That’s extraordinary. Technically, that’s the most extraordinary—“ “Stop it,” said Wren. He stopped. She was sitting on the floor against the counter with Nettle half asleep in her lap. She did not look at the lamp. She did not want to look at it. For the first time since she had found it in the flue at Thornbury House, it frightened her — more than the Hollows had, more than Mott ever had. Because she understood it now, a little, and she did not like what she understood. All her life Wren had known how the world worked. Everything costs. You want bread, you pay for it or you nick it. You want a roof, you work it off. You want somebody to look after you, you’d better be useful, or they’ll stop. It was a hard way to live, but at least you knew where you were. You knew the rules. You could be clever about them. But you could not be clever about this. You could not trick it, or bargain with it, or make it do anything. It only did what it did when you let go. When you gave it away. And Wren had never in her life given anything away without a reason, and she did not know how to do it twice, and she did not know what it would cost her in the end. “It’s not fair,” she said in a low voice. “What isn’t?” “That it won’t fight. That it’s got to be given.” She glared at the lamp. “What use is that? What use is a thing you can’t keep hold of?” Tobin opened his mouth, and then, for once in his life, shut it again without saying anything. In the corner Mrs Fenn sat in her chair with her floury hands in her lap, grey and quiet, her five children round her knees. Wren looked at her for a long moment. Then she lifted Nettle gently off her lap, and got up, and picked up the lamp. Her hands were not quite steady. She had taken one step towards Mrs Fenn’s chair when Cinder began to growl. It was not her Hollow-growl. It was lower, angrier. Tobin went to the window and lifted a corner of the blind. “Lights,” he said. “Lanterns. Lots of them. Coming up the lane.” Wren came and looked. Up from the canal end of Soot Lane came a procession of lanterns, swinging, a dozen at least, and in their yellow glow she could see the dark coats and brass buttons of the Warden’s guard, and the glint of their pikes. And walking in front of them all, puffing and wheezing, his big red knuckles wrapped round a lantern of his own, was a man she would have known anywhere, by his shape alone, by the way he walked, by the smell of gin she could almost smell from here. Gristle Mott stopped in the middle of the lane. He lifted his lantern high. And then he turned to the guards behind him and pointed straight at the bakery window. “In there,” he said. “That’s her. That’s the witch-girl. Now where’s my reward?”

fields.title: Taken
fields.body_html:
There was no back door to Mrs Fenn’s bakery. Wren knew that before she looked, because she had known every door in Soot Lane since she was four years old, but she looked anyway. Then she looked at the chimney, which was far too narrow, and at the window, which had a guard outside it, and at last she stopped looking and stood in the middle of the shop with the lamp in her hand and Nettle clinging to her coat.

“Wren,” said Tobin quickly. “Listen. If you go out the front with the lamp held up, they won’t dare—“

“They’ll dare,” said Wren. “There’s a reward.”

Someone knocked on the door. It was not a loud knock. It was a tired one.

“Open up, lass,” said a voice. “It’s Sergeant Bracken. I know you’re in there, and you know I know, so let’s not make a night of it. My knees won’t stand it.”

Wren opened the door.

Sergeant Bracken was a grizzled, square man with a grey moustache and a face like a worn-out boot. He looked down at her, and at Nettle hanging on her coat, and at the five Fenn children peering round their grey mother’s chair, and something in his face went sorry.

“Right,” he said heavily. “Right, then.”

Behind him, in the lantern-light, Gristle Mott was holding out his big red hand to a guardsman with a leather purse. The guardsman dropped the purse into it. Mott weighed it, grinned, and put it in his waistcoat.

“Pleasure doing business,” he wheezed. He caught Wren’s eye and had the grace, for one moment, to look away. Then he looked back, and the grace was gone. “Don’t look at me like that, girl. You’d have done the same. Everybody would.”

“No,” said Nettle suddenly, from behind Wren. “Wren wouldn’t.”

Mott laughed, and walked off down the lane, jingling.

They did not tie Wren’s hands. Bracken would not allow it. “She’s twelve,” he said, when one of his men brought out a cord. “And she’s not going anywhere. Are you, lass?” Wren said nothing. There was nowhere to go. A pair of the Warden’s men in better coats than Bracken’s had already taken hold of Tobin by both arms, and he was struggling and saying, “Let go — I’m the Warden’s son — let go of me—“ and one of them said, “We know who you are, young sir. That’s why we’re taking you home.”

Wren gave Nettle to Hettie Fenn. “Stay with them,” she said. “Don’t go out. Not for anything. Not for me.”

“Promith?” said Nettle.

“Promise.”

As they marched her up out of the Low Quarter, the guards talked among themselves in low voices, the way men do who think a child is not listening. Wren listened. She heard that the grey soldiers had come along the North Wall an hour ago, and taken the mad old lamplighter right off the battlements as he was lighting a lamp, pole and all. She heard that he had not fought them. She heard that his fox had bitten one of them through the boot and got away into the dark, and that nobody had been able to catch it.

She put her hand on the lamp inside her coat. It was warm. It was the only warm thing left.

The Warden’s Hall was the biggest, coldest building Wren had ever been inside, and the room they brought her to was the biggest and coldest room in it. It had a floor of grey stone and a ceiling so high she could not see it, and a fire in a great carved fireplace that gave no heat at all, as if it were only a picture of a fire. Tobin was there already, held by the two men in good coats, his face white and streaked with soot and tears he had not quite wiped off. And in front of the fire, very tall and very still, with silver at his temples and his hands clasped behind his back, stood Lord Edric Harrowgate.

He did not shout. Wren had expected shouting. Mott shouted. Grubb shouted. But the Warden of Emberwick only looked at her, the way you might look at a stain on a good tablecloth, and when he spoke his voice was low and perfectly even.

“You have something that belongs to this city,” he said. “Give it to me.”

“It doesn’t belong to the city.”

“It belongs,” said Lord Edric, “to whoever can keep the city safe. At dawn I will hand it to a man who has promised me that the Hollows will leave Emberwick and never come back. The Ring will hold. Your Low Quarter will hold. The little girl in the bakery will be safe. Do you understand me? I am offering you a bargain. A good one.”

“Father, he’s lying,” said Tobin. “Varrick’s lying, you heard him, I heard him, he never—“

“Be quiet, Tobin.”

“He let the lamps go out tonight! While you were waiting for him! Doesn’t that tell you—“

“I said be quiet.”

Tobin went quiet. Wren looked at him, and then at his father, and then at the guards on every side of her, and at the great cold fire that gave no heat. And a very old feeling came up inside her, the oldest feeling she had. It was the feeling she’d had every time Mott counted out her wages and docked them, and every time the baker’s boy chased her off, and every time she had lain in her garret and known — just known — that anything good she ever got would be taken off her in the end. Because that was how it worked. That was always how it worked. Nobs took. Mott took. The Guild took. Everybody always took everything in the end, and the only question was whether you let go of it before they broke your fingers.

She was frightened. She was so tired. And she was angrier than she had ever been in her life.

She pulled the lamp out of her coat. Its golden light ran across the grey stone floor, and for a moment the whole hall was warm, and her ribbon was red on her wrist.

Then she threw it down at Lord Edric’s feet.

“Take it, then!” she shouted. “I never asked for it! I never asked for any of it!”

The lamp struck the stone with a dull brassy clang and rolled over once on its side.

And it went out.

It did not flicker. It did not gutter. One moment it was burning, and the next it was simply dark — a small, dented, ugly brass thing lying on the floor with a cracked glass chimney, like something from the bottom of Grubb’s junk-tray. The warmth went out of the room. Wren’s ribbon, on her wrist, was a dull pinkish grey again.

She waited for the flame to come back. It always came back. She had thrown it in the canal and buried it in the tannery yard, and every time, every single time, it had come back to her.

It did not come back.

Lord Edric looked down at it for a long moment. He did not pick it up with his hands. He took a handkerchief from his pocket and lifted the lamp in that, carefully, the way you might pick up something that had once bitten you. But the brass was only cold.

“Take it to the strongroom,” he said to his steward. “Lock it in. I will bring it up myself at dawn.” He turned to Bracken. “And put the girl below.”

“My lord—“ said Bracken.

“Below, Sergeant.”

The cells under the Warden’s Hall were dry, at least, and they were not very dark, because a lantern hung at the end of the passage where Bracken sat on a stool with his back to the wall. Wren’s cell had a stone bench and a barred iron door with a heavy old lock. She sat on the bench and drew her knees up to her chin.

She was not going to cry. She never cried. Crying was for people who had somebody to hear it.

She thought of the lamp lying on the floor, dark. She thought of how it had blazed on Mrs Fenn’s step, when she had held it out to Nettle and asked for nothing. She thought of how she had said I never asked for it — and that was true, that was the whole point, she never had asked for it. Nobody had made her pay for it. It had just been there, in the flue, warm, waiting for her. It had come back every time she threw it away. It had been given.

And she had thrown it in the man’s face like a stone.

Wren put her forehead down on her knees, and for the first time in a very long time, she cried. She cried quietly, because Bracken was at the end of the passage. She cried for Nettle, and Mrs Fenn, and Old Ash taken off the wall, and Cinder alone in the dark. But mostly she cried because she had wanted the lamp, she had wanted it, more than she had ever wanted anything, and she had told it she didn’t. And it had believed her.

“I didn’t mean it,” she whispered to nobody. “I didn’t mean it.”

She tried to hum the song her mother used to sing. Morning comes, morning comes. But she could not get past the first line, and in that cold place it did not sound like a song about morning at all.

Tobin Harrowgate had been sent to bed, which was the sort of thing that happened to you, he reflected, even on the worst night in the history of Emberwick, if you happened to be thirteen.

He did not go to bed. He sat on the edge of it in his attic workshop with his mother’s night-lamp on the table in front of him and the Orrery of the Ring gleaming dimly in the corner, and he looked at the Orrery for a long time. All along the Low Quarter wall, its little glass beads were dark.

He knew where the strongroom was. Everybody in the Hall knew where it was. It was under the oldest part of the building, at the bottom of a long stone stair that went down and down into the rock, and the stair had no windows and no lamps, because his great-grandfather had thought lamps on a strongroom stair were an invitation to thieves. Tobin had been down it exactly once, when he was six, holding his father’s hand. He had counted the steps because counting was what he did when he was frightened. There were sixty-one. He had had nightmares about them for a year.

He also knew where the key-ring hung. It hung on a hook behind the door of his father’s study, under a dull painting of a horse, and the study was directly beneath the crawlway Tobin used for listening. He had seen his father hang the keys there a hundred times.

Nobody else can do it, said a small, sensible voice inside him. Ash is taken. Cinder’s gone. Wren’s locked up. It’s you or nobody.

Then it’s nobody, said another voice, a smaller and much more frightened one. Because I can’t. You know I can’t. It’s dark down there. It’s the darkest place in the whole city.

Tobin picked up the night-lamp. He looked at its little steady flame, the one that had been his mother’s, the one he had never once in eight years let go out.

Then he stood up.

The crawlway, the study, the hook behind the door: those were easy. He had done harder things that very night on top of a glass dome. The keys were cold and heavy and he wrapped them in his scarf so they would not jingle. The door to the strongroom stair was at the end of a passage in the old wing, and it opened with a groan, and beyond it the steps went down into a blackness so thick it looked solid.

He held up the night-lamp, and started down.

“One,” he whispered. “Two. Three.”

The walls were close on either side, and damp, and cold enough to steam his breath. The little lamp lit three steps below him and three above, and nothing else in the world. He went down slowly, one hand on the wall.

“Fifteen. Sixteen.”

The flame dipped.

“Twenty-two. Twenty-three.”

It dipped again, and spat, and hissed. Tobin stopped. He held the lamp up to his spectacles and looked at it, and with a horrible sinking feeling he understood. He had filled it two days ago from the Hall’s own store. Guild oil. Canal water added. He had read the very page.

“No,” he whispered. “No, please, not now—“

On the thirtieth step, the night-lamp went out.

I do not know whether you have ever been in total darkness. Not the darkness of a bedroom at night, where there is always a little grey at the window or a line of light under the door — but real darkness, the kind there is under the ground, where there has never been any light at all. It is not like closing your eyes. When you close your eyes you know you could open them. In real darkness you open your eyes as wide as they will go, and it makes no difference whatever.

Tobin stood on the thirtieth step and could not move.

His hands were shaking so hard he nearly dropped the keys. His heart was going so fast it seemed to fill his whole chest. He could not tell which way was up. He could not tell how far down the stair went, or whether there were still steps in front of him at all, or whether he was standing on the edge of nothing. The dark pressed on his eyes and on his face and on his mouth. He wanted to turn and run back up. He could not even remember which way back up was.

He thought he would stand there forever.

And then, without at all meaning to, Tobin did something he had never done in his life. He had heard his mother do it, long ago, when he was very small and she thought he was asleep. His father said it was Lamplighter nonsense, and he had never tried it. He did not know how. He did not even know who he was talking to.

“If you’re there,” he whispered into the dark. His voice shook. “Whoever — whoever lit the first lamp. I can’t do this. I really can’t. Please.”

Nothing happened. No light came. The dark was exactly as dark as before.

But Tobin found, rather to his own surprise, that he had put out his foot and found the next step. And then the next.

“Thirty-one,” he whispered. “Thirty-two.”

He did not stop again. He counted every step out loud, one hand on the wet wall, and at sixty-one his foot came down on flat stone, and his outstretched hand touched iron. He felt for the lock. It took him a long time, in the dark, to find the right key. It took him even longer to fit it, because his hands would not stop shaking. But at last the bolt slid back, and the strongroom door swung open onto more darkness, and Tobin went in on his hands and knees, feeling his way along the cold floor.

His fingers touched brass.

He knew it at once — the dents, the little hook on top, the glass chimney with its hairline crack. He picked the lamp up in both hands. It was as cold as the floor. It was as cold as the stair. It was as cold as a thing that had never been lit at all.

Tobin sat back on his heels in the dark and held it.

“I know you’re not mine,” he said to it. His voice was hoarse. “I’m not going to keep you. I’m not even going to use you. I’m only taking you back to her. That’s all. She didn’t mean it. I’m taking you back to Wren.”

And in his hands, the lamp grew warm.

It came slowly, like the first warmth of a cup of tea in cold fingers. Then a spark woke in the heart of the brass, gold as a buttercup. Then a flame, small and steady and white-gold, that smelled of bread and summer — and the strongroom was full of light, and Tobin could see his own ink-stained hands, and the walls, and the open door, and the long stair climbing up and up away from him, every one of its sixty-one steps lit and golden and perfectly plain.

He was crying, a little. He did not mind.

He took the stairs two at a time.

Sergeant Bracken was asleep on his stool at the end of the passage, with his chin on his chest and his moustache going in and out. The key to the cells hung on his belt. Tobin looked at it for a long moment, and then decided he had stolen enough from grown-ups for one night.

He knelt at the door of Wren’s cell instead. She was sitting on the bench with her knees drawn up, staring at the light he carried as if she could not believe it was real.

“Hold this,” said Tobin, and passed the lamp through the bars without thinking.

Then he took out his mother’s compass. He opened the lid — Home is where the light is, said the little engraved letters inside, in the lamp’s gold glow — and very carefully, with the tip of his penknife, he prised up the glass and lifted out the long fine steel needle.

“That’s your mum’s,” said Wren.

“I can put it back. Probably. Technically, it’s only a matter of re-seating the pivot.” He bent the end of the needle against the stone floor, very slightly, and slid it into the keyhole. “It’s an old warded lock. Not like the Pellingham. You just have to feel for the — there’s a lever, and if you lift it while you turn—“

“Less talking,” whispered Wren. “More clicking.”

There was a click.

The cell door swung open with a long iron creak. Down the passage, Sergeant Bracken snorted and shifted on his stool, and did not wake.

Wren stepped out. She looked down at the lamp in her hands. She had not even noticed that she was holding it — that Tobin had simply given it to her, through the bars, the way you might hand someone back a thing they had dropped.

“I didn’t mean it,” she whispered, to the lamp, or to Tobin, or to someone else. “I never meant it. I want it. I want it.”

The lamp blazed up so brightly that the whole passage turned to gold. The ribbon on her wrist flushed red as a rose. And far away, beyond the walls of the Warden’s Hall, out across the dark city, the bells began to ring — not the slow bells of the hours, but quick, wild, jangling bells, one tower after another, all over Emberwick.

Something was terribly wrong.
fields.body_text: There was no back door to Mrs Fenn’s bakery. Wren knew that before she looked, because she had known every door in Soot Lane since she was four years old, but she looked anyway. Then she looked at the chimney, which was far too narrow, and at the window, which had a guard outside it, and at last she stopped looking and stood in the middle of the shop with the lamp in her hand and Nettle clinging to her coat. “Wren,” said Tobin quickly. “Listen. If you go out the front with the lamp held up, they won’t dare—“ “They’ll dare,” said Wren. “There’s a reward.” Someone knocked on the door. It was not a loud knock. It was a tired one. “Open up, lass,” said a voice. “It’s Sergeant Bracken. I know you’re in there, and you know I know, so let’s not make a night of it. My knees won’t stand it.” Wren opened the door. Sergeant Bracken was a grizzled, square man with a grey moustache and a face like a worn-out boot. He looked down at her, and at Nettle hanging on her coat, and at the five Fenn children peering round their grey mother’s chair, and something in his face went sorry. “Right,” he said heavily. “Right, then.” Behind him, in the lantern-light, Gristle Mott was holding out his big red hand to a guardsman with a leather purse. The guardsman dropped the purse into it. Mott weighed it, grinned, and put it in his waistcoat. “Pleasure doing business,” he wheezed. He caught Wren’s eye and had the grace, for one moment, to look away. Then he looked back, and the grace was gone. “Don’t look at me like that, girl. You’d have done the same. Everybody would.” “No,” said Nettle suddenly, from behind Wren. “Wren wouldn’t.” Mott laughed, and walked off down the lane, jingling. They did not tie Wren’s hands. Bracken would not allow it. “She’s twelve,” he said, when one of his men brought out a cord. “And she’s not going anywhere. Are you, lass?” Wren said nothing. There was nowhere to go. A pair of the Warden’s men in better coats than Bracken’s had already taken hold of Tobin by both arms, and he was struggling and saying, “Let go — I’m the Warden’s son — let go of me—“ and one of them said, “We know who you are, young sir. That’s why we’re taking you home.” Wren gave Nettle to Hettie Fenn. “Stay with them,” she said. “Don’t go out. Not for anything. Not for me.” “Promith?” said Nettle. “Promise.” As they marched her up out of the Low Quarter, the guards talked among themselves in low voices, the way men do who think a child is not listening. Wren listened. She heard that the grey soldiers had come along the North Wall an hour ago, and taken the mad old lamplighter right off the battlements as he was lighting a lamp, pole and all. She heard that he had not fought them. She heard that his fox had bitten one of them through the boot and got away into the dark, and that nobody had been able to catch it. She put her hand on the lamp inside her coat. It was warm. It was the only warm thing left. The Warden’s Hall was the biggest, coldest building Wren had ever been inside, and the room they brought her to was the biggest and coldest room in it. It had a floor of grey stone and a ceiling so high she could not see it, and a fire in a great carved fireplace that gave no heat at all, as if it were only a picture of a fire. Tobin was there already, held by the two men in good coats, his face white and streaked with soot and tears he had not quite wiped off. And in front of the fire, very tall and very still, with silver at his temples and his hands clasped behind his back, stood Lord Edric Harrowgate. He did not shout. Wren had expected shouting. Mott shouted. Grubb shouted. But the Warden of Emberwick only looked at her, the way you might look at a stain on a good tablecloth, and when he spoke his voice was low and perfectly even. “You have something that belongs to this city,” he said. “Give it to me.” “It doesn’t belong to the city.” “It belongs,” said Lord Edric, “to whoever can keep the city safe. At dawn I will hand it to a man who has promised me that the Hollows will leave Emberwick and never come back. The Ring will hold. Your Low Quarter will hold. The little girl in the bakery will be safe. Do you understand me? I am offering you a bargain. A good one.” “Father, he’s lying,” said Tobin. “Varrick’s lying, you heard him, I heard him, he never—“ “Be quiet, Tobin.” “He let the lamps go out tonight! While you were waiting for him! Doesn’t that tell you—“ “I said be quiet.” Tobin went quiet. Wren looked at him, and then at his father, and then at the guards on every side of her, and at the great cold fire that gave no heat. It was the feeling she’d had every time Mott counted out her wages and docked them, and every time the baker’s boy chased her off, and every time she had lain in her garret and known — just known — that anything good she ever got would be taken off her in the end. Because that was how it worked. That was always how it worked. Nobs took. Mott took. The Guild took. Everybody always took everything in the end, and the only question was whether you let go of it before they broke your fingers. She was frightened. She was so tired. And she was angrier than she had ever been in her life. She pulled the lamp out of her coat. Its golden light ran across the grey stone floor, and for a moment the whole hall was warm, and her ribbon was red on her wrist. Then she threw it down at Lord Edric’s feet. “Take it, then!” she shouted. “I never asked for it! And it had believed her. “I didn’t mean it,” she whispered to nobody. “I didn’t mean it.” She tried to hum the song her mother used to sing. Morning comes, morning comes. Tobin Harrowgate had been sent to bed, which was the sort of thing that happened to you, he reflected, even on the worst night in the history of Emberwick, if you happened to be thirteen. He did not go to bed. He sat on the edge of it in his attic workshop with his mother’s night-lamp on the table in front of him and the Orrery of the Ring gleaming dimly in the corner, and he looked at the Orrery for a long time. All along the Low Quarter wall, its little glass beads were dark. He knew where the strongroom was. Everybody in the Hall knew where it was. It was under the oldest part of the building, at the bottom of a long stone stair that went down and down into the rock, and the stair had no windows and no lamps, because his great-grandfather had thought lamps on a strongroom stair were an invitation to thieves. Tobin had been down it exactly once, when he was six, holding his father’s hand. He had counted the steps because counting was what he did when he was frightened. There were sixty-one. He had had nightmares about them for a year. He also knew where the key-ring hung. It hung on a hook behind the door of his father’s study, under a dull painting of a horse, and the study was directly beneath the crawlway Tobin used for listening. He had seen his father hang the keys there a hundred times. Nobody else can do it, said a small, sensible voice inside him. Ash is taken. Cinder’s gone. Wren’s locked up. It’s you or nobody. Then it’s nobody, said another voice, a smaller and much more frightened one. Because I can’t. You know I can’t. It’s dark down there. It’s the darkest place in the whole city. Tobin picked up the night-lamp. He looked at its little steady flame, the one that had been his mother’s, the one he had never once in eight years let go out. Then he stood up. The crawlway, the study, the hook behind the door: those were easy. He had done harder things that very night on top of a glass dome. The keys were cold and heavy and he wrapped them in his scarf so they would not jingle. The door to the strongroom stair was at the end of a passage in the old wing, and it opened with a groan, and beyond it the steps went down into a blackness so thick it looked solid. He held up the night-lamp, and started down. “One,” he whispered. “Two. Three.” The walls were close on either side, and damp, and cold enough to steam his breath. The little lamp lit three steps below him and three above, and nothing else in the world. He went down slowly, one hand on the wall. “Fifteen. Sixteen.” The flame dipped. “Twenty-two. Twenty-three.” It dipped again, and spat, and hissed. Tobin stopped. He held the lamp up to his spectacles and looked at it, and with a horrible sinking feeling he understood. It is not like closing your eyes. When you close your eyes you know you could open them. In real darkness you open your eyes as wide as they will go, and it makes no difference whatever. The dark pressed on his eyes and on his face and on his mouth. He wanted to turn and run back up. He could not even remember which way back up was. He thought he would stand there forever. His voice shook. “Whoever — whoever lit the first lamp. I can’t do this. I really can’t. Please.” Nothing happened. No light came. The dark was exactly as dark as before. He counted every step out loud, one hand on the wet wall, and at sixty-one his foot came down on flat stone, and his outstretched hand touched iron. He felt for the lock. It took him a long time, in the dark, to find the right key. It took him even longer to fit it, because his hands would not stop shaking. He knew it at once — the dents, the little hook on top, the glass chimney with its hairline crack. He picked the lamp up in both hands. It was as cold as the floor. It was as cold as the stair. It was as cold as a thing that had never been lit at all. Tobin sat back on his heels in the dark and held it. “I know you’re not mine,” he said to it. His voice was hoarse. “I’m not going to keep you. I’m not even going to use you. I’m only taking you back to her. That’s all. She didn’t mean it. I’m taking you back to Wren.” And in his hands, the lamp grew warm. It came slowly, like the first warmth of a cup of tea in cold fingers.
