fields.title: The Last Lamps of Emberwick
fields.body_html:
The bells of Emberwick had not all rung together for a hundred years, and they had forgotten how. The Guild Hall bell clanged, the cracked canal-watch bell clattered, a little tin bell in the Low Quarter went tink-tink-tink like a spoon in a cup, and none of them kept time. It was the most frightened sound Wren had ever heard a city make.

“That’s not the hour,” said Tobin, holding the cell door open. His hands were still shaking from the stair. “That’s the alarm. That’s every alarm. Technically speaking, they only do that if—“

“If what?”

Tobin did not answer. He was already running, and Wren, with the lamp warm against her chest and her ribbon glowing red as a robin on her wrist, ran after him.

They did not go down, towards the boots and shouts at the great doors. They went up, through a door that looked like a cupboard and a staircase that looked like a ladder, into the long, slanting workshop under the roof. Clocks ticked on every shelf. And on its round table sat the Orrery of the Ring.

It was a brass model of Emberwick’s wall, as wide as a cartwheel, set all round with a hundred and forty-four tiny glass beads, one for each Ring-lamp. Thin copper wires ran from every bead inwards, under a little brass city, to meet in the very middle at a single larger bead on a tall brass spire. On any ordinary night the beads glowed a weak, tired yellow, like the real lamps they copied.

As Wren and Tobin watched, the beads began to go out.

There was a sound, very small, like a breath let go, and a shiver ran round the whole brass ring. Every bead flickered and held, the way a candle holds when you have nearly blown it out. Then all hundred and forty-four went grey at once.

Tobin made a noise in his throat. “No. They can’t all go. Not at once. Some of them are Ash’s, he relit them only tonight—“

“Tobin.” Wren had gone to the little round window under the eaves. “Come and look.”

From the top of the Hill you could see the whole of Emberwick spread out like a map, and all the way round it, like a necklace on a dark neck, the wall with its Ring-lamps. Wren had never once thought it beautiful. It had only been there, the way the sky was there.

Now it was gone. The wall was a black line against a blacker sky. There was not one lamp burning on it anywhere.

And over the wall, everywhere at once, came the Hollows.

They came the way fog comes off a river: not climbing, not hurrying, only arriving, like grey water sliding over a weir. Wherever they went, the lit windows went dull, and the painted signs went dull, and the faces of the people running went dull, and a cold rose up the Hill that Wren could feel through the glass.

Then the voice began.

If you have ever been very tired, and somebody has tucked a blanket round you and told you that you need not get up after all, you will know a little of what that voice was like. It came out of the dark itself, from the gutters and chimneys and the black spaces under the eaves, and it was the sweetest voice Wren had ever heard. It was like warm milk. But it was like warm milk that has been left standing, and is going cold, and has a skin on it.

“Hush now,” said the voice, softly, all over the city at once. “Hush, little city. Where would you run to? You have been fighting the dark so long. Aren’t you tired? Lie down. It is easier in the grey.”

Down in the streets, Wren saw people stop running. Some of them sat down, right where they were, in the middle of the road.

“There is a child among you,” said the voice, and it grew warmer still, and somehow it seemed to be speaking straight into Wren’s ear. “A little sweep, with a little lamp. Give me the lamp, child, and I will let them all sleep. Give it to me, and no one need be cold any more.”

Wren’s hand had closed tight round the lamp under her coat. “Rot,” she said, but it came out as a whisper.

Tobin’s face had gone the colour of candle-wax. “It’s her,” he said. “Isn’t it? The Queen. The one in Ash’s story.”

“Don’t listen to it,” said Wren. She did not know how she knew this, but she knew it. “Whatever you do, don’t listen.”

They went out of the window and onto the roof, because there was nowhere else to go. Tobin was bad at roofs. He went along the lead gutter on his hands and knees, saying “Oh dear, oh dear” under his breath like a little old lady crossing an icy road. But he did not stop, and Wren, who had once laughed at him for exactly this, did not laugh now.

Halfway along the east side of the Hall, the gutter ran past a tall lit window, and Tobin stopped so suddenly that Wren nearly walked into him.

It was his father’s study.

Lord Edric Harrowgate stood in the middle of the room in his long dark coat. In the doorway, with his helmet in his hands and mud on his boots, stood Sergeant Bracken.

The window was shut, but the glass was thin and old, and Bracken was not a quiet man when he was upset.

“—never meant to keep it, my lord,” he was saying. “Never meant to. He’s opened the Grey Gate himself. The Hollows aren’t going round the city, they’re coming into it. He’s not after any peace. He’s after the girl, and he’ll have every street greyed to get her.”

Lord Edric said something too low to hear.

“Her cell’s empty, my lord.” Bracken turned his helmet in his hands. “What are your orders? The men are asking. The people are asking. They want the Warden.”

For a long moment Lord Edric said nothing. Then he went to the door, and Wren thought he was going to go down the Hill to stand in the streets with his people.

He did not. He shut the door in Bracken’s face. He turned the key. He went to his big desk and sat down behind it, and put his face in his hands.

Tobin made no sound at all. Wren was never sure, afterwards, whether that was worse than if he had cried out.

Then Lord Edric lifted his head, and his eyes went to the window, and he saw his son.

I am sorry to tell you that this is how it was. Father and son looked at one another through the old glass for perhaps two seconds: the boy out on the roof in the dark with his elbows scraped and his fair hair blowing, and the man in his warm room with the door locked. Wren saw something move in Lord Edric’s face. It might have been shame. It might have been fear. It might, just a little, have been love.

Then the Warden of Emberwick stood up, and crossed to the window, and drew the heavy curtain across it, and the light went out of the glass.

Tobin stayed where he was, on his hands and knees in the gutter.

“Tobin,” said Wren.

“He knew,” said Tobin, in a flat, careful voice, the voice of someone carrying something heavy and trying not to drop it. “He knew Varrick was lying and he— He’s just going to sit there. He’s going to sit there while—“ He stopped.

Wren did not know what to say. In Soot Lane nobody’s father drew curtains on them, because nobody in Soot Lane had a father, or curtains. In the end she reached out and took hold of his sleeve, the way Nettle sometimes took hold of hers, and gave it a small tug.

“Come on, you great lump,” she said, as kindly as she knew how. “He’s drawn his curtain. That doesn’t mean you have to draw yours.”

Tobin looked at her. He pushed his spectacles up his nose with a finger that was still shaking. Then he nodded, once, and kept going.

They had got as far as the corner of the roof, where the gutter met a forest of chimney-pots, when something small and grey shot out from behind the nearest chimney and hit Wren in the middle of the chest.

She very nearly fell off the Warden’s Hall. Then she saw the tail-tip, glowing like a coal that had just been blown on, and she sat down hard on the leads and threw both arms round it.

“Cinder! Oh, you daft thing, you daft thing—“

The ember-fox wriggled and licked her chin and then sneezed a little shower of sparks all over Tobin, which seemed to make her feel better. Her coat was singed and one ear had a new notch in it. But her spark was burning brighter than Wren had ever seen it, because she was near the Flame again and because she was glad.

And she was not alone.

Behind her, peering round the chimney-pot with two enormous white eyes, was a knee-high creature as black as the inside of a flue, looking at Wren’s coat-buttons the way a hungry dog looks at a sausage.

“Snib,” said Wren.

“Sweepy-girl!” squeaked the Gutterling, and bobbed. “Sweepy-girl, shiny-boy, fox-with-fire, all in a row! Snib knows roofs. Snib knows ways. Fox says come, so Snib says go!”

“Cinder brought you?” said Tobin. “But how could she— she can’t talk—“

“Fox bites,” said Snib, with feeling, and rubbed his bottom. “Fox bites, Snib comes. Old man says.” He hopped from one long foot to the other. “Old man broke the grey-cage! Old man’s out and in a rage! Old man’s coming to the square, old man says meet him there!”

Wren and Tobin looked at one another.

“Ash,” said Wren. “He’s escaped. They had him in a cage? At the Grey Gate?”

“Grey-cage, grey-cage,” agreed Snib. “Bent the bars with his long stick. Knights all fell down, very quick. Now old man’s fighting, street by street. Beacon Square is where we meet.”

“Beacon Square,” said Tobin slowly. “Why would he want us to go to—“ And then he stopped, and his eyes went wide behind his spectacles, and he said, “Oh.”

“What?”

“Oh.” He grabbed Wren’s arm so hard that she yelped. “The Orrery! The wires! I copied it from the old Lamplighter plan and I knew the wires all ran to the middle, but I never once asked why, I thought it was just plumbing, and they go to the middle because that’s where the fire comes from—“

“Tobin. Slower. Words.”

“The Beacon!” He was almost dancing on the gutter, which was not a safe thing to do. “The Great Beacon isn’t just a tower. It’s the source. Copper flame-pipes run from it under the whole city to every Ring-lamp on the wall. It’s a network! The Guild stopped lighting the Beacon years ago because it cost too much oil, and they’ve filled each lamp by hand ever since, which is why they keep failing, but the pipes are still there. If the source burns, the whole Ring burns. If you could light the Beacon—“

He looked at the lamp in Wren’s hands. Wren looked at it too. Its little flame burned golden-white and steady, no bigger than her thumb, and smelled of bread and summer.

“With this?” she said. “Tobin, it’s tiny.”

“Yes,” said Tobin, and swallowed. “Technically speaking, that is the part I haven’t worked out.”

“Buttons later?” said Snib hopefully, from behind the chimney. “Buttons later? Buttons later?”

“Buttons later,” said Wren. “Lots. Now get us to Beacon Square.”

I do not think anyone but a Gutterling could have done it. The roofs of Emberwick are like a sea frozen in the middle of a storm, all peaks and troughs and sudden drops, and the Gutterlings have their own paths across it: a plank between two gables, a rope of knotted rags over an alley, a gap between chimneys exactly wide enough for someone small. Snib scampered ahead, his white eyes shining back at them, squeaking “This way, this way, mind the slate, this way, quick, or we’ll be late!”

Below them, the streets were full of Hollows.

Wren could not help looking. On the steps of a big house, a lady in a fine coat sat quite still, staring at nothing. Her coat had been green, perhaps, or blue. It was grey now. On a bridge, a man turned slowly round and round, as if he had forgotten which way his house was.

“Lie down,” sang the sweet voice, out of the dark. “Lie down, lie down. It is so much easier.”

At the bottom of the Hill they crossed above the Guild Hall, and there they saw something that made Wren stop, crouching on a ridge-tile, with her mouth open.

The gilded doors of the Guild Hall stood wide. Guild clerks were staggering out under heavy iron strongboxes and heaving them into a covered wagon, and at the front of the wagon, his gold chain of office glinting, sat Guild Master Cuthbert Prowle.

“Faster, you snails, you sluggards!” he hissed. “Leave the candlesticks, there’s no time—“

A Hollow came drifting round the corner of the square.

Prowle shrieked like a trodden cat and flung a handful of little stamped tin discs at it. They bounced off the grey shape and lay in the road, and the Hollow did not even slow down.

“Flame tokens,” said Tobin, in great disgust. “He knows they don’t work. It’s in his own ledger—“

The wagon lurched off with a crack of the whip, the clerks clinging to the back. The tin tokens lay where they had fallen.

It was the most frightened sound Wren had ever heard a city make. “That’s not the hour,” said Tobin, holding the cell door open. His hands were still shaking from the stair. “That’s the alarm. That’s every alarm. Technically speaking, they only do that if—“ “If what?” Tobin did not answer. He was already running, and Wren, with the lamp warm against her chest and her ribbon glowing red as a robin on her wrist, ran after him. They did not go down, towards the boots and shouts at the great doors. fields.title: Given Away
fields.body_html:
The stair of the Great Beacon was black stone, worn into a dip in every step by three hundred years of Lamplighters’ boots. It went round and round, and it never seemed to go anywhere except further into the dark.

Wren counted. It was Tobin’s habit, not hers, but when you are climbing in the dark and cannot see the top or the bottom, numbers are something to hold on to. Twenty-one. Twenty-two. Twenty-three.

Tobin climbed behind her, breathing hard. Cinder ran ahead and then back, ahead and then back, her spark bobbing like a firefly.

At fifty-eight, the voice found them.

“Such a long way up,” it said, sweetly, out of the stones. “And what will you find at the top? An empty bowl. Nothing, little sweep. There is never anything at the top. Sit down and rest.”

“Don’t,” said Wren, through her teeth, before Tobin could say a word. “Don’t answer it. Just count.”

Fifty-nine. Sixty.

Far below them, iron clanged on stone.

They both stopped. Then, curling up the stairwell, came a breath of air so bitter that Wren’s fingers went numb round the lamp.

“The coal-door,” whispered Tobin. “They’ve found the coal-door.”

Down where the lamplight did not reach, something grey was moving up the stair. Not climbing. Drifting. And another behind it.

“Run,” said Wren.

They ran. Seventy, eighty, ninety. Her legs burned. The cold came after them faster than they could climb. At a hundred and twelve there was a little landing, where a narrow slit of a window let in a smear of grey night, and there Tobin stopped.

“Go on,” he said.

“What? Don’t be daft. Come on—“

“No.” His face was as white as his knuckles. “They’ll catch us both before we’re halfway. Hollows don’t get tired. It’s simple arithmetic. Somebody has to hold the stair, and it can’t be you, because you’ve got the lamp, so it has to be—“ His voice cracked in the middle. “It has to be me.”

“You haven’t even got a light!”

“I’ve got Cinder.” The ember-fox stood beside him, ears flat, spark blazing, growling so low that Wren felt it more than heard it. “And technically speaking, a narrow stair is the best place there is to hold anything. That’s why castles have them—“

“Tobin, you’re scared of the dark.”

“Yes,” said Tobin. “I know. I’m aware.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose, and his hand was shaking so badly that he nearly poked himself in the eye. “I’m going to be scared of it anyway. I’d rather be scared here than scared somewhere else.”

Wren opened her mouth to argue. But the first Hollow came round the curve of the wall, grey and faceless, and Cinder flew at it in a burst of sparks, and it drew back — only a little — and stopped.

And then, from somewhere below the Hollows, came a sound that Wren knew.

Tap. Pause. Tap. Pause. Tap.

It was a brass-hooked pole striking stone, the way it had struck the North Wall every night for thirty years. The grey shapes below shrank against the wall, and up through them came a little swinging lantern on the hook of a lamplighter’s pole. And behind it came Old Ash.

He looked dreadful. His coat was torn half off one shoulder, his beard was singed on both sides now instead of one, and he was limping. But he came up through the Hollows as if they were a draught, and they drew back from his little oil-light the way cats draw back from water. He reached the landing and looked at the two of them over his beard.

“Hm,” said Old Ash. “Good. You didn’t wait for me.”

“Ash! They said you were in a cage—“

“I was. It was a poor sort of cage.” He turned to face down the stair beside Tobin, old man and boy, with Cinder between their feet. Below them the Hollows were gathering again, a thick grey tide, and Ash’s lantern looked very small. “Hm. Up you go, child.”

“But—“

“Up,” said Ash. “You know what to do. The lad and I will hold the stair.”

Tobin’s teeth were chattering. “I don’t think I’m much good at holding stairs,” he said. “I should tell you, sir, I’m frightened of the dark. Quite badly, actually.”

“So was I, at your age,” said Old Ash. “So am I now, as it happens. Stand here anyway.” He glanced sideways at the boy, and something in his face softened. “That’s all courage is, lad. Being frightened, and standing here anyway.”

Tobin swallowed. Then he set his feet, and stood.

Wren looked at them both for one more moment — the tall bent old man with his pole, the gangly boy with his spectacles, the small grey fox with her tail on fire — and she found there was a lump in her throat that she did not know what to do with. So she did the only thing she could. She turned, and she climbed.

A hundred and fifty. A hundred and sixty.

She was alone now, with the lamp, and the dark, and the voice.

“Poor little sweep,” it murmured, so gently. “They’ve left you to do it all by yourself. That is what people do, you know. They always leave you. You learned that a long time ago.”

Two hundred. Two hundred and ten.

Below her, very faint, she heard Cinder snarl, and once Tobin’s voice, high and shaking, shouting “Get back!” She did not stop. If she stopped she would go back down.

Two hundred and ninety-eight. Two hundred and ninety-nine.

Three hundred.

The stair ended at a small iron door. Wren pushed it, and it swung open, and the wind hit her in the face.

She was at the top of the whole city. There were no stars, only a low, heavy sky. Far below, Emberwick lay in the dark like something drowned, and the wall round it was a black ring with not one light on it.

In front of her was the Beacon-bowl.

It was as big as a pond, a vast round dish of black iron on three great legs, its rim at the height of her chest. Inside lay the wick-bed: a matted floor of old wick like a field of dead grass, grey with dust and dry as bone. Round its edges gaped the dark mouths of the copper flame-pipes, going down.

It was the coldest, emptiest thing she had ever seen. It did not look like something that had ever been on fire. It looked like something that had forgotten fire was possible.

And standing beside it, his grey cloak stirring in the wind, was Captain Varrick.

“You’re quick,” he said. He nodded at the top of an iron stair that came spiralling up the outside of the tower. “The Lamplighters built that for carrying oil. I used to know a great many things like that.” He rubbed his right palm with his thumb. “Good evening, Wren Ashby.”

“I’m not going to take it from you,” said Varrick, spreading his empty hands. “I can’t. It must be given. I know that better than you might think. I’m here to make you an offer.”

“Don’t want it,” said Wren.

“You haven’t heard it yet.” He smiled. It was not an unkind smile, and that was the worst of it. “Here is my offer. Keep the lamp. Keep it, and walk away. Go down my stair, and through the Grey Gate, tonight. No Knight will stop you. No Hollow will touch you. You will never be cold again, or hungry, or anyone’s sweep, or in anyone’s debt. You keep everything. You lose nothing.”

The wind blew. The ribbon on Wren’s wrist fluttered red in the lamplight.

“And why not?” said Varrick softly. “Think about it. Why should you give anything to them?” He nodded down at the drowned city. “They called you a witch. Your own master sold you for a handful of silver. The Warden locked you in a cell. What has that city ever given you? Cold, and soot, and debt. You said it yourself, didn’t you? Everything costs. You were right. You have always been right. So why should you be the only one who pays?”

And Wren, standing at the top of the Beacon in the wind, found that she could not think of an answer.

Because he was right. She had known it since she was four years old and alone. Nobody gives you anything. If it doesn’t cost you now, it’ll cost you later. That rule had kept her alive. And here was a grown man in armour telling her she had been right all along — and offering her, at last, a way out.

Then the other voice came, from just behind her ear, so close she could almost feel its breath; and it was not speaking.

It was humming.

Wren went cold all over, colder than any Hollow had ever made her.

It was the tune. Her tune. The one with no words, the one she hummed to herself in the garret when she could not sleep. Morning comes, morning comes — and then, where Wren’s memory always stopped, where there was only a blank and an ache, the humming went on. It went on into the part she had lost. And there were words in it — she could hear that there were words, just on the other side of the humming, the way you can hear that someone is talking in the next room.

It was her mother’s voice. Or it was so like her mother’s voice that Wren could not tell the difference, and did not want to.

“I know the rest of it,” said the sweet voice, very softly. “I know all of it, every word. She sang it to you every night, did you know that? You used to fall asleep before the end. Come with me, little one. Come with me, and I will sing you the rest.”

Wren’s eyes stung. She held the lamp so tightly that the brass bit into her palms.

I will tell you now what she was really afraid of, because it was not Varrick, and it was not even the voice. She was afraid of the bowl.

She looked at that vast cold dish with its field of dead wick, and then at the little flame in her lamp, no bigger than her thumb. And she knew what would happen if she gave it. The bowl would swallow it, like one cup of water poured into the Soot Canal. It would be gone.

And then she would have nothing.

No warmth in the garret at night. No red ribbon. She would be what she had always been: a hungry nobody in a cold city, owing money she could never pay. The lamp was the only thing that had ever been hers.

Everything costs. And this would cost her everything.

Wren shut her eyes.

She saw, all over the dark city below, hundreds of people sitting down in the streets because a sweet voice had told them it was easier.

And she remembered kneeling beside Nettle with the lamp held out, saying here, it’s for you, you don’t have to do anything — and how it had blazed.

It cannot be bought, stolen or earned, said Old Ash, in her memory, in his slow dry voice. Only given.

Wren opened her eyes.

“I don’t want the rest of the song,” she said. Her voice came out small and wobbly, and she hated it, and she kept going anyway. “Not from you. It’s not yours to give me. And I don’t want your road, either.” She swallowed hard. “You’re right. Everything costs. But I reckon — I reckon some things are worth what they cost.”

She turned her back on Varrick. She climbed up onto the iron rim of the Beacon-bowl, knelt there with the wind tugging at her hair, and held the lamp out over the dead grey field of the wick-bed.

Her hands were shaking. She could not make them stop.

And then, quite clearly, she felt a hand on her shoulder.

It was a warm hand. Large, and steady, and kind, and very warm, as if it had been held near a fire for a long time. It did not push her, or pull her. “Here,” she whispered, to the city, to the dark, to all the grey people sitting in the streets. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

And she tipped the lamp, and gave the Flame away.

For one dreadful heartbeat, nothing happened. The little golden flame slid off the lip of the lamp like a drop of honey and fell into the grey wick, and Wren saw it there, tiny, a single spark in a field of dust, and she thought: it’s gone. I knew it. It’s gone.

Then the next. Then the next and the next and the next, running round the city wall in both directions at once, faster than a horse could gallop, faster than Wren could turn her head to follow. Down in the streets, the Hollows screamed.

A high thin shriek rose from every lane and alley. They poured back towards the wall like smoke before a gale, and fled over it into the Greywaste, and were gone.

And the colour came back.

It came running into the city like the tide over sand. The roofs below, which had always been grey, turned a deep warm colour she had no word for, the colour of a fox’s back. Then she looked down at the lamp in her hands.

Old Ash looked at him across the Beacon. The old man’s face, in the gold light, was full of a grief so deep that Wren had to look away from it.

Varrick lowered his arm.

fields.title: Into the Greywaste
fields.body_html:
The sun came up the next morning exactly as pale as it always had.

I would like to tell you otherwise. I would like to tell you that Solenne rose gold and blazing over Emberwick, and that everyone who saw it wept for joy. But it was not so. The Beacon could light the Ring, and the Ring could keep out the dark; but the sun had been cursed three hundred years ago by a bargain on a far-off mountain, and no lamp in a single city could mend that. It crept up over the Greywaste like a coin seen through dirty water, the same as ever.

And yet, for the first time in anyone’s memory, nobody in Emberwick was looking at the sun. They were looking at the wall, where a hundred and forty-four lamps still burned white-gold in the morning, as if they had no intention of ever going out again. And they were looking at their own streets, which had colours in them.

Wren walked down from Beacon Square with the lamp in her hands and Nettle at her elbow, and she did not know where to look first.

“That door’th blue,” said Nettle, pointing. Nettle had been restored a whole night longer than anybody else, and so she considered herself an expert. “Mithter Ath told me. Blue. And that one’th green, and that’th yellow, and your ribbon’th red, and Tobin’th hair ith yellow too, only a different yellow, and—“

“How d’you know all that?”

“I athked,” said Nettle simply.

Wren had never thought of asking. It had never occurred to her that colours were something you could have names for, like people.

They came down into Soot Lane. And there, all along the crooked little street, in the doorways and on the steps and sitting on the cold cobbles where the Hollows had left them, were the greyed.

The light of the Ring had driven the Hollows out. But it had not brought back what they had taken. There were people still sitting quite still in the morning air, grey from their hair to their boots, staring at nothing: old men and young mothers, a boy from the tannery, the woman who sold eels in Crookback Market. Their families stood round them, holding their hands, saying their names, getting no answer.

On the step of the bakery, with flour still on her grey hands, sat Mrs Dolly Fenn. Her five children were huddled round her like chicks. The smallest was patting her cheek.

Wren stopped.

You might think, after all that had happened at the top of the Beacon, that it would be easy now. It was not. It is one thing to give something away once, on a mountain-top, with a great roaring fire and the whole city watching. It is quite another to do it again on an ordinary morning in your own street, with nobody watching but a lot of tired, frightened neighbours, some of whom had shouted “witch-light” at you only days before.

Wren knelt down on the bakery step anyway. She held out the lamp.

“Here,” she said, a bit gruffly. “It’s for you, Mrs Fenn. You don’t have to do anything.”

The flame leaned out of the lamp towards Mrs Fenn, the way a flower leans towards a window. Warmth spread over the step. And the colour came back into Mrs Fenn the way it had come back into Nettle — slowly at first, then all in a rush: the pink in her cheeks, the brown of her hair, the faded red of her apron. She blinked. She looked down at the children round her knees, and her face crumpled up.

“Pip,” she said. “Hettie. Sam. Molly. And — and my little Jem.” She seized them, all five of them at once, in a hug so enormous that flour went everywhere. “Pip, Hettie, Sam, Molly and Jem! I know you! I know every one of you, my lambs—“

Wren stood up quickly and turned away, because her eyes had gone hot and she did not want anyone to see.

When she looked down at the lamp, it was brighter.

She went down Soot Lane door by door, all that morning.

Word spread ahead of her faster than she could walk. By the time she reached the third house, people were coming out to meet her. By the tenth, they were carrying their greyed ones out into the street on chairs and in barrows, and laying them in a row on the cobbles for her, which made her feel like a doctor and also slightly like a fishmonger.

At every one she knelt down and held out the lamp and said, “Here. It’s for you.” And every time, the flame leaned out, and the colour came back, and names came back, and somebody started crying, usually the person who had been doing the holding.

And every time, the lamp burned a little brighter.

Some of the people tried to pay her. A man pushed a copper penny into her hand, and when she gave it back he looked frightened, as if she had refused him on purpose. A woman tried to give her a ring. The eel-seller offered her a whole eel, which Nettle said was the worst present she had ever heard of.

“It’s not for sale,” Wren kept saying. “It’s given. You can’t pay for it. It doesn’t work like that.”

She heard herself saying it, over and over, and every time it sounded a little stranger, and a little less strange. She had spent her whole life saying everything costs. She was not sure when she had stopped believing it. She thought it might have been at the top of the Beacon, with a warm hand on her shoulder. Or it might have been earlier, in the market, with a warm loaf in her hands and an old man saying no charge. Or it might only be happening now, door by door, the way a frozen pond thaws — not all at once, but from the edges in.

Near the bottom of Soot Lane, by the gate of the sweep yard, she stopped.

Sitting against the yard wall, grey as a sack of ashes, with his big red knuckles gone the colour of putty and the reward purse still in his lap, was Gristle Mott. He had gone home through Soot Lane just before the whole Ring went dark, and the Hollows had found him at his own gate.

Nettle took hold of Wren’s sleeve. “Wren,” she whispered. “That’th him. He thold you. For the reward.”

“I know,” said Wren.

She stood and looked at him for a long time. She thought of all the cold nights in the garret with no coal, and the board money that went up every week however hard she worked, and the shouting, and the docked pay. She thought of him in the lantern-light at the bakery door, pointing at her.

Then she thought about the warm hand on her shoulder, and about who it had been given to. Not to the deserving. Not to the ones who had earned it. To her — Wren Ashby, liar and pickpocket, who had thrown it down at a Warden’s feet.

She knelt down in front of Gristle Mott and held out the lamp.

“Here,” she said. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

The colour came back into Mott like wine into a glass. He wheezed, and blinked, and his little eyes focused on Wren, and he looked — for the first time in all the years she had known him — afraid of her. Not because she was dangerous. Because he did not understand what she had just done.

And he got up, and shuffled into his yard, and shut the gate, and Wren did not see him again.

“Well,” said Nettle, after a while. “I’d have let him thtay grey.”

“Yes,” said Wren. “So would I, yesterday.”

At noon, if you could call it noon, Tobin found them in Beacon Square.

He looked as if he had not slept, which he hadn’t, and he had a large leather-bound book under his arm, which he had carried all the way from the Leaning Tower. Sergeant Bracken was there with a dozen guardsmen, looking exhausted and puzzled and rather pleased, and Tobin marched straight up to him and held out the book with both hands.

“The ledger of the Lamp Guild, Sergeant,” he said. “From the vault. It shows that the oil’s been watered for years, and the money’s gone into Guild Master Prowle’s own accounts, and the Flame tokens are just tin. Technically speaking, I stole it. I thought you ought to have it anyway.”

Bracken took the ledger and opened it. He read for a while, his grizzled eyebrows going up and up.

“Well,” he said at last. “That’ll be why Master Prowle left town in such a hurry.” The Guild Master’s wagon, it turned out, had gone out through the South Gate in the night, strongboxes and all, and not stopped. Nobody knew where he had gone. I am afraid that we have not seen the last of Cuthbert Prowle; men like him have a way of turning up again, smelling of lavender. But that is another story.

“I arrested you,” he said. “I’m sorry for it.”

Wren did not know what to say to that. No grown-up had ever said sorry to her before. So she said, “You weren’t rough,” which was true.

Sergeant Bracken held out his big hand. After a moment, Wren took it, and he shook it firmly, the way you shake hands with someone you respect.

Tobin went up the Hill alone that afternoon. He was gone an hour. When he came back to the Leaning Tower he was very quiet, and he sat down on the step and polished his spectacles for a long time, though they were perfectly clean.

“He was in his study,” he said at last, when Wren sat down beside him. “He’d heard. Everyone’s heard. I told him it was over and the Ring was lit and Varrick had gone.” He held his spectacles up to the light. “He didn’t say anything. He just stood at the window. I waited and waited, and he never turned round. He couldn’t look at me.”

“Maybe he couldn’t look at himself,” said Wren.

Tobin thought about that. “Maybe,” he said. He put his spectacles back on. “That’s worse, though, isn’t it? In a way.”

Wren didn’t answer. She just sat beside him on the step until the light went.

That evening, in the Leaning Tower, Old Ash made tea.

It was, if possible, worse than ever. It tasted, Tobin said afterwards, like a garden shed that had been left out in the rain. Cinder took one sniff at Wren’s cup, sneezed sparks all over the stuffed owl, and went to steal a biscuit off the shelf instead.

Old Ash sat in his big chair by the round window with his bandaged leg up on a stool. Out beyond the wall, the Greywaste stretched away into the dusk, flat and colourless and endless. And beyond the Greywaste, so far off that it might have been only a cloud, there was something on the edge of the sky that Wren had never noticed before: a faint, pale point, like the tip of a tooth.

“She’ll come back,” said Ash.

He did not say who. He did not need to.

And next time she’ll know what she’s looking for.”

Ash nodded at the round window, at the pale point on the edge of the sky. “The Bright Mountain,” he said. “Where the Flame began. Where he came from. If there is an answer anywhere in Gloamhaven, it’s there.” He was quiet for a moment. “I mean to go. I should have gone years ago. I was waiting.” He looked at the lamp burning on the table among the teacups. “Hm. I think I was waiting for that.”

“We’re coming,” said Wren at once.

Ash raised one shaggy eyebrow. “It’s a long road, child. Across the Greywaste, and beyond. I can’t promise there’ll be bread at the end of it. I can’t promise there’ll be an end of it at all.”

“Somebody’s got to come,” said Wren, “or you’ll poison yourself with that tea before you’re past the Grey Gate.” She lifted her chin. “Anyway, it’s my lamp. It was given to me. I’m not letting it go off without me.”

Ash looked at Tobin.

Tobin had gone pale. He was thinking — Wren could see it — of the dark, and of the long nights out on the Greywaste with no Ring round them at all, and of his father standing at the window and not turning round. He pushed his spectacles up his nose.

Father, I have gone with the Lamplighter to the Bright Mountain. I am not running away. I am going to find out how to make the light last. I know you were frightened. I was too. I love you. Tobin.

He folded it and sealed it, and Sergeant Bracken promised to take it up the Hill in the morning.

Then, just as they were going to bed, Old Ash held out one long hand to Tobin.

“Your compass, lad,” he said. “Lend it me. Just for tonight.”

Tobin hesitated. Then he took the little brass compass from his pocket, the one with his mother’s words inside the lid, and put it in the old man’s palm. Ash closed his fingers round it and said “Hm,” and went up the crooked stair to the top of the tower, and they heard his footsteps moving about up there long after the candles were out.

She lay for a moment listening to Cinder snoring and Tobin muttering in his sleep about gear-ratios. Then she got up and went down to the door of the tower. Someone was sitting on the step outside.

It was Nettle, wrapped in a shawl of Mrs Fenn’s that was six sizes too big for her. She had walked all the way up to the North Wall in the dark to be there in time. She was not going to the Bright Mountain. “For the road,” said Nettle, and held out her hand.

In it was a heel of bread. A heel of yesterday’s loaf, a bit squashed, a bit warm from being held.

Wren looked at it.

A month ago — a week ago — she would have looked for the catch. It did not come.

The Greywaste lay beyond it, wide and flat and silent, the colour of old porridge, all grey grass and dead trees and a road that went away into the mist. Behind them the Ring burned gold along the wall. Ahead there was nothing at all but grey.

Far behind them, on the long grey road from Emberwick, so far off that it was hardly more than a smudge against the mist, a single rider in grey was following.

Wren saw it. She looked down at the lamp, burning warm and steady in her hands. Then she turned her face towards the Bright Mountain, and kept walking, and kept humming; and the little flame she carried, which had been given away and was not one bit the less for it, lit the grey road in front of them, step by step, all the way to the edge of the world.

She looked down at the lamp, burning warm and steady in her hands. Then she turned her face towards the Bright Mountain, and kept walking, and kept humming; and the little flame she carried, which had been given away and was not one bit the less for it, lit the grey road in front of them, step by step, all the way to the edge of the world.
